docs.title: Dashboard and administration
docs.text: Start a development node with the quick start. For production, follow the release requirements and Docker deployment guide.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
Release binaries and the container include a React dashboard at /ui/ on the HTTP listener. With the quick-start node, open http://127.0.0.1:8080/ui/.

The dashboard shows topology, partition health, replication lag, consumer groups, schemas, and operations. Its retention and compaction actions use the same admin service as the CLI. Tenant usage currently shows zeros because tenant limits are not configured; the rebalance action reports that placement is driven by membership rather than initiating a rebalance itself.

When authentication is enabled, sign in with a JWT whose subject has "admin": true in the server's policy file (see permissions). cronos-admin generate-token can sign a token for testing; see test tokens.

Source builds need make build to compile and embed the dashboard. See the dashboard architecture for routes, authentication, and implementation details.

docs.title: Administration tool
docs.text:
cronos-admin is included in each release and at /app/cronos-admin in the container. The examples below assume it is on PATH. To build it from source:

go build -o bin/cronos-admin ./cmd/admin

Use bin/cronos-admin.exe as the output on Windows. For the quick-start container, an equivalent invocation is:

docker exec cronos-dev /app/cronos-admin --server=localhost:9000 admin topology

Each command asks one node and reports that node's view. The command reference lists every command and flag.

docs.title: Connecting to a node
docs.text:
--server (default localhost:9000) names the node and port. The admin, partition, consumer and debug commands use the public client port (--grpc-addr, default :9000). cluster voters and cluster remove-node use the internal cluster port (--cluster-grpc-addr, default :7947). Match the connection flags to how the server was started:

Server setting What cronos-admin needs --tls-enabled (public port) --tls, and --tls-ca unless the server certificate chains to a CA the system trusts. The certificate must cover the host given in --server. --tls-client-auth (public port) Also --tls-cert and --tls-key: a client certificate signed by the CA in the server's --tls-ca-file. --auth-enabled (public port) --jwt-token on every command that uses the public port. See permissions. --replication-tls-enabled (cluster port) --tls, --tls-ca, --tls-cert and --tls-key with the cluster's certificates: the CA in --replication-tls-ca-file and a certificate it signed. The cluster port does not check --jwt-token.

Production mode requires --tls-enabled, --auth-enabled and --replication-tls-enabled; --tls-client-auth is optional. Without --tls the CLI connects in plain text and sends any --jwt-token unencrypted.

cronos-admin --server=node1.example.com:9000 --tls --tls-ca=ca.crt \
  --jwt-token="$TOKEN" admin topology

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
With --auth-enabled, every RPC on the public port needs a token signed with the server's --auth-jwt-secret or matching --auth-jwt-public-key. A missing, expired or badly signed token is refused with Unauthenticated. The server's --auth-policy-file then decides what the token's subject (its sub claim) may do. The file is a JSON object keyed by subject:

{
  "ops": {"admin": true},
  "orders-app": {"topics": {"orders": {"publish": true, "subscribe": true}}}
}
  • "admin": true allows every admin command, cluster status, the dashboard, all consumer-group RPCs, and the compact, retention and split RPCs of the partition service. It does not allow publishing to or subscribing from any topic.
  • topics allows publish and subscribe on each named topic; names must match exactly. A per-topic "admin" key is accepted, but no RPC checks it.
  • The read-only partition list, partition info and partition wal commands need only a valid token. consumer list and consumer lag require global admin permission because they expose group progress.

A refused permission is reported as PermissionDenied with the subject's name. With auth disabled (the default) no command needs a token. --dev does not disable auth.

docs.title: Public admin commands
docs.text:
These commands connect to the public client gRPC listener:

cronos-admin --server=localhost:9000 admin topology
cronos-admin --server=localhost:9000 admin partition-health 0
cronos-admin --server=localhost:9000 admin replication-lag
cronos-admin --server=localhost:9000 admin consumer-groups list
cronos-admin --server=localhost:9000 admin consumer-group-lag my-group 0
cronos-admin --server=localhost:9000 admin schema-list
cronos-admin --server=localhost:9000 admin tenant-usage
cronos-admin --server=localhost:9000 admin retention-run --max-age-hours=168
cronos-admin --server=localhost:9000 admin compaction-run

Partition 0 is a valid target for health and consumer-group lag. For retention, compaction and replication lag, 0 means every applicable partition on this node, including partition 0.

docs.title: Cluster membership
docs.text:
cluster voters and cluster remove-node connect to the internal cluster gRPC listener, whose production connections require the cluster's client certificate:

cronos-admin --server=node1:7947 \
  --tls --tls-ca=ca.crt --tls-cert=tls.crt --tls-key=tls.key cluster voters

cluster voters shows whether the node asked coordinates the cluster, its Raft term, and the Raft addresses of the nodes that count towards a majority. Use the same connection options with cluster remove-node <node-id> for a node that is permanently lost. A node that is still running is refused, and a node cannot remove itself: ask another one. See node replacement and removal before changing a production cluster's membership. A standalone node has no Raft service and answers these commands with Unimplemented.

docs.title: Offline recovery tools
docs.text:
Run these against the data directory of a stopped node:

cronos-admin restore --from=/backups/<backup> --data-dir=/data
cronos-admin check-log --data-dir=/data
cronos-admin check-log --data-dir=/data --partition=3 --repair

Restore checks every file against the backup's manifest and refuses a data directory that already holds any of the backup's partitions. check-log reports damage; --repair cuts out damaged log content and reports what was lost. Preserve backups before repair. Neither tool contacts a server or checks that the node is stopped, so stop it first. See the maintenance validation record and backup and restore requirements.

docs.title: Test tokens
docs.text:
generate-token signs a token on the machine it runs on. It is meant for testing:

TOKEN=$(cronos-admin generate-token --secret="$(cat jwt-secret)" --subject=ops --ttl=1h)
cronos-admin --server=localhost:9000 --jwt-token="$TOKEN" admin topology

The token is signed with HS256 using --secret, which must equal the server's --auth-jwt-secret. It holds only the subject (sub and sub_id), the time it was issued and its expiry, --ttl later; permissions come from the policy file. A server that verifies only with --auth-jwt-public-key refuses it. Anyone who has the secret can sign a token for any subject, including an admin, and a secret given on the command line can be kept in shell history and seen in process listings. Issue production tokens from the system that manages your JWTs.

docs.title: Global flags
docs.text:
Every command accepts these flags; they only matter for commands that connect to a node.

Flag Default Meaning -s, --server localhost:9000 host:port of the node to ask --tls off Connect with TLS instead of plain text --tls-ca system CAs PEM file of the CA that signed the server's certificate --tls-cert, --tls-key none Client certificate and key for mutual TLS. Give both: one alone is ignored --tls-skip-verify off Do not verify the server's certificate (development only) --jwt-token none Token sent as authorization: Bearer <token> with every RPC

--tls-ca, --tls-cert, --tls-key and --tls-skip-verify take effect only with --tls. --help shows the value of --jwt-token as authorization: Bearer <token>; pass the token alone.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
"Port" is the listener the command uses. "Needs with auth" is what the command needs when the server runs with --auth-enabled: admin means "admin": true in the policy file, and "cluster certificate" means a client certificate signed by the cluster's CA when the server runs with --replication-tls-enabled.

Command What it does, and when to use it Port Needs with auth admin topology Nodes, and each partition's leader, replicas, in-sync replicas and high watermark. Check placement and replica health public admin admin partition-health <id> A partition's high watermark, segments, timers, ready events, cold-store entries and replay error on this node. Check one partition public admin admin replication-lag [<id>] Leader high watermark and each follower's offset, lag and in-sync state. Check that followers keep up public admin admin consumer-groups list Consumer groups on every partition of this node, with member count public admin admin consumer-group-lag <group> <id> A group's committed offset, the partition's high watermark, and the lag between them. Check that consumers keep up public admin admin schema-list Topics with a schema, their latest version and compatibility mode public admin admin schema-get <topic> <version> One schema version; 0 is the latest public admin admin tenant-usage [<tenant>] In-flight and storage usage of one tenant, or of all public admin admin retention-run Applies age or size retention once. Free disk now, or apply a limit once, without changing --retention-max-age-hours or --retention-max-size-gb public admin admin compaction-run [--partition-id <id>] Removes finished log segments without waiting for --compaction-interval; 0 or omitted means every partition on this node public admin admin cluster-rebalance Changes nothing: reports that on-demand rebalance is not available, since placement follows membership public admin partition list Partitions with their topic and leader public valid token partition info <id> A partition's leader, replicas, high watermark, last offset, segment count and disk usage, as JSON public valid token partition wal <id> Last offset, segment file count and total size of this node's log for a partition public valid token consumer list Consumer groups with their topic and partitions public admin consumer lag <group> A group's topic, partitions and committed offset per partition public admin debug publish <topic> <payload> Publishes one test event, due 5 seconds later, and prints its partition and offset. Check that a node accepts writes public publish on the topic cluster voters Whether the node asked coordinates the cluster, its Raft term, and the Raft addresses of the voters cluster cluster certificate cluster remove-node <node-id> Removes a stopped node that is gone for good from Raft and from every node's member list cluster cluster certificate cluster status Calls AdminService.GetClusterTopology, as admin topology does public admin generate-token Signs a test token; see test tokens none none restore Restores a backup into a data directory files node stopped check-log Checks the partition logs for damage; --repair cuts it out files node stopped completion <shell> Prints a completion script for bash, zsh, fish or powershell none none

A command waits 5 seconds for an answer; admin retention-run and admin compaction-run wait 60, cluster voters 10 and cluster remove-node 30.

docs.title: Arguments and results
docs.text:
Command Details admin topology A partition whose leader does not answer within 2 seconds shows isr=unknown. A standalone node lists itself and no partitions admin partition-health <id> Only partitions on this node; ID 0 is valid. disk always prints 0; partition info shows disk usage admin replication-lag [<id>] Omitted or 0: every partition this node leads, with the follower lines merged and hwm summed. Only replicated partitions led here list followers; others print hwm=0 admin consumer-group-lag <group> <id> ID 0 is valid. -1 means the partition is not on this node or the group has not committed there admin schema-list, admin schema-get Schemas the node loaded from <data-dir>/schemas when it started. No RPC registers a schema, so the list is normally empty admin tenant-usage [<tenant>] Omitted: the sum over all tenants. Tenant limits cannot be set in this release, so it reports limits_configured=false and zero usage partition list In a cluster, every partition in the cluster's metadata; standalone, the node's partitions. watermark always prints 0; partition info shows the high watermark partition info <id> Fields that are zero are left out of the JSON. In a cluster, a partition this node does not hold shows only its topic, leader and replicas partition wal <id> Only partitions on this node consumer list, consumer lag Read the groups of partition 0 only; see limitations. consumer lag prints committed offsets, not lag; -1 means nothing committed debug publish <topic> <payload> Sends the payload as bytes with message ID admin-<nanoseconds>; the server picks the partition. "admin": true alone does not allow it

admin retention-run flags:

Flag Default Meaning --partition-id 0 Partition to clean; 0 means every partition on this node --max-age-hours 0 Remove segments older than this; 0 sets no age limit --max-size-bytes 0 Remove the oldest segments until the log fits; 0 sets no size limit. For every partition, this is a budget for the node's total log size

With both limits at 0 it removes nothing. It never removes a partition's active segment, applies the same completion checks as background retention, and on a replicated partition only the leader removes segments.

admin compaction-run flags:

Flag Default Meaning --partition-id 0 Partition to compact; 0 means every partition on this node

It prints segments_removed=N with the number of removed segments. The RPC's bytes_reclaimed remains 0; compare partition wal <id> before and after for disk usage. On replicated partitions, cleanup requires leadership; a request over every local partition can fail on a follower. Use an explicit partition and ask its leader when ownership is spread across nodes.

generate-token flags:

Flag Default Meaning --secret none (required) HMAC key; must equal the server's --auth-jwt-secret --subject admin Subject of the token; it gets the permissions of that key in the policy file --ttl 24h How long the token is valid, as a duration such as 30m or 1h

restore flags:

Flag Default Meaning --from required One backup generation: the backup-* directory that holds backup.json, under --backup-dir (default backups in the data directory) --data-dir required Data directory of the stopped node --encryption-key-file none Master key of an encrypted backup; checked against the backup before anything is copied

check-log flags:

Flag Default Meaning --data-dir required Data directory of the stopped node --partition -1 (all) Check only this partition. Required with --repair --encryption-key-file none Master key, when the logs are encrypted --repair off Cut each damaged segment after its last valid record; the events it reports as unreadable are given up

check-log exits with an error while damaged segments remain.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• admin retention-run, admin compaction-run and admin replication-lag use 0 for every applicable partition. They cannot target only partition 0. Use PartitionService.Compact or PartitionService.RunRetention below when cleanup must be scoped to partition 0 alone.
  • consumer list and consumer lag read only partition 0's consumer groups. A group that subscribes only to other partitions is missing there, and consumer lag reports consumer group not found. Use admin consumer-groups list and admin consumer-group-lag, which read every partition on the node.

docs.title: Server RPCs without a command
docs.text:
The public port also serves these RPCs, which cronos-admin does not call. Use any gRPC client; the port serves gRPC reflection. The contracts are in events.proto and admin.proto.

RPC Use Needs with auth PartitionService.GetSchedulerStatus Timers, ready events and timing-wheel settings of a partition valid token PartitionService.Compact Compaction of any partition, including 0, optionally only before before_ts; reports what it removed admin PartitionService.RunRetention Retention of one partition, including 0, also below min_offset admin ConsumerGroupService.CreateConsumerGroup, RebalanceConsumerGroup Create a group; reassign a group's partitions to its members admin EventService.GetEventState, CancelEvent, RescheduleEvent Inspect, cancel or move one scheduled event; use the Go SDK lifecycle methods or see the lifecycle contract publish on the topic EventService.Replay Read a topic's events from an offset or a time subscribe on the topic

docs.title: Go client guide
docs.text:
The SDK provides publishing, consumer groups, replay, cancellation and rescheduling, metadata-based leader routing, pooled connections, and reconnect handling.

Start a development node with the README quick start. Server binaries are also available on the releases page. For source builds, see Contributing.

docs.title: Install and connect
docs.text:
Use Go 1.26.10 or later:

go get github.com/jatin711-debug/cronos_db_golang@v0.10.0

Import github.com/jatin711-debug/cronos_db_golang/pkg/client. The README publisher example is a complete program that dials a local node and schedules a JSON event ten seconds in the future.

client.DefaultConfig accepts one or more bootstrap addresses. The client uses partition metadata to find leaders. Updated servers advertise client addresses through --advertise-grpc-addr; explicit NodeIDToAddress mappings take precedence. Advertised addresses must be reachable from the client.

The examples use plaintext development connections. For production, configure Config.Security: TLS verification, CA/server name, optional client certificates, and bearer credentials. The subject must have permissions in the server's authorization policy. See the production configuration and the SDK API reference.

docs.title: Consume with automatic acknowledgements
docs.text:
Run this program against the development node to consume the orders topic. It accepts both single-event and batched deliveries:

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "log"
    "os"
    "os/signal"

    client "github.com/jatin711-debug/cronos_db_golang/pkg/client"
    "github.com/jatin711-debug/cronos_db_golang/pkg/types"
)

func main() {
    ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt)
    defer stop()

    c, err := client.Dial(ctx, client.DefaultConfig("127.0.0.1:9000"))
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer c.Close()

    cfg := client.DefaultConsumerConfig("orders", "order-processors")
    err = c.Subscribe(ctx, cfg, func(_ context.Context, d client.Delivery) error {
        events := d.Batch
        if d.Event != nil {
            events = append([]*types.Event{d.Event}, events...)
        }
        for _, event := range events {
            var payload map[string]any
            if err := json.Unmarshal(event.GetPayload(), &payload); err != nil {
                return err
            }
            log.Printf("message_id=%s payload=%v", event.GetMessageId(), payload)
        }
        return nil
    })
    if err != nil && ctx.Err() == nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
}

The default PartitionID=-1 opens a stream for every partition, covering the topic regardless of producer partition keys. Handlers can run concurrently across partitions.

Automatic acknowledgement is the default: a successful handler return queues an acknowledgement; a handler error marks processing as failed. Acknowledgements are batched asynchronously by default. Delivery is at least once, so handlers should tolerate duplicates and partial processing of a batch.

For manual control, use AckModeManual and Delivery.AckSuccess or Delivery.AckFailure to queue acknowledgements explicitly. With CommitStrategySync these calls return the server's answer: nil once it has recorded the acknowledgement, an error when it refused it, the stream ended first or the context expired. With the default asynchronous strategy they return once the acknowledgement is queued. See the SDK reference for checkpoint stores, retries, and flow-control options.

docs.title: Run the end-to-end demo
docs.text:
With the development node running, run from a repository checkout:

go run ./examples/pubsub_demo

The demo subscribes, publishes a JSON event scheduled ten seconds ahead, and prints its delivery metadata and payload. Use -addr=host:port to select a different node. make demo runs the same example.

Source: examples/pubsub_demo/main.go.

docs.title: Cancel or reschedule an event
docs.text:
A node started with --event-lifecycle lets you cancel an event or move it to a new time, as long as it is not yet due. See the lifecycle contract for the server setup and its limits. With authentication enabled, the caller needs publish permission on the event's topic.

The server finds an event by its reference: topic, partition, offset, term and message ID, not by message ID alone. Keep the reference from the publish result with your own record of the event:

sent, err := producer.Send(ctx, client.Message{
    Topic:      "orders",
    MessageID:  "order-1002-reminder",
    Value:      map[string]string{"order_id": "ord-1002"},
    ScheduleAt: time.Now().Add(24 * time.Hour),
})
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
ref := sent.Reference() // store it, for example as JSON next to the order

Every change names the revision it replaces, so that two writers cannot silently overwrite each other's changes, and a request ID, so that it can be retried safely:

state, err := c.GetEventState(ctx, ref)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
state, err = c.RescheduleEvent(ctx, ref, client.EventChange{
    RequestID:        "order-1002-move-1",
    ExpectedRevision: state.Revision,
}, time.Now().Add(48*time.Hour))
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
_, err = c.CancelEvent(ctx, ref, client.EventChange{
    RequestID:        "order-1002-cancel",
    ExpectedRevision: state.Revision,
})

For an event never changed, ref.InitialRevision() is its revision and GetEventState can be skipped. The calls go to the partition's leader and retry by themselves while the outcome is unknown. When they give up, the error's Kind says what to do:

Kind Meaning What to do ErrorKindUnavailable The outcome is unknown: the leader may have changed, or the change has not reached enough replicas yet Retry with the same EventChange and time. The server applies it at most once ErrorKindTimeout The deadline expired or the context was canceled; a mutation may already have applied Use a fresh context and retry with the same EventChange and time ErrorKindConflict The event changed after ExpectedRevision Read the state again and decide whether your change still applies ErrorKindPrecondition The event is canceled or already due, or the server runs without --event-lifecycle Do not retry ErrorKindNotFound The reference does not match an event the server still keeps Do not retry. The event was removed by retention, or the reference is wrong ErrorKindValidation A missing request ID, a past time or an incomplete reference Fix the request

Use a new request ID for every new change, and the same one only to retry it. Keep the requested time too: recomputing time.Now().Add(...) changes the request. A retry can resolve even after that time has passed, while the server still retains the request's result. A later change can supersede that result; read the current state if the retry reports a revision conflict. SendBatch results carry complete references only when ProducerConfig.ReturnReferences is set.

docs.title: SDK settings
docs.text: Start from client.DefaultConfig, client.DefaultProducerConfig and client.DefaultConsumerConfig and change only what you need. Many zero values fall back to defaults, but booleans and values such as partition 0 and offset 0 have their own meaning; use the constructors first. The SDK API reference documents every field.

docs.title: Connection (client.Config)
docs.text: Field Default What it is for BootstrapAddresses required One or more nodes' gRPC addresses. The client learns the rest of the cluster from them NodeIDToAddress empty Maps node IDs to addresses when nodes do not advertise one (--advertise-grpc-addr) PartitionCount 0 Partition count to hash keys with while metadata is not yet loaded. 0 waits for the server's count ConnectionsPerNode 2 gRPC connections kept per node. Raise it for very high request rates DialTimeout 5s How long connecting to a node may take RequestTimeout 10s Deadline of a call whose context has none ResolveDNS true (DefaultConfig) Resolve bootstrap host names KeepaliveTime, KeepaliveTimeout 10s, 5s How fast a node that stops answering is noticed: after about the sum. The server refuses pings more often than every 5 seconds MaxRecvMsgSize, MaxSendMsgSize 16 MiB Largest message the client receives or sends. Must cover your largest event ReadBufferSize, WriteBufferSize 4 MiB gRPC transport buffers Metadata.TTL, Metadata.RefreshInterval 15s, 5s How long partition and leader information is trusted, and how often it is refreshed. The interval must not exceed the TTL Security plaintext Insecure: false plus CACertFile/ServerName for TLS; ClientCertFile and ClientKeyFile for mutual TLS; BearerToken or PerRPCCredentials when the server runs with --auth-enabled. InsecureSkipVerify is for development only Hooks none Callbacks for metrics: metadata refreshes, every request, and errors with their ErrorKind CircuitBreaker 5 failures, 10s, 2 recovery successes Shared by producers of this client, per node. Pauses publishes after consecutive failures; probes after the timeout and closes after SuccessThreshold successes. FailureThreshold: 0 disables it. It does not gate lifecycle or consumer calls

docs.title: Publishing (client.ProducerConfig)
docs.text: Field Default What it is for AutoMessageID true Generate a message ID when a message has none. Set your own IDs when a retry after a crash must not publish twice: the server does not store a message ID again on the same topic within --dedup-ttl. The same ID on two topics names two events DefaultAllowDuplicate false Publish even if the message ID was already stored. For tests Codec JSON Encodes Message.Value when Payload is empty MaxPayloadBytes MaxSendMsgSize Refuse larger payloads before sending them RetryPolicy 4 attempts, 50ms to 2s backoff Retries after transient failures and leader changes MaxInFlight 1024 Concurrent publishes; further calls wait AsyncQueueSize, AsyncWorkers 4096, 2 Queue and workers behind SendAsync BlockOnQueueFull true SendAsync waits when the queue is full; false returns an error instead MaxQueuedBytes 256 MiB Payload bytes the async queue may hold CircuitBreaker reserved Currently unused; configure client.Config.CircuitBreaker instead Hedging disabled Also send a slow publish to the next node after Delay, to cut tail latency at the cost of extra requests ReturnReferences false Make SendBatch results carry complete event references, for cancel and reschedule Partitioner server hash How a partition key picks a partition. Keep the default unless you also route by partition ID

docs.title: Consuming (client.ConsumerConfig)
docs.text: Field Default What it is for Topic, ConsumerGroup required What to consume, and the group whose progress (acknowledged offsets) the server tracks PartitionID -1 -1 consumes every partition; a number consumes only that one StartOffset -1 Where redelivery of retained, unacknowledged events starts. -1 continues from the group's progress; a higher offset skips events before it MaxBufferSize 1024 How many deliveries may be unacknowledged at once (at most 50000). Higher means more throughput and more events redelivered after a crash WorkerConcurrency 1 Handler goroutines per partition stream AckMode, AutoAck auto, true AckModeAuto acknowledges when the handler returns; AckModeManual needs Delivery.AckSuccess or AckFailure. AutoAck is the older compatibility field; prefer an explicit AckMode CommitStrategy async Async batches acknowledgements (AckBatchSize 64, every AckFlushInterval 50ms); sync sends each one at once and returns the server's answer from Ack AckQueueSize 4096 Acknowledgements waiting to be sent CheckpointStore, ResumeCheckpoint none, true Optional local store of progress, used as StartOffset for a single pinned partition. It holds the group's completion floor as the server reports it: every offset below it is complete. Events are delivered in schedule order, not offset order, so the offset of the last acknowledged delivery is not saved MaxPayloadBytes MaxRecvMsgSize Larger deliveries skip the handler and, in auto mode, count as failed PreferredCodec JSON Codec for Delivery.Decode NodeAddress empty Try this node first ReconnectBackoff, MaxReconnectBackoff, ReconnectJitter 1s, 15s, 0.2 Delay between reconnect attempts MaxReconnectAttempts 0 Give up after this many failed reconnects in a row; 0 never gives up HeartbeatInterval and On* callbacks 3s Notifications on connect, assignment, reconnect and disconnect

docs.title: Replay and routing
docs.text:
• Client.Replay, ReplayByOffsetRange, and ReplayByTimeRange read retained events. ReplayToLive combines historical replay with live consumption.
  • Client.DetectCapabilities and RequireCapabilities check server support.
  • Client.RouteForPartition exposes routing for diagnostics.

Replay availability depends on retention and the supported read path; it is not an archive of events already removed from the log. See the replay architecture.

docs.title: Inspect the gRPC API
docs.text:
The wire contracts are in events.proto and admin.proto; the API architecture distinguishes public and internal listeners.

For a development node, a Bash shell with grpcurl can publish an event:

grpcurl -plaintext \
  -d '{"event":{"messageId":"example-1","topic":"orders","scheduleTs":'"$(($(date -u +%s) * 1000))"',"payload":"eyJvcmRlcl9pZCI6Im9yZC0xMDAyIn0="}}' \
  localhost:9000 cronos_db.EventService.Publish

Use a fresh message ID for each new event. Use the SDK consumer above when you need acknowledgements and reconnect handling.

docs.title: Three-node publish validation — 2026-09-29
docs.text:
This is a historical measurement record. It does not measure v0.8.0, current-term format activation or lifecycle operations. For the released scope and remaining capacity limits, see release requirements; no v0.8.0 throughput claim is made.

These measurements use three local Windows/amd64 processes on one AMD Ryzen 7 6800H host, Go 1.26.7, 256-byte payloads, periodic fsync, and the gRPC batch load test. All reported runs had a nonzero share of partition leaders on each node, 100% PublishedCount, and zero reported publish errors. The load-test counter measures accepted publish responses, not consumer delivery or survival of a power loss. The three nodes share one CPU, memory pool, and SSD.

scripts/compare-cluster-throughput.ps1 starts each node after the previous one is healthy, checks the leader distribution in the load-test output, and saves per-node logs and metrics under ignored build/perf-comparison/. Build the server and cluster_loadtest.go with -tags clustertest before using it. The harness keeps WAL data unless -RemoveData is passed; allocate enough disk or clear only its temporary node directories after saving the evidence you need. It does not start with less than -MinFreeMB of available memory and stops the load if that falls below -AbortFreeMB. -Pprof saves CPU, block, and mutex profiles for each node.

docs.title: RF=1 raw publish ceiling
docs.text:
The matched comparison uses 32 partitions, 128 MiB WAL segments, 32 publishers per node, 50,000 events per publisher (4.8 million total), batches of 4,000, and AllowDuplicate=true. This bypasses deduplication and uses one replica. Both versions used the same load-test binary and fresh data in each sample.

Build Run 1 Run 2 Run 3 Median v0.5.0, CGO disabled 717,695 732,563 743,281 732,563 events/s Current branch after quorum guard, CGO disabled 621,230 597,596 612,095 612,095 events/s

The current median is 16.4% lower. A separate matched native Rust/CGO pair measured 625,338 events/s on v0.5.0 and 453,924 on the current branch (27.4% lower); it is one pair, so it is less precise. All eight runs above reported zero publish errors. The code changes after v0.6.0-rc.1 affect the epoch and replication guard; RF=1 continues to use the unlocked WAL append path.

An earlier short 1.92-million-event pair with 512 MiB segments measured 601,735 events/s on v0.5.0 and 727,042 on v0.6.0-rc.1. Its opposite result shows that short local tests vary. It is not evidence for a sustained 1M+ ceiling. The 19.2-million-event Makefile preset could not complete on this machine: three nodes reserved 48 GiB of WAL segments during the attempt.

docs.title: RF=3 quorum path
docs.text:
The current branch was tested with replication-factor=3, min-insync-replicas=2, AllowDuplicate=false, 16 partitions, 128 MiB segments, and 256-byte payloads. Followers were registered, the three leaders shared partitions, and captured cronos_replication_lag gauges were zero at the end of successful runs.

Publishers per node Batch Accepted events Go fallback Native Rust/CGO 4 1,000 240,000 62,348 events/s — 16 4,000 960,000 130,128 events/s 110,773 events/s 32 4,000 1,920,000 125,390 events/s —

Every listed run reported zero publish errors. These are publish acceptance rates, not a fault campaign or independent per-ID follower reconciliation. Periodic fsync does not imply each acknowledged write is safe against a simultaneous power loss. Quorum loss, failover, and restart correctness remain production release blockers in the audit.

docs.title: Correctness finding
docs.text:
The v0.6.0-rc.1 source could acknowledge RF=3/minISR=2 batches while no replication leader was installed. New router assignments used epoch zero, promotion rejected nonpositive epochs, and the publish handler then fell through to the single-replica WAL path. The current branch starts new epochs at one and rejects replicated publishes if the local replication leader is absent. Unit tests cover the missing-leader rejection and RF=1 fast path. The safety fix is not in the v0.6.0-rc.1 tag.

The historical 1,010,933 events/s entry in ARCHITECTURE.md had no preserved run artifacts or independent durability check. The README's older ~790K RF=1 and ~200K RF=3 figures used different conditions and should not be treated as current capacity. The matched results above show an RF=1 regression requiring investigation before a production throughput target is set.

docs.title: Follow-up — 2026-10-06
docs.text:
Cause of the RF=1 regression. The post-v0.5.0 epoch fencing persists the partition epoch with an fsynced file write. PromoteToLeader did that on every 5-second leadership reconcile, for every locally led partition, while holding the partition manager's write lock. Every publish takes that lock for reading, so each tick stalled all publishes on the node for the duration of about ten fsyncs. The write is now skipped when the epoch is unchanged.

Two older stalls on the same path, present in v0.5.0 as well, were removed at the same time: the periodic WAL flush did its disk I/O while holding the WAL append lock, and each flush re-walked the whole mapped segment instead of the bytes written since the previous flush.

Measurement. The host had 2–6 GiB of free memory and other workloads during this session, so runs were kept to 1.2–1.8 million events (4 publishers per node with 100,000 events each unless noted, 32 partitions, 64 MiB segments, batch 4,000, dedup bypassed) and run with the harness's memory guard and -RemoveData. Block profiles (--pprof-addr) give the direct evidence: goroutine time publish handlers spent blocked on the partition-manager lock, summed over the three nodes.

Build Batch A (1.2M events) Batch B (1.2M) Batch C (1.8M) Branch head before the fixes 599,018 / 585,141 / 602,217 476,561 / 466,365 658,743 / 666,085 / 717,273 With the fixes 736,857 / 723,716 631,854 / 659,751 823,516 / 821,356 / 646,450

Values are accepted events per second. Each batch interleaved the two builds; the batches ran under different background load, so compare within a batch. "With the fixes" is the working tree at the time of the batch; the three publish-path fixes above were in place before batch A. Batch C used 12 publishers per node with 50,000 events each. In batch A the profiled time blocked on the manager lock was 2.7 s, 3.0 s, and 3.1 s per run before the fixes and 0.03 s and 0.04 s with them.

These are short runs and are not comparable with the 4.8-million-event medians above; the matched comparison has not been repeated at that size. Run-to-run variance on this host is large: one further 1.2M run of each build was several times slower because file syncs on the shared SSD took far longer than usual (151,058 events/s before the fixes, 271,279 with them), and one batch C run with the fixes was slower than two of the runs without them.

RF=3 with min-insync-replicas=2 and dedup enabled could only be run at 240,000 events (4 partitions, 32 MiB segments); four attempts at 480,000 events were stopped by the memory guard on both builds. Before the fixes: 138,090, 131,594, and 145,413 events/s. With them: 164,630 and 187,973. Every run reported zero publish errors, and all cronos_replication_lag gauges were zero when scraped, at most three seconds after the load ended. The sample is too small to size a deployment from.

docs.title: Second follow-up — 2026-10-06
docs.text:
batch fsync. In batch mode every append flushed and synced the segment while holding the WAL lock, so concurrent writers queued behind each other's disk writes. The sync now happens after the lock is released, and writers that append while one is in flight share the next. BenchmarkWAL_AppendBatch_Matrix with 16 writers and 256-byte payloads, time per batch, four runs each:

Events per batch Before After 10 3.2-6.1 ms 0.44-0.51 ms 100 3.2-3.9 ms 0.68-1.10 ms 1,000 6.0-6.7 ms 2.1-2.3 ms (one run 13.2 ms)

A writer still returns only after a sync that began after its append.

Memory per partition. An empty partition held 146 MB of heap at default settings: a bloom filter sized for 100 million message IDs and a one-million-entry consumer queue, both allocated at creation. They are now allocated on first use, leaving 12 MB. The filter is still built, at full size, by the first deduplicated publish to the partition.

Cluster formation. Leadership now comes only from Raft-committed assignments, and partitions that never had a leader are assigned five seconds after membership last changed (since 2026-10-07: as soon as --cluster-expected-nodes nodes are up, with the wait as the fallback). Without that wait the first node of a new cluster led every partition and handed most of them over as the others joined, refusing publishes for those partitions meanwhile. A node also unloads a partition once it is neither its leader nor a replica. /health/ready answers 503 until every partition has a leader that has loaded it, and scripts/compare-cluster-throughput.ps1 waits for it before starting the load; a fixed pause was not enough on a slow host.

Measurement. Free memory on the host moved between 0.7 and 4.5 GiB during this session for reasons outside the test, so the comparison was limited to 480,000 events (16 publishers per node with 10,000 events each, 32 partitions, 64 MiB segments, batch 4,000, dedup bypassed, RF=1), interleaving the working tree with the branch head from before this session's changes:

Build Events/s Server CPU per event Peak working set, three nodes Working tree 629,769 / 711,887 10.1 / 10.3 us 958 / 972 MB Branch head before the fixes 704,335 / 60,367 10.1 / 16.0 us 1,498 / 1,662 MB

The slow baseline run coincided with a drop in free memory. Runs this short (under a second of load) do not include a leadership reconcile tick, so they neither show nor contradict the gain measured in the first follow-up; they do show that the later changes cost no CPU on the publish path and that the servers need about a third less memory. The first run of each newly built binary was repeatedly several times slower than its second and is not listed. Larger matched runs were not repeated: two attempts were stopped by the memory guard.

RF=3 with min-insync-replicas=2 and dedup enabled was run as a failover check rather than a throughput test: 60,000 events across four partitions, one node killed, 40,000 more events to the two survivors, zero publish errors, and identical logs on the survivors.

docs.title: Container release implication
docs.text:
Superseded: images of v0.6.0-rc.2, rc.3 and rc.4 have been published since, built from source without the quorum defect; the current one, v0.6.0-rc.4, was scanned before it was pushed (audit F19 has the scan history). The paragraph below is what held on 2026-09-29.

The rc.1 CI built a container and started the production Helm chart in kind, but it did not publish or scan a release image. There is no Docker CLI on this Windows host. Do not publish an image from the rc.1 tag: it contains the quorum acknowledgement bug. A future image candidate needs the corrected source, a scan of that exact image, and release notes stating the measured profile and remaining production blockers.

docs.title: Three-node throughput validation — 2026-10-16
docs.text:
These are v0.7.0/v0.6.0 results, not measurements of v0.8.0 or its opt-in lifecycle operations. They remain unchanged as a dated record. See current release limits.

These measurements compare v0.6.0 (babee9c) with the hardening-v0.7.0 branch at fd84f4b, whose server code is that of d5c7269 and of v0.7.0. All runs use three server processes on one AMD Ryzen 7 6800H laptop (16 logical processors, 15 GB of memory, one Micron 2450 NVMe SSD), Windows/amd64, Go 1.26.9 with cgo disabled (the Go bloom filter), and 256-byte payloads. The two server builds ran alternately with the same load generator. The three nodes share one CPU, memory pool and SSD, and Windows syncs files differently from Linux, so these are results for this machine, not a capacity to size a deployment on.

docs.title: Production settings, every event checked as delivered
docs.text:
scripts/measure-throughput-native.ps1, which runs the nodes as Windows processes:

  • RF=3 with min-insync-replicas=2 and 3 partitions;
  • batch fsync with a 2 ms flush interval, deduplication on;
  • public TLS, replication mTLS, JWT authentication and encryption at rest.

Each node is capped and watched:

  • 2 CPUs (GOMAXPROCS=2), a 150 MiB Go memory target and a 384 MiB budget (--memory-limit);
  • below-normal priority;
  • the supervisor stops the run at 75% of the budget or below 1.5 GiB of free host memory.

One consumer group reads every partition with a buffer of 64 deliveries and one worker per partition. Publishers pause while 20,000 accepted events are undelivered. A trial is valid only when every accepted message ID was delivered.

Accepted events per second over 15-second trials, round 1 / round 2. Delivered per second is within a few percent below the accepted rate except where noted.

Batch × publishers v0.6.0 Current Publish p99, v0.6.0 Publish p99, current 1 × 1 40 / 49 50 / 46 159 / 32 ms 31 / 35 ms 1 × 4 72 / 81 82 / 73 268 / 115 ms 106 / 126 ms 100 × 1 3,964 / 3,172 4,044 / 3,582 50 / 107 ms 47 / 52 ms 100 × 4 9,068 / 8,712 7,873 / 6,970 115 / 118 ms 225 / 159 ms 100 × 8 10,347 / 9,418 9,920 / 9,251 230 / 214 ms 204 / 248 ms 1,000 × 1 18,061 / 16,582 18,599 / 17,525 64 / 100 ms 86 / 61 ms 1,000 × 4 12,526 / 12,460 13,794 / 10,918 250 / 324 ms 188 / 595 ms 1,000 × 8 12,666 / 11,792 14,257 / 11,592 426 / 540 ms 502 / 280 ms 1,000 × 16 13,158 / 11,126 6,598 / 11,060 480 / 951 ms 1,741 / 917 ms

Every trial delivered every accepted event; no ID was missing.

  • Peak. Batches of 1,000 from one publisher gave the highest rate for both builds, about 17,000–18,600 accepted events per second. A separate run of the current build reached 18,256 events/s accepted and 16,199 delivered, and 19,691 in its repeat before the server refused a batch with "partition 1 is at capacity".
  • Ceiling. In the larger configurations the consumer, not the publish path, set the ceiling. Delivery lateness p99 was 2 to 6 seconds, and publishers paused for the backlog.
  • More publishers. Beyond one publisher of large batches, adding publishers only grew the backlog.
  • Single-event publishes. These are bound by the fsync each waits for, about 19 ms here.
  • One configuration to watch. 100 × 4 was slower on the current build in both rounds, by about 15%. Runs on this host vary by ±20%, so two rounds do not settle it.
  • One outlier. The current build's first 1,000 × 16 run coincided with host CPU at 91%.
  • At-least-once. One trial redelivered 20 events, which at-least-once delivery allows.

Peak memory per node was 213–225 MiB of the 384 MiB budget. Host CPU peaked at 55–91% and free host memory stayed above 6.5 GiB.

docs.title: Publish acceptance, as in the 2026-09-29 record
docs.text:
scripts/compare-cluster-throughput.ps1 with --dev, no TLS, authentication or encryption, periodic fsync (which production mode refuses), no CPU caps and no consumer. It counts accepted publish responses only. A run is stopped below 1.5 GiB of free host memory.

RF=1, dedup bypassed: 32 partitions, 128 MiB segments, 32 publishers per node, batch 4,000, 4.8 million events:

Build Run 1 Run 2 v0.6.0 705,374 357,331 events/s Current 856,003 646,826 events/s

RF=3, minISR=2, dedup enabled: 16 partitions, 32 MiB segments, 16 publishers per node, batch 4,000, 240,000 events:

Build Run 1 Run 2 Run 3 Median v0.6.0 165,189 190,709 199,019 190,709 events/s Current 216,916 177,276 203,791 203,791 events/s

Every completed run reported zero publish errors.

  • No regression. Neither profile shows the current build slower.
  • Variance. The 357,331 run of v0.6.0, with unchanged settings, shows how much a single run varies here.
  • 1M+. The figure of earlier versions of the README was not reached by either build; the best run was 856,003 events/s.

The same RF=3 profile at the earlier record's 960,000 events (128 MiB segments) did not complete on either build: all four runs were stopped by the memory guard. In one v0.6.0 run free memory had reached 795 MiB before the load stopped. Publishing into three replicas with no consumer and no pause outgrows this laptop's memory at that size; where the memory goes has not been diagnosed. The 2026-09-29 record completed 960,000 events with both the Go (130,128 events/s) and the native Rust/CGO build (110,773), and a later session of that record was stopped by the guard at 480,000. That is consistent with this host's free memory varying between sessions. It is not evidence of a change in either direction.

docs.title: Server configuration
docs.text: Use this page to choose server settings. For Go application settings, see the SDK guide; for operator commands, see administration. The defaults below are the binary's defaults. Docker Compose and Helm supply their own values.

docs.title: Set a value
docs.text:
Every flag has an environment variable. Defaults are loaded first, then nonempty environment values, then explicit command-line flags. A flag wins over its environment variable. Invalid environment values fail startup even if a flag would override them; an empty environment value keeps the default.

These Bash examples start the same local development node:

cronos-api --dev --node-id=local --ack-timeout=45s
CRONOS_DEV=true CRONOS_NODE_ID=local CRONOS_ACK_TIMEOUT=45s cronos-api

Durations take a unit, such as 250ms, 30s, 10m or 1h. Flags ending in -ms and the interval flags whose tables say milliseconds take an integer instead. Byte counts take integers, such as 67108864 for 64 MiB. Booleans take true or false. Use --flag=false to turn a boolean off explicitly.

Most environment names are CRONOS_ followed by the uppercase flag name with dashes replaced by underscores. Two differ: --dedup-ttl uses CRONOS_DEDUP_TTL_HOURS, and --min-insync-replicas uses CRONOS_MIN_IN_SYNC_REPLICAS. Every exact name is in the tables below.

docs.title: Choose a deployment
docs.text:
For local development, --dev --node-id=local is enough. It bypasses the production startup requirements. It does not turn off security settings you explicitly enable.

For production, use the deployment requirements and Docker guide. Startup requires TLS, JWT authentication with a policy file, WAL encryption with a key file, mutual TLS between nodes, at least three replicas, at least two write acknowledgements, and batch or every_event fsync. Cluster nodes also need seeds. Experimental features, exactly-once commits, and a profiling listener outside loopback are refused. Passing validation alone does not create a working cluster: configure --cluster, reachable node addresses, certificates and persistent storage as described in the deployment guide.

Start with the defaults and change a setting for a measured need. For slow handlers, increase the acknowledgement timeout. For memory pressure, inspect the scheduler budget and admission limits. For disk pressure, inspect retention and unfinished events before shortening retention limits. Limits that refuse new work let clients retry; they do not delete accepted events.

docs.title: Node and listeners
docs.text: Flag Environment variable Default What it does and when to change it --node-id CRONOS_NODE_ID required Stable, unique identity of this node. Keep it with the node's persistent data; give each node a different ID. --data-dir CRONOS_DATA_DIR ./data Root for partition logs, offsets and other node data. Mount persistent storage here. --grpc-addr CRONOS_GRPC_ADDR :9000 Public gRPC listen address for applications and the admin CLI. :9000 listens on all interfaces. --http-addr CRONOS_HTTP_ADDR :8080 Health, metrics, dashboard and HTTP admin API listen address. Use HTTP TLS below when this port needs TLS. --partition-count CRONOS_PARTITION_COUNT 1 Number of logical partitions. Partitions let work run in parallel; more partitions also need more memory and files. Keep the cluster's nodes consistent. --replication-factor CRONOS_REPLICATION_FACTOR 1 Copies of each partition, including its leader. Production requires at least 3; also choose the write acknowledgement count below. --dev CRONOS_DEV false Bypass production startup requirements for local tests. Use true only for development. --experimental-features CRONOS_EXPERIMENTAL_FEATURES false Expose unverified transactions, online partition splitting and cross-region replication. Requires --dev; incompatible with event lifecycle mode.

docs.title: Storage, retention and backups
docs.text:
Retention proposes old closed log segments for removal. Completion, replication and lifecycle safety checks can keep a segment longer. An event scheduled far into the future can pin a segment. These are cleanup targets, not guaranteed disk quotas. See the retention contract.

Flag Environment variable Default What it does and when to change it --segment-size CRONOS_SEGMENT_SIZE 536870912 WAL segment size in bytes before rotation (512 MiB). Smaller segments allow finer cleanup at the cost of more files. --index-interval CRONOS_INDEX_INTERVAL 1000 Events between sparse log index entries. A smaller value speeds seeking at the cost of a larger index. --fsync-mode CRONOS_FSYNC_MODE batch batch groups disk syncs and waits for durability; every_event syncs each event. periodic can acknowledge before disk sync and is refused in production. --flush-interval CRONOS_FLUSH_INTERVAL 1000 Background WAL flush interval in milliseconds. Must be positive. In periodic mode this affects the unsynced-data window. --compaction-interval CRONOS_COMPACTION_INTERVAL 10m How often each partition removes closed segments whose events are finished. 0 disables scheduled compaction; an admin command can still run it. --retention-max-age-hours CRONOS_RETENTION_MAX_AGE_HOURS 168 Age in hours after which closed segments may be removed, subject to safety checks. 0 disables the age target. --retention-max-size-gb CRONOS_RETENTION_MAX_SIZE_GB 0 Size target for WAL cleanup in GiB. 0 disables it; pinned work can keep usage above the target. --event-lifecycle CRONOS_EVENT_LIFECYCLE false Enable inspecting, canceling and rescheduling future events. Standalone requires RF=1/minISR=1; a cluster requires majority acknowledgements and capable replicas/voters. Incompatible with CDC sinks and experimental features. Activation changes the persistent format; turning it off is not a supported downgrade. --wal-relocation-bytes CRONOS_WAL_RELOCATION_BYTES 0 Encoded future-event bytes that a retention pass may copy forward to release pinned old segments. Requires lifecycle mode. 0 disables copying. --backup-interval CRONOS_BACKUP_INTERVAL 1h Back up partitions at wall-clock multiples of this duration. 0 disables scheduled backups. Choose an interval that matches how much recovery work you can tolerate. --backup-retention CRONOS_BACKUP_RETENTION 168h How long backup generations are kept. 0 keeps them indefinitely, so monitor free space. --backup-dir CRONOS_BACKUP_DIR empty Backup destination; empty uses backups under the data directory. Use a separate volume/failure domain to survive loss of the data volume.

docs.title: Scheduling
docs.text:
The hot timing wheel holds near-term work in memory. Distant events and memory overflow wait on disk, and the hydrator brings them back toward their delivery time. Reducing the tick improves timing granularity but increases scheduler activity; it does not guarantee an exact delivery deadline.

Flag Environment variable Default What it does and when to change it --tick-ms CRONOS_TICK_MS 10 Scheduler tick in milliseconds. Use a smaller tick only when measurements show a timing benefit. --wheel-size CRONOS_WHEEL_SIZE 600 Slots per timing-wheel level. Changes how times are spread through the wheel; normally keep the default. --hot-window-minutes CRONOS_HOT_WINDOW_MINUTES 60 Keep events due beyond this many minutes in the cold store. 0 disables time-based spill; the memory budget can still spill events. --hydrator-min-interval CRONOS_HYDRATOR_MIN_INTERVAL 5000 Shortest adaptive cold-store scan interval, in milliseconds. Lower values scan more often. --hydrator-max-interval CRONOS_HYDRATOR_MAX_INTERVAL 300000 Longest adaptive cold-store scan interval, in milliseconds. Keep it at least as large as the minimum.

docs.title: Delivery and acknowledgement
docs.text:
These settings govern server-to-consumer delivery. They differ from the SDK producer's retries of a failed publish. An acknowledgement timeout or failed handler can cause redelivery, so handlers must tolerate duplicates. Zero values for timeout, retries, credits, backoff and breaker settings fall back to dispatcher defaults; they do not disable those mechanisms.

Flag Environment variable Default What it does and when to change it --ack-timeout CRONOS_ACK_TIMEOUT 30s Time a delivery may remain unacknowledged before retry. Allow enough time for normal handler work; longer timeouts delay recovery after a consumer stops. --max-retries CRONOS_MAX_RETRIES 5 Delivery attempt limit before dead-lettering (the initial attempt counts). Increase only when failures are expected to recover. --retry-backoff CRONOS_RETRY_BACKOFF 1s Base delay before redelivery, multiplied by the attempt number. Increase to avoid repeatedly hitting a failing dependency. --max-credits CRONOS_MAX_CREDITS 1000 Maximum unacknowledged deliveries for a subscription that does not request its own limit. A requested buffer size wins, capped at 50000. The Go SDK requests 1024 by default. --max-consumer-groups CRONOS_MAX_CONSUMER_GROUPS 10000 Consumer groups a partition holds at most. Subscribe creates a group for any new name and groups are kept with their progress, so a subscription for a new group beyond the limit is refused with RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED. Groups that exist are kept, and a negative value removes the limit. Group names are limited to 255 bytes. --cb-failure-threshold CRONOS_CB_FAILURE_THRESHOLD 0.5 Delivery failure fraction at which the server's breaker pauses a failing subscription. 0.5 means 50 percent. Distinct from the SDK's node breaker. --cb-min-attempts CRONOS_CB_MIN_ATTEMPTS 10 Minimum delivery samples before evaluating that fraction. A larger value avoids reacting to a few early failures. --cb-open-duration-ms CRONOS_CB_OPEN_DURATION_MS 30000 Milliseconds the delivery breaker stays open before probing for recovery.

docs.title: Admission, memory and rate limits
docs.text:
These limits refuse new publishes when the node is busy. Set client retry backoff so rejected work does not immediately overwhelm it again. Counts are per partition unless the table says otherwise. The scheduler budget covers payloads held by the scheduler, not the whole process.

Flag Environment variable Default What it does and when to change it --max-ready-queue CRONOS_MAX_READY_QUEUE 1000000 Refuse publishes that would exceed this many ready events. 0 disables this admission check. Increase only when consumers can drain the backlog. --max-timing-wheel-size CRONOS_MAX_TIMING_WHEEL_SIZE 10000000 Refuse publishes that would exceed this many active hot timers. 0 disables this check. --max-in-flight CRONOS_MAX_IN_FLIGHT 500000 Admission limit based on active, unacknowledged deliveries. 0 disables this check; subscription credits remain separate. --load-shedding-threshold CRONOS_LOAD_SHEDDING_THRESHOLD 0 Refuse new work earlier, at this fraction of --max-ready-queue; 0.8 means 80 percent. 0 disables early shedding. Requires a positive ready-queue limit. --max-disk-usage CRONOS_MAX_DISK_USAGE 0.95 Refuse publishes once the data filesystem is 95 percent full; resume two percentage points below. Accepts 0 (disabled) or 0.05 to 1. Delivery and cleanup continue; followers refuse growth but can acknowledge data already stored. --max-memory-percent CRONOS_MAX_MEMORY_PERCENT 80 Refuse publishes at this process memory usage as a percentage of its memory limit. 0 disables it. Unlike disk usage, this takes 80, not 0.8. --memory-limit CRONOS_MEMORY_LIMIT 0 Memory limit in bytes used by admission. 0 detects the container's cgroup limit or falls back to machine memory. Set it explicitly when detection does not match your deployment. --memory-check-interval CRONOS_MEMORY_CHECK_INTERVAL 1000 Milliseconds a memory measurement may be reused. A shorter interval responds sooner at extra measurement cost. --scheduler-memory CRONOS_SCHEDULER_MEMORY 67108864 Node-wide scheduler payload budget in bytes (64 MiB). Minimum 32 MiB; 0 uses the default. Overflow waits as log references. Leave headroom for other memory. --max-ingest-rate CRONOS_MAX_INGEST_RATE 0 Sustained publish events per second per partition. Requires a positive ingest burst size too; 0 disables this limiter. --ingest-burst-size CRONOS_INGEST_BURST_SIZE 0 Token-bucket capacity for ingest bursts. Both this and the rate must be positive to enable limiting. --topic-rate-limit CRONOS_TOPIC_RATE_LIMIT 0 Events per second per JWT subject and topic, with authentication enabled. 0 disables this limit. Use with a positive burst size. --topic-rate-burst CRONOS_TOPIC_RATE_BURST 0 Token-bucket capacity for that topic limit; nonpositive rate or burst disables the topic limiter.

docs.title: Duplicate detection and replay
docs.text: Flag Environment variable Default What it does and when to change it --dedup-ttl CRONOS_DEDUP_TTL_HOURS 168 Hours to retain message-ID deduplication records. Cover your longest publish retry/backfill window. After expiration, a repeated ID can be accepted again. --bloom-capacity CRONOS_BLOOM_CAPACITY 100000000 Expected IDs per partition for the Bloom filter that avoids disk lookups. Larger capacity uses more memory; the durable dedup store remains authoritative. --follower-reads CRONOS_FOLLOWER_READS false Allow followers to serve replay reads. Their view can lag the leader; leave off when replay must use the leader. --exactly-once-commits CRONOS_EXACTLY_ONCE_COMMITS false Experimental commit-ID storage. Refused in production and unused by the normal Ack path; enabling it does not provide end-to-end exactly-once delivery.

docs.title: Cluster and replication
docs.text:
Applications connect to the public gRPC port. Nodes use membership, internal gRPC and Raft addresses to communicate with each other. Make those addresses reachable by the other nodes, and put the corresponding DNS names in the certificates. Changing the replication factor does not create missing nodes.

Flag Environment variable Default What it does and when to change it --cluster CRONOS_CLUSTER false Enable cluster membership, placement and replication. Without it the server runs standalone. --cluster-seeds CRONOS_CLUSTER_SEEDS empty Comma-separated membership addresses, for example node1:7946,node2:7946,node3:7946. Name all nodes on every node, including itself. Required in production cluster mode. --cluster-bootstrap CRONOS_CLUSTER_BOOTSTRAP false Allow this node to create a new cluster if it has no state and no seed belongs to one. Give this to exactly one node. Existing state is reused on restart. --cluster-expected-nodes CRONOS_CLUSTER_EXPECTED_NODES 0 Number of nodes expected at first formation. Assign first partition leaders once that many are up; 0 leaves the count unknown. --cluster-formation-wait CRONOS_CLUSTER_FORMATION_WAIT 5s If the expected count is unknown or not yet reached, wait this long with stable membership before first placement. 0 assigns immediately. --cluster-gossip-addr CRONOS_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_ADDR :7946 TCP membership listen/advertised address. In a cluster use a host and port peers can reach. --cluster-grpc-addr CRONOS_CLUSTER_GRPC_ADDR :7947 Internal RPC address for replication, Raft control and experimental cross-region RPCs. Keep separate from the public listener. --cluster-raft-addr CRONOS_CLUSTER_RAFT_ADDR :7948 Raft transport address used by the cluster coordinators. Peers must reach it. --advertise-grpc-addr CRONOS_ADVERTISE_GRPC_ADDR empty Public host:port advertised to SDKs in partition metadata. Set when applications must discover nodes beyond bootstrap addresses. Must be reachable by clients and covered by the public TLS certificate. --raft-dir CRONOS_RAFT_DIR ./raft Persistent Raft state directory. Put it on persistent storage; the container/chart use a path under the data volume. --raft-join CRONOS_RAFT_JOIN empty Parsed but unused. Join through --cluster-seeds; changing this value has no effect. --virtual-nodes CRONOS_VIRTUAL_NODES 2048 Hash-ring positions per node. More positions spread partition ownership more evenly; nodes should agree on this value. --heartbeat-interval CRONOS_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL 1s Time between membership heartbeats. Shorter intervals increase traffic and detect failures sooner. --failure-timeout CRONOS_FAILURE_TIMEOUT 5s Heartbeat silence before failure detection escalates. Allow for expected network pauses to avoid unnecessary leadership changes. --suspect-timeout CRONOS_SUSPECT_TIMEOUT 3s Time a suspected node remains suspect before it is considered dead. --use-memberlist CRONOS_USE_MEMBERLIST false Unsupported. Setting true fails startup; the server uses its own membership protocol. --clock-skew-threshold-ms CRONOS_CLOCK_SKEW_THRESHOLD_MS 5000 Parsed but unused; this setting currently enforces no clock-skew limit. Synchronize node clocks operationally. --node-rack CRONOS_NODE_RACK empty Rack or availability-zone label used by topology-aware placement. Label nodes to describe independent failure domains. --node-zone CRONOS_NODE_ZONE empty Zone label for placement. Keep labels consistent across nodes in the same zone. --node-region CRONOS_NODE_REGION empty Region label for placement and experimental cross-region identity. --replication-batch CRONOS_REPLICATION_BATCH 100 Events per replication batch. Larger batches trade request overhead for batch size and latency. --replication-timeout CRONOS_REPLICATION_TIMEOUT 10s Time allowed for replication. A timeout can leave a write's outcome unknown; retry the same message/request ID. --min-insync-replicas CRONOS_MIN_IN_SYNC_REPLICAS 1 Replicas, including the leader, required before a write is acknowledged. 0 means 1; production requires at least 2. Lifecycle mode in a cluster requires a majority of the replication factor. Higher values tolerate fewer unavailable replicas. --snapshot-catchup-threshold CRONOS_SNAPSHOT_CATCHUP_THRESHOLD 10000 Parsed but unused. Startup synchronization installs snapshots; connected followers catch up incrementally. Changing this does not trigger snapshots based on lag.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
TLS protects transport, JWTs identify callers, and the policy file grants permissions. They serve different purposes. Public gRPC, HTTP and internal node connections have separate TLS switches. See permissions.

Flag Environment variable Default What it does and when to change it --tls-enabled CRONOS_TLS_ENABLED false Enable TLS on public gRPC. Requires the certificate and key below. --tls-ca-file CRONOS_TLS_CA_FILE empty PEM CA bundle for verifying public gRPC client certificates when client authentication is enabled. --tls-cert-file CRONOS_TLS_CERT_FILE empty PEM server certificate; names must cover addresses clients use. Also used by HTTP TLS. --tls-key-file CRONOS_TLS_KEY_FILE empty Private key matching that certificate. Mount it as a secret. --tls-client-auth CRONOS_TLS_CLIENT_AUTH false Require a client certificate on public gRPC (mTLS). Applications must supply their own certificate and key. --http-tls-enabled CRONOS_HTTP_TLS_ENABLED false Serve health, metrics, dashboard and HTTP admin endpoints over TLS using the public certificate/key. HTTP callers are not asked for a client certificate. --replication-tls-enabled CRONOS_REPLICATION_TLS_ENABLED false Require mutual TLS for replication, membership and Raft. Requires all three replication TLS files. --replication-tls-ca-file CRONOS_REPLICATION_TLS_CA_FILE empty CA bundle trusted to identify cluster nodes. --replication-tls-cert-file CRONOS_REPLICATION_TLS_CERT_FILE empty This node's PEM certificate for both server and client use between nodes. --replication-tls-key-file CRONOS_REPLICATION_TLS_KEY_FILE empty Private key matching the node certificate. --auth-enabled CRONOS_AUTH_ENABLED false Require JWTs on public RPCs and protected HTTP endpoints. Requires a verification secret or public key. --auth-jwt-secret CRONOS_AUTH_JWT_SECRET empty Shared HMAC verification secret. Use a secret-backed environment variable rather than a command-line argument visible in process listings. --auth-jwt-public-key CRONOS_AUTH_JWT_PUBLIC_KEY empty PEM Ed25519, RSA or ECDSA public key for asymmetric JWT verification. --auth-policy-file CRONOS_AUTH_POLICY_FILE empty JSON permissions keyed by JWT subject. Required in production. Explicitly grant topic publish/subscribe or global admin as needed. --encryption-enabled CRONOS_ENCRYPTION_ENABLED false Encrypt WAL segments with AES-256-GCM. Requires the key file; this is separate from TLS. --encryption-key-file CRONOS_ENCRYPTION_KEY_FILE empty 32-byte master key file. Preserve it securely with the recovery plan; encrypted backups need the matching key.

docs.title: Tracing and profiling
docs.text: Flag Environment variable Default What it does and when to change it --tracing-enabled CRONOS_TRACING_ENABLED false Create OpenTelemetry traces. Choose an exporter as well; tracing has runtime cost. --tracing-exporter CRONOS_TRACING_EXPORTER none none, stdout or otlp. Use stdout for local inspection or OTLP to send to a collector. --tracing-otlp-endpoint CRONOS_TRACING_OTLP_ENDPOINT 127.0.0.1:4317 OTLP gRPC collector host:port; used with the OTLP exporter. --tracing-sample-ratio CRONOS_TRACING_SAMPLE_RATIO 0.01 Fraction of traces sampled, from 0 to 1. 0.01 samples about one percent; raise briefly when debugging. --tracing-insecure CRONOS_TRACING_INSECURE true Send OTLP without TLS. Set false when the collector requires TLS. --pprof-addr CRONOS_PPROF_ADDR empty Separate Go runtime profiling listener, for example 127.0.0.1:6060. Empty disables it. Production requires loopback.

docs.title: Additional environment variables
docs.text:
These have no command-line flag. CDC captures accepted event changes; it is not a substitute for consumer delivery acknowledgements. CDC sinks cannot be combined with event lifecycle mode. See CDC.

Variable Default Use CRONOS_CDC_KAFKA_BROKERS empty Comma-separated Kafka brokers; nonempty registers a CDC Kafka sink. CRONOS_CDC_KAFKA_TOPIC cronos-cdc Destination topic when the Kafka sink is configured. CRONOS_CDC_WEBHOOK_URL empty Nonempty registers an HTTP webhook CDC sink. CRONOS_REGIONS empty Comma-separated region=address entries for experimental cross-region peers. Requires --dev --experimental-features. See replication.

docs.title: Apply changes and SIGHUP limits
docs.text:
Restart the node to apply configuration changes consistently. Updating a parent shell's environment does not update an already running process. On Unix, the SIGHUP listener re-reads a small set of variables from the process's existing environment. It updates the shared config object without reconfiguring most running components; it is not a general live reload. Windows has no usable SIGHUP reload path.

Re-read variable Effect in the running server CRONOS_MAX_CREDITS Existing dispatchers keep their startup value; partitions constructed later use the new config. CRONOS_ACK_TIMEOUT Same dispatcher limitation. Startup takes durations such as 30s; the reload parser instead takes integer seconds. CRONOS_MAX_RETRIES Existing dispatchers keep their startup value; new partitions use the new config. CRONOS_CB_FAILURE_THRESHOLD Existing delivery breakers keep their startup value; new partitions use the new config. CRONOS_LOAD_SHEDDING_THRESHOLD Admission reads the shared field on each check, so this value can affect existing partitions. This does not provide coordinated reload of the other limits. CRONOS_TRACING_SAMPLE_RATIO The tracer was constructed at startup and keeps its original sampler. CRONOS_STATS_PRINT_INTERVAL_MS Reload-only variable; the running stats ticker keeps its startup interval. There is no startup flag for it.

The listener registers no component-update callbacks in cmd/api/main.go. Its parsers also differ from startup validation. Use a restart rather than depending on SIGHUP to tune production behavior.

docs.title: Docker and Helm
docs.text:
With Docker, pass variables with -e/--env-file and mount any named files inside the container. A host path is not automatically available in the container. Inspect Compose and chart values for deployment-specific defaults.

The Helm chart has named values for common settings, and extraEnv for any remaining variable. Values are Kubernetes EnvVar entries, including valueFrom for secrets. Explicit environment entries override ConfigMap values. Avoid duplicate names in extraEnv and the chart's explicit env entries; prefer the named chart setting for TLS, auth, addresses and storage.

# Additional values file, used together with values-production.yaml.
config:
  minInSyncReplicas: 2
extraEnv:
  - name: CRONOS_EVENT_LIFECYCLE
    value: "true"
  - name: CRONOS_RETENTION_MAX_AGE_HOURS
    value: "72"
  - name: CRONOS_BACKUP_INTERVAL
    value: "6h"

Apply changed environment values by rolling/restarting pods. Use backupPersistence for a separate backup PVC and values-production.yaml for the production security settings. The chart's base values enable dev mode; they are intended for testing.

docs.title: Check the effective setup
docs.text: Use cronos-api --help to inspect the binary's accepted flags. Check both explicit arguments and container/pod environment when a setting surprises you; deployment defaults can differ from binary defaults. The administration guide describes topology, health, lag and log checks. The configuration architecture links the implementation and explains how values reach components.

docs.title: CronosDB Developer Architecture Guide
docs.text:
Comprehensive codebase walkthrough for developers and code readers.

This document explains the production architecture as implemented in code, not only at a conceptual level. Use it as a map to navigate subsystems, understand reliability decisions, and trace end-to-end flows.

The v0.8.0 lifecycle contract and current-term commitment protocol define the one-way format activation, mutation and recovery rules. The release requirements separate implemented behavior from unvalidated operating conditions.

Related docs:

  • Feature-split architecture index: docs/architecture/README.md
  • Inline-rendered diagrams: see the Diagram Index

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
• 1. Why This Guide Exists
  • 2. How To Read This Codebase
  • 3. System Overview
  • 4. Startup Composition and Lifecycle
  • 5. End-to-End Runtime Flows
  • 6. Feature Deep Dive by Module
  • 7. Reliability and Production Decisions
  • 8. Debugging and Navigation Playbook
  • 9. Extension Points for Future Development
  • 10. Suggested Reading Order

docs.title: 1. Why This Guide Exists
docs.text:
CronosDB is a distributed, timestamp-triggered event platform with many cooperating modules. The architecture is intentionally layered but operationally dense. This guide helps you:

  • Understand how requests move through data and control planes.
  • Find the right file quickly for a feature or bug.
  • Understand reliability tradeoffs behind current implementation choices.
  • Onboard engineers without relying on tribal knowledge.

docs.title: 2.1 Repository Shape
docs.text:
• cmd/api/main.go: composition root and runtime lifecycle owner.
  • internal/*: production implementation by subsystem.
  • pkg/*: reusable SDK and shared types/utilities.
  • proto/events.proto: contract source for all gRPC services.

docs.title: 2.2 Mental Model
docs.text:
Think in three planes:

  • Data plane: publish, schedule, dispatch, ack, replay.
  • Control plane: cluster membership, routing, leader metadata.
  • Reliability plane: dedup, auth, audit, retention, metrics, tracing, SLO.

docs.title: 3. System Overview
docs.text:
The canonical system-overview diagram lives in docs/architecture/README.md (rendered inline on GitHub). In brief:

  • Clients (Producer/Consumer SDKs, ops CLI + dashboard) hit the process edge: public gRPC :9000, HTTP :8080 (health/metrics/UI), internal gRPC :7947.
  • The data plane (handlers → partition manager → per-partition WAL, scheduler, worker, dispatcher, consumer groups, DLQ, dedup) serves event traffic.
  • The control plane (cluster manager, hash-ring router, gossip membership, Raft metadata, leader-follower replication, and experimental cross-region replication) manages placement and consistency.
  • Guardrails (JWT+RBAC, audit, schema registry, tenant accounting, SLO/metrics/tracing, retention/backup) and production security (public TLS, optional HTTP TLS, encryption at rest v2, replication mTLS, --dev bypass) wrap both planes.
  • Experimental features — transactions (2PC), online partition splitting and cross-region replication — run only with --dev --experimental-features; production validation refuses the flag.

docs.title: 4.1 Composition Root
docs.text:
The runtime is composed in cmd/api/main.go in this order:

  1. Load config (includes production validation unless --dev), determine the memory limit (--memory-limit, else the cgroup limit, else machine memory), start the optional --pprof-addr listener, and install the hot-reload listener.
  2. Initialize guardrails (audit, schema, tenant, cdc, slo, tracing).
  3. Initialize partition manager with shared Pebble cache (its backpressure manager refuses publishes above --max-memory-percent), and give it the change feed for CDC and, when CRONOS_REGIONS is set with --experimental-features, cross-region replication before any partition exists.
  4. Start operational loops (disk_pressure, backup_scheduler, retention enforcer).
  5. If cluster mode: start cluster manager (raft + membership + router), join seeds.
  6. Create initial partitions (standalone: all; cluster: partition 0 then lazy-create). Each partition created, now or later, starts its change feed.
  7. Build public gRPC (:9000): Event, ConsumerGroup, Partition, Admin; the Transaction handler (tx.NewHandler(pm)) only with --experimental-features.
  8. Build internal gRPC (:7947): Replication, Raft (cluster mode); CrossRegion only with --experimental-features (replication mTLS in production).
  9. Start HTTP (:8080): health, metrics, embedded dashboard /ui/, /api/admin/*; over TLS with --http-tls-enabled.
  10. Start serve monitors, the autoscaler (always started; it only logs CPU, memory, disk and lag threshold warnings), and the stats loop.
  11. On signal: graceful stop public/internal gRPC and HTTP, stop retention and backups, stop partitions, stop the cluster manager, then a final WAL flush.

docs.title: 4.2 Startup and Shutdown Sequence
docs.text:
This is the canonical startup/shutdown diagram:

sequenceDiagram
    participant Main as cmd/api/main.go
    participant Config as internal/config
    participant Guard as audit schema tenant cdc slo tracing
    participant PM as internal/partition
    participant Cluster as internal/cluster
    participant Pub as Public gRPC :9000
    participant Int as Internal gRPC :7947
    participant HTTP as HTTP :8080
    participant BG as Background loops

    Main->>Config: LoadConfig + ValidateConfig
    Main->>Main: --dev relaxes production security gates
    Main->>Main: Memory limit, optional pprof listener, SIGHUP reload
    Main->>Guard: Init audit, schema, tenant, CDC sinks, tracing, SLO
    Main->>PM: NewPartitionManagerWithCache(shared Pebble cache)
    Main->>PM: SetChangeFeed (CDC sinks + experimental cross-region, echo guard)
    Main->>BG: Disk monitor, backup scheduler, retention ticker
    alt cluster enabled
        Main->>Cluster: NewManager + SetPartitionAccessor
        Main->>Cluster: Start Raft then membership/router
        Main->>Cluster: JoinCluster seeds when provided
    end
    Main->>PM: Create/start partitions<br/>(standalone: all, cluster: partition 0 then lazy)
    Main->>Pub: NewGRPCServer + interceptors
    opt --experimental-features
        Main->>Pub: SetTransactionHandler (PM-injected 2PC)
    end
    Main->>Int: NewInternalGRPCServer
    Main->>Int: Register Replication, Raft (cluster)
    opt --experimental-features
        Main->>Int: Register CrossRegion
    end
    Main->>Pub: RegisterServices: Event, ConsumerGroup, Partition, Admin (+ Transaction if set)
    Main->>HTTP: Health + metrics + WebHandler /ui + /api/admin (TLS if --http-tls-enabled)
    Main->>Pub: Start + ServeError monitor
    Main->>Int: Start + ServeError monitor
    Main->>HTTP: ListenAndServe with timeouts
    Main->>BG: Autoscaler (logs only) + stats loop
    Note over Main,BG: SIGINT / SIGTERM
    Main->>Pub: GracefulStopWithTimeout 25s then Stop
    Main->>Int: GracefulStopWithTimeout then Stop
    Main->>HTTP: Shutdown
    Main->>BG: Stop retention enforcer and backup scheduler
    Main->>PM: Close (stop all partitions)
    Main->>Cluster: Stop when enabled
    Main->>PM: Final WAL flush across partitions
    Note over Main,Cluster: 60s overall shutdown budget

docs.title: 5.1 Publish to Delivery Flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Producer
