    participant API as EventService.Publish
    participant PM as PartitionManager
    participant Dedup
    participant WAL
    participant Scheduler
    participant Worker
    participant Dispatcher
    participant Consumer
    participant Group as ConsumerGroup

    Producer->>API: Publish(event)
    API->>PM: Resolve partition for topic or key
    API->>Dedup: Claim message_id and reconcile an appended retry
    alt duplicate
      Dedup-->>API: duplicate=true
      API-->>Producer: duplicate error
    else new event
      Dedup-->>API: duplicate=false
      API->>WAL: Append event and assign offset
      Note over API,WAL: Release claims only on definite pre-append failure
      API->>PM: Replicate to minISR with current-term proof gating commitment
      API->>Scheduler: Schedule by schedule_ts
      API-->>Producer: success with offset and term
    end

    Scheduler->>Worker: ready notification
    Worker->>Dispatcher: dispatch batch
    Dispatcher->>Consumer: delivery stream message
    Consumer->>API: Ack stream (delivery_id, success)
    API->>Group: CommitDeliveries (acks read ahead, one durable write per partition per batch)
    Group-->>API: completions recorded

docs.title: 5.2 Delivery Reliability State Machine
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
  direction LR

  [*] --> Pending
  Pending --> Delivered: stream send ok
  Delivered --> Acked: ack success
  Acked --> [*]

  Pending --> RetryQueued: send failed
  Delivered --> RetryQueued: nack or ack timeout
  RetryQueued --> Pending: retry_at reached
  RetryQueued --> DLQ: max retries exceeded
  DLQ --> [*]

  RetryQueued --> OpenCircuit: failure threshold reached
  OpenCircuit --> HalfOpen: open duration elapsed
  HalfOpen --> Pending: probe delivery succeeds
  HalfOpen --> OpenCircuit: probe fails

docs.title: 6. Feature Deep Dive by Module
docs.text: This section is organized by feature area and tells you where to read first, what the control flow is, and which reliability decisions matter.

docs.title: 6.1 API Layer (gRPC, handlers, middleware)
docs.text:
• Purpose: external and internal RPC surface.
  • Key files:
  • internal/api/grpc_server.go (public listener on :9000)
  • internal/api/internal_grpc_server.go (internal cluster listener on :7947; registers ReplicationServiceServer, RaftServiceServer in cluster mode, and CrossRegionServiceServer only with --experimental-features)
  • internal/api/handlers.go
  • internal/api/consumer_handler.go
  • internal/api/partition_handler.go
  • internal/api/replication_server.go
  • internal/api/raft_server.go (Raft join/leave/status, node removal)
  • internal/api/crossregion_server.go (experimental)
  • internal/tx/transaction_handler.go (registered on the public listener via RegisterTransactionServiceServer only with --experimental-features)
  • internal/api/tls.go (public gRPC and HTTP TLS configuration; certificates re-read when their files change)
  • internal/api/admin_handler.go (operator-facing AdminService)
  • internal/api/web_handler.go (HTTP JSON proxy for AdminService + embedded dashboard SPA)
  • internal/api/health.go
  • Main flow:
  • Requests enter interceptor chain (tracing, SLO, version, auth, topic limit, audit, metrics, IP limit).
  • Handlers enforce request validation, routing, dedup, and downstream invocation.
  • Partition admin methods provide WAL/scheduler status, compaction, retention, and split (split refused unless --experimental-features).
  • Reliability decisions:
  • Explicit gRPC message size limits and keepalive policy.
  • Start() returns listen errors; asynchronous serve errors are surfaced via ServeError().
  • GracefulStopWithTimeout(ctx) drains in-flight RPCs and falls back to forced Stop if the context expires.
  • Health/metrics server startup errors are propagated so the node fails fast on bind or serving failures.
  • Unavailable vs failed precondition semantics for cluster ownership and follower-read gating.
  • Acks on a stream are read ahead and recorded in batches (up to 256), one durable write per partition (processAcks).
  • --exactly-once-commits is refused in production; the Ack path does not read it.
  • With --http-tls-enabled the HTTP port serves TLS with the --tls-cert-file certificate; --pprof-addr is a separate listener, loopback-only in production.

docs.title: 6.2 Configuration and Runtime Reload
docs.text:
• Purpose: unify defaults, flags, env overrides, and runtime reload.
  • Key files:
  • internal/config/defaults.go
  • internal/config/config.go
  • internal/config/reload.go
  • charts/cronos-db/values.yaml
  • charts/cronos-db/values-production.yaml
  • Main flow:
  • Config is loaded once at startup from flags and environment variables. Every flag reads CRONOS_<FLAG> (upper-cased, - replaced by _; aliases CRONOS_DEDUP_TTL_HOURS, CRONOS_MIN_IN_SYNC_REPLICAS); an explicit flag wins.
  • SIGHUP re-reads selected environment values into the shared config; most running components keep their startup values. Restart to apply changes consistently; see reload limits.
  • New flags include retention controls (--retention-max-age-hours, --retention-max-size-gb) and the full security surface (TLS, auth, replication mTLS, encryption at rest).
  • Reliability decisions:
  • Default WAL fsync mode is batch.
  • --dev disables production security requirements; production mode requires TLS, auth with a policy file, encryption at rest, replication mTLS, --replication-factor>=3, --min-insync-replicas>=2, fsync mode batch or every_event, and --cluster-seeds in cluster mode, and refuses --experimental-features, --exactly-once-commits and a non-loopback --pprof-addr.
  • Environment variables: every flag has one (see above). Others read by the binary: SIGHUP-reloadable CRONOS_* tunables (internal/config/reload.go), CDC sinks (CRONOS_CDC_*), and CRONOS_REGIONS (experimental cross-region; refused without --experimental-features).
  • Helm chart defaults to config.dev=true; values-production.yaml disables dev mode and requires TLS, auth, encryption, and replication-mTLS secrets.
  • Conservative defaults for durability and cluster behavior.
  • Feature flags for controlled rollout (follower-reads, tracing, TLS, auth); --experimental-features (requires --dev) gates transactions, online splitting and cross-region replication.

docs.title: 6.3 Partition Runtime and Lifecycle
docs.text:
• Purpose: aggregate per-partition components and lifecycle operations.
  • Key files:
  • internal/partition/manager.go
  • internal/partition/retention.go (PruneWAL, FollowLogStart)
  • internal/partition/split.go (experimental)
  • internal/partition/disk_pressure.go
  • internal/partition/backpressure.go (admission control and the memory guard)
  • internal/partition/lifecycle.go, replicated_lifecycle.go, term_start.go
  • internal/partition/recovery_snapshot.go, internal/recoverystate/file.go
  • Main flow:
  • Partition creation wires WAL, scheduler, dedup, consumer group, dispatcher, worker.
  • A partition start replays timers (replayWALTimers) only for events whose time has not come. Events already due stay in the log; each subscription reads what its group has not finished at its consumers' pace (redriveRetained), so a restart does not load the backlog into memory.
  • Lookup can be lazy in cluster mode via hash-derived partition IDs.
  • Manager also handles leader promotion/demotion and follower registration.
  • Reliability decisions:
  • Epoch fencing to reduce split-brain risk.
  • Admission control across ready queue, timing wheel depth, and in-flight deliveries.
  • Memory guard: publishes are refused while the process holds --max-memory-percent (default 80) of its memory limit.
  • Disk-pressure callback triggers emergency compaction.
  • Lifecycle mode reconstructs a payload-free index before serving. Mutations and delivery share a gate: staged successors suppress predecessors but do not release retention, and only accepted replacements can be delivered.
  • Lifecycle snapshots and backups carry the WAL cut's epoch, accepted boundary, group progress and dead letters; interrupted state import resumes before serving. Suffix replacement clears stale completions before offset reuse.

docs.title: 6.4 Storage (WAL, segments, index, backup, crypto)
docs.text:
• Purpose: durable ordered log with seekability and maintenance loops.
  • Key files:
  • internal/storage/wal.go
  • internal/storage/segment.go
  • internal/storage/index.go
  • internal/storage/backup_scheduler.go
  • internal/storage/backup.go
  • internal/storage/crypto.go
  • pkg/utils/atomicfile.go
  • Main flow:
  • Append assigns offsets and writes WAL v2 records to the active segment; each record carries an 8-byte Raft term and a 4-byte trailing checksum, and the sparse index is updated.
  • Compaction runs through Partition.PruneWAL. Active events must be due, accepted, completed and exported; accepted terminal controls and superseded copies have no consumer obligation. Lifecycle partitions prune a prefix even when standalone. Optional --wal-relocation-bytes moves never-due work within a byte budget, waiting for acceptance before pruning an original copy.
  • In a cluster only the partition's leader prunes, and only from the start of the log; followers drop what lies below the leader's log start (FollowLogStart), and a replica whose log ends before it restarts its log there.
  • Backup scheduler checkpoints every partition at wall-clock multiples of --backup-interval and keeps backups for --backup-retention. cronos-admin restore copies a backup into an empty data directory, checking every file against the manifest; cronos-admin check-log reports (and with --repair cuts) a damaged segment.
  • Reliability decisions:
  • WAL v2 includes a Raft term and trailing checksum. Pre-v2 layouts are not automatically migrated; that is distinct from the capability-gated v0.8.0 upgrade of an existing v0.7.0 WAL. See the release upgrade notes.
  • CRC32 validation for integrity checks.
  • Default fsync mode is batch; every_event and periodic remain available for stricter or looser durability.
  • Critical metadata (transaction logs, encryption key files, backup manifests/checkpoints) is persisted via utils.AtomicWriteFile (temp file + fsync + rename + parent-dir fsync).
  • Optional encryption at rest with key-file managed segment cipher.

docs.title: 6.5 Scheduler (timing wheel + cold store)
docs.text:
• Purpose: time-accurate delivery scheduling at scale.
  • Key files:
  • internal/scheduler/timing_wheel.go
  • internal/scheduler/scheduler.go
  • internal/scheduler/cold_store.go
  • Main flow:
  • Near-future events stay in hot timing wheel.
  • Far-future events move to cold store and are hydrated as due time approaches.
  • Ready events are pushed to worker for dispatch.
  • Reliability decisions:
  • O(1) wheel operations for predictable behavior under load.
  • Adaptive hydrator intervals to balance IO and readiness.
  • Recovery path from WAL/checkpoints.

docs.title: 6.6 Deduplication (Rust bloom + Pebble fallback)
docs.text:
• Purpose: message idempotency and duplicate suppression.
  • Key files:
  • internal/dedup/store.go
  • internal/dedup/bloom_store.go
  • internal/dedup/pebble_store.go
  • internal/dedup/rust_bloom_unix.go
  • internal/dedup/rust_bloom_windows_cgo.go / internal/dedup/rust_bloom_nocgo.go
  • Main flow:
  • Fast probabilistic check first, persistent confirmation fallback when needed.
  • Store update keeps recent message IDs with TTL behavior.
  • Reliability decisions:
  • Two-tier design balances speed and correctness.
  • Persistent fallback prevents false-positive-only behavior from dropping valid messages.

docs.title: 6.7 Delivery (dispatcher, worker, retry, circuit breaker, DLQ)
docs.text:
• Purpose: robust subscriber delivery with backpressure and failure handling.
  • Key files:
  • internal/delivery/dispatcher.go
  • internal/delivery/worker.go
  • internal/delivery/retry_queue.go
  • internal/delivery/circuit_breaker.go
  • internal/delivery/dlq.go
  • internal/delivery/dlq_segment.go
  • Main flow:
  • Worker drains ready events and submits to dispatcher.
  • Dispatcher tracks credits, in-flight deliveries, and timeout/retry progression.
  • Failed deliveries escalate to retry queue and eventually DLQ.
  • Reliability decisions:
  • Circuit breaker isolates bad subscribers.
  • Non-blocking retry heap avoids hot-loop blocking.
  • DLQ segments preserve failure evidence for replay and forensics.

docs.title: 6.8 Consumer Groups and Offset Store
docs.text:
• Purpose: group membership and durable commit position tracking.
  • Key files:
  • internal/consumer/group.go
  • internal/consumer/offset_store.go
  • Main flow:
  • Subscribe/ack APIs feed into group manager.
  • Offsets, group metadata/assignments and per-event completions are persisted in the PebbleDB OffsetStore.
  • Reliability decisions:
  • Delivery ID parsing routes ack to correct partition path.
  • OffsetStore.CommitOffsetExactlyOnce (commit IDs) exists but is not called by the Ack path; --exactly-once-commits is refused in production.
  • The leader sends progress on changed maintenance ticks and at least every 30 s. Completions not yet transferred can be redelivered after failover. Lifecycle snapshots import progress with a consistent WAL generation; legacy RF=1 handoff does not provide that atomic state transfer.

docs.title: 6.9 Cluster Control Plane (membership, router, raft)
docs.text:
• Purpose: ownership, routing, and metadata consensus for distributed mode.
  • Key files:
  • internal/cluster/manager.go
  • internal/cluster/leadership.go — reconcileLocalLeadership, fenced elections (electNewLeader, fencedPositions), staged handoff (handoffMayStart, advanceTransfers), syncClusterState
  • internal/cluster/election.go — ChooseFailoverLeader, fallback used only without a replica-position source
  • internal/cluster/autoscaler.go — logs CPU, memory, disk and lag threshold warnings; changes nothing
  • internal/cluster/router.go
  • internal/cluster/membership.go
  • internal/cluster/transport.go — mutual TLS for the membership and Raft ports
  • internal/cluster/memberlist_adapter.go — not connected: the server refuses --use-memberlist
  • internal/cluster/raft.go
  • internal/cluster/hashring.go
  • Main flow:
  • Membership events update the ring, which proposes replicas and a preferred leader per partition.
  • The Raft-committed assignment is the only source of leadership: each node leads what is committed to it, follows what it is a replica of, and releases the rest (reconcileLocalLeadership). A partition with no committed assignment has no leader.
  • The Raft leader commits ring placement (syncClusterState). A move of a live leader is a staged handoff: the intent is committed, the leader refuses publishes, and leadership changes once the target's log ends at the same entry; a handoff that takes too long is abandoned.
  • A dead leader is replaced by a fenced election: the Raft leader first commits that the partition has no leader at a new epoch, asks the replicas where their logs end (ReplicationService.Position with fence_epoch; each replica refuses older leaders before it answers), and commits the most complete one at a higher epoch.
  • Each node logs under-replication for the partitions it leads (updateReplicaOffsets, noteInSync); the admin topology reads in-sync replicas from each partition's leader (ReplicationService.LeaderReport).
  • cronos-admin cluster remove-node <node-id> removes a node that is lost for good from Raft and from every node's member list; a running node is refused.
  • Reliability decisions:
  • Configured virtual nodes reduce leadership skew.
  • Join/rebalance includes state transfer hooks to avoid empty ownership.
  • Raft persistence via Bolt-backed log store.
  • Durable format requirements activate term-start commitment only after all assigned replicas, handoff targets and voters are capable. Lifecycle operations are separately opt-in and require majority acknowledgements. Requirements constrain future elections, placement and replacement voters; incompatible downgrade is unsupported.
  • Membership and Raft ports use the replication mTLS certificates; certificates, keys and CAs are re-read when their files change (internal/tlsfiles).

docs.title: 6.10 Cluster Rebalance Flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    NodeJoin[Node joins or leaves]
    Membership[Membership service emits event]
    Router[Router updates hash ring placement]
    RaftSync["Raft leader commits placement<br/>leader moves by staged handoff"]
    Promote["Each node acts on the committed assignment<br/>reconcileLocalLeadership"]
    Follower[Leader adds followers; followers catch up]
    Sync["Joining node: bulk snapshot install<br/>SyncPartitionFromLeader"]
    Healthy[Cluster converged]

    NodeJoin --> Membership --> Router --> RaftSync --> Promote --> Follower --> Healthy
    NodeJoin -.-> Sync -.-> Follower

docs.title: 6.11 Replication (intra-cluster and cross-region)
docs.text:
• Purpose: keep intra-cluster followers in sync for durability, and push events to remote regions for geo-resilience.
  • Key files:
  • internal/replication/leader.go — Leader.Replicate, Leader.catchUpFollower, FollowerInfo and ISR/quorum accounting.
  • internal/replication/follower.go — Follower.InstallSnapshot, Follower.dialCredentials.
  • internal/replication/mtls.go — MTLSConfig, BuildClientTLS (re-reads certificate, key and CA when their files change), BuildClientTLSConfig, BuildServerTLSConfig.
  • internal/replication/region.go — CrossRegionReplicator, per-region batched async push (experimental).
  • internal/api/replication_server.go — ReplicationServiceHandler.Append, .Sync, .Snapshot, .Position, .LeaderReport, .SyncConsumerProgress.
  • internal/api/internal_grpc_server.go — InternalGRPCServer on the dedicated internal listener (default :7947).
  • internal/api/crossregion_server.go — CrossRegionServiceServer.
  • internal/partition/manager.go — PartitionManager.SyncPartitionFromLeader (trigger for bulk install).
  • internal/cluster/manager.go — Manager.JoinCluster (calls SyncPartitionFromLeader on join; the cluster router also calls it during partition moves).
  • Main flow:
  • Happy path — Leader.Replicate(events) fans a contiguous batch out to connected followers. Legacy partitions use Append; term-start partitions use AppendTermStart, naming the formats, with no plain-append fallback. Requests carry offset/term matching and a batch CRC32.
  • Quorum — Leader.Replicate returns success to the client only after min-insync-replicas replicas including the leader have appended via WAL.AppendReplicatedBatch. In every_event and batch fsync modes a follower syncs the batch before it acknowledges (batch through group commit); only periodic acknowledges before the data is on disk, and production mode refuses periodic.
  • Incremental catch-up — when a follower reports NextOffset < events[0].Offset, Leader.catchUpFollower slices [from, to) from the leader's WAL into batchSize-sized chunks and replays them through Append. For very long ranges the leader also serves the server-streaming ReplicationService.Sync RPC.
  • Bulk install — Follower.InstallSnapshot(ctx, leaderAddr, partitionID, 0) dials the leader over the internal listener and calls ReplicationService.Snapshot. The leader flushes its active segment and streams each segment + sparse-index file with a ReplicationSnapshotHeader (per-file IEEE CRC32, first/last offset, file size, is_index) followed by 1 MB data chunks and a final trailer carrying {success, last_offset, epoch}. The follower stages files under <dataDir>/snapshot-staging/{segments,index}/ and checks every file's size and CRC32 against its header as it completes. An interrupted transfer resumes: staged files are reported to the leader, which answers unchanged ones with a reuse header. A trailer epoch below the epoch this replica has accepted is refused. WAL.InstallCheckpoint then swaps the logs under a journal (snapshot-install.state): old segments/index moved to *.old, staged dirs moved in, the new log loaded and verified, then *.old removed; a crash before completion restores the old log.
  • Trigger — bulk install is invoked by PartitionManager.SyncPartitionFromLeader under a 10-minute context, called from Manager.JoinCluster when a node joins and iterates its router.GetLocalPartitions(), and from the router during partition moves. After formation, Manager.reconcileLocalLeadership runs every 5s and idempotently wires up PromoteToLeader + AddFollower on every locally-led partition, which is what enables streaming Append on a healthy cluster.
  • Cross-region (experimental) — CrossRegionReplicator queues per region, batches (100 events / 100 ms), and pushes via CrossRegionService.ReplicateEvents. Best-effort, no ISR semantics. Runs only with --dev --experimental-features.
  • Reliability decisions:
  • Channel isolation — replication traffic runs over InternalGRPCServer (default :7947), a separate listener from the public API on :9000. Public clients cannot reach replication.
  • Per-batch CRC32 on ReplicationAppendRequest — computed by the leader and verified by the follower handler before anything is applied, along with each event's payload checksum and contiguous offsets.
  • Per-file CRC32 and size on ReplicationSnapshotHeader; the follower verifies every file and aborts on a mismatch, leaving the local log untouched.
  • Term fencing in ReplicationServiceHandler.Append: rejects req.Term < p.Epoch, rejects a second leader at the current term, and on a newer term persists it to epoch.json (stepping down first if this node was leading) before applying the sender's entries. Elections use fence epochs (fence_epoch on Position), so a replaced leader cannot gather confirmations once the replicas have answered.
  • Gap rejection — the handler rejects a batch whose ExpectedNextOffset does not match its first event and a batch that starts beyond the local log end ("log gap: catch-up required"); WAL.AppendReplicatedBatch also rejects non-contiguous offsets. Both drive leader-side catch-up.
  • Quorum durability — min-insync-replicas enforced before client ack. With RF=3 / minISR=2 the leader + at least one follower must ack; cluster degradation below minISR fails closed rather than silently succeeding on leader-only.
  • Commitment — replica counting alone cannot commit earlier-term entries. A term-start leader appends/fsyncs a current-term record and gets it onto the required replicas, including on idle partitions. Readers, held writes, pruning and export share this boundary. Mixed clusters retain legacy accounting until capability agreement.
  • Lifecycle recovery — snapshots transfer a validated recovery file bound to the WAL generation. Import clears old completions, makes dead letters durable, and syncs matching progress before serving; a crash after the WAL swap resumes that import on open.
  • Journaled swap during snapshot install — WAL closed before rename; every crash point recovers to one complete generation (RecoverSnapshot on WAL open).
  • mTLS between nodes — --replication-tls-enabled plus --replication-tls-{ca,cert,key}-file, all three required. The same certificates secure the membership and Raft ports (internal/cluster/transport.go). Server enforces tls.RequireAndVerifyClientCert; both sides pin against the cluster CA. Certificates, keys and CAs are re-read when their files change, so they are replaced without a restart. Follower.dialCredentials falls back to insecure credentials when the flag is off (intentional for --dev, refused by config.ValidateConfig in production).
  • Cross-region (experimental) is intentionally separate from intra-cluster — no ISR, last-write-wins conflict handling, fire-and-forget.
  • Trigger caveat — --snapshot-catchup-threshold (default 10000) is a dead config key (parsed, never read). Automatic mid-flight lag-driven InstallSnapshot is not wired; a far-behind connected follower still uses incremental Sync/Append catch-up.

docs.title: 6.12 Cross-Region Topology
docs.text:
Experimental: only with --dev --experimental-features and CRONOS_REGIONS.

flowchart TB
    subgraph RegionA
      ALeader[Leader Partition]
      AFollower1[Follower 1]
      AFollower2[Follower 2]
    end
    subgraph RegionB
      BIngress[CrossRegionService]
      BLeader[Leader Partition]
      BFollower[Follower]
    end

    ALeader -->|Change feed batch| BIngress
    BIngress -->|PublishBatch| BLeader
    BLeader -->|Replication Append| BFollower
    ALeader -->|Replication Append| AFollower1
    ALeader -->|Replication Append| AFollower2

docs.title: 6.13 Replay Engine
docs.text:
• Purpose: stream historical events by time or offset.
  • Key files:
  • internal/replay/engine.go
  • internal/api/handlers.go (Replay handler)
  • Main flow:
  • Replay query maps to partition WAL scans.
  • Results stream in chunks to avoid memory spikes.
  • Reliability decisions:
  • Context cancellation safe exits.
  • Optional follower-read support via config gate.
  • Public replay omits term-start records and emits only active lifecycle copies with internal metadata removed, bounded by the committed prefix. It is not a physical replica inventory.

docs.title: 6.14 Transactions (2PC coordinator)
docs.text:
• Purpose: multi-step prepare/commit orchestration with crash recovery. Experimental: TransactionService is registered only with --dev --experimental-features.
  • Key files:
  • internal/tx/coordinator.go
  • internal/tx/transaction_handler.go
  • Main flow:
  • tx.NewHandler(pm) injects PartitionManager so participants write durable markers.
  • PrepareTransaction executes prepare-only path.
  • Commit path proceeds from prepared state with idempotent behavior.
  • Reliability decisions:
  • Durable coordinator log (tx_log.json) for recovery replay.
  • Explicit state transitions reduce phase conflation bugs.

docs.title: 6.15 Transaction State Model
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Pending: BeginTransaction
    Pending --> Prepared: PrepareTransaction - all participants vote yes
    Pending --> Aborted: AbortTransaction or recovery timeout
    Pending --> Committing: CommitTransaction auto-prepares
    Prepared --> Committing: CommitTransaction
    Prepared --> Aborted: AbortTransaction
    Committing --> Committed: all commit callbacks succeed
    Committing --> Committing: callback failure; recovery retries
    Committed --> [*]
    Aborted --> [*]

docs.title: 6.16 Schema Registry and Compatibility
docs.text:
• Purpose: prevent unsafe payload evolution on topic contracts.
  • Key files:
  • internal/schema/registry.go
  • internal/schema/compatibility.go
  • internal/schema/avro.go
  • internal/schema/protobuf.go
  • Main flow:
  • Register schema version per topic.
  • Validate new versions against compatibility mode.
  • Publish path can enforce schema checks before storage.
  • Reliability decisions:
  • Type-aware validators and compatibility modes reduce deployment breakage.

docs.title: 6.17 Compliance, Retention, and Data Governance
docs.text:
• Purpose: automated data lifecycle enforcement and protected paths.
  • Key files:
  • internal/compliance/retention.go
  • internal/api/partition_handler.go (admin compaction/retention)
  • Main flow:
  • An hourly loop applies the max age and max size policies (--retention-max-age-hours, --retention-max-size-gb).
  • The retention enforcer parses each segment's header (firstOffset, createdTS) to pick candidates and always preserves the active segment per partition. It removes nothing itself: each candidate goes through the partition (PartitionManager.RemoveRetainedSegment then Partition.PruneWAL), with the same checks as compaction. In a cluster only the partition's leader removes segments, and only from the start of the log.
  • Matching .index files are deleted alongside reclaimed segments.
  • Partition admin RPC can trigger immediate retention and compaction actions.
  • Reliability decisions:
  • Protected directories are skipped to prevent accidental cleanup.
  • The enforcer honors context cancellation so shutdown does not leave partial deletes.
  • Admin actions return explicit success/error and reclaimed counters.

docs.title: 6.18 CDC (Change Data Capture)
docs.text:
• Purpose: stream write-side changes to external sinks.
  • Key files:
  • internal/cdc/sink.go
  • internal/cdc/kafka_sink.go
  • internal/cdc/webhook_sink.go
  • Main flow:
  • Each partition's change feed (internal/partition/changefeed.go) reads the log behind the accepted watermark and hands events over in log order, on the partition's leader only.
  • cdc.Manager.Deliver writes each batch to every sink in order and reports failure; the feed then offers the same events again.
  • The feed's position is stored per partition and sent to followers, so restarts and failovers continue it.
  • Reliability decisions:
  • Publishing never waits for a sink: a failing sink makes its partition's feed lag, and nothing is dropped.
  • Nothing queues in memory; events stay in the log until they are handed over.
  • Term-start controls advance feed cursors without being emitted. Lifecycle v1 refuses CDC and cross-region feeds: a raw publish sink has no mutation contract.

docs.title: 6.19 Auth and Audit
docs.text:
• Purpose: security and traceability.
  • Key files:
  • internal/auth/auth.go
  • internal/api/audit_interceptor.go
  • internal/audit/audit.go
  • Main flow:
  • Auth interceptors validate JWT and enforce policy.
  • Audit interceptor records important request actions.
  • Reliability decisions:
  • Auth enabled requires a valid policy; production requires auth and policy. --dev does not disable explicitly enabled authentication.
  • Audit writes are guarded for thread safety.

docs.title: 6.20 SLO, Metrics, and Tracing
docs.text:
• Purpose: operational visibility and target tracking.
  • Key files:
  • internal/slo/slo.go
  • internal/api/metrics.go
  • internal/tracing/tracing.go
  • internal/tracing/grpc_interceptor.go
  • Main flow:
  • Interceptors capture request latency and errors.
  • Recorder aggregates p95/p99 and error rates.
  • Prometheus endpoint and tracing exporters expose telemetry.
  • Reliability decisions:
  • Bounded recording windows prevent unbounded memory growth.
  • Tracing can degrade gracefully to no-op mode.

docs.title: 6.21 Tenant Resource Accounting
docs.text:
• Purpose: optional per-tenant accounting; limits are not runtime-configurable in the shipped server.
  • Key files:
  • internal/tenant/tenant.go
  • internal/api/handlers.go (tenant extraction and accounting hooks)
  • Main flow:
  • With limits configured, identity is the JWT subject (default without claims), and publishes use receipt-based reservations.
  • No production caller sets limits. Publishing skips the accountant and usage reports zero with limits_configured: false.
  • Reliability decisions:
  • Reservation/refund regressions cover the optional accountant; they do not enable quotas. See tenant architecture.

docs.title: 6.22 Admin Dashboard and CLI
docs.text:
• Purpose: operator-facing visibility and control without writing custom clients.
  • Key files:
  • internal/api/admin_handler.go — gRPC AdminService implementation (topology, partition health, replication lag, consumer groups, schemas, tenant usage, retention, compaction, rebalance).
  • internal/api/web_handler.go — HTTP JSON proxy for AdminService and SPA static file serving.
  • web/dashboard/* — React 19 + Vite admin dashboard, embedded via //go:embed.
  • cmd/admin/main.go — cronos-admin gRPC CLI.
  • Main flow:
  • The dashboard calls /api/admin/* endpoints served by the JSON proxy.
  • With auth disabled the proxy allows anonymous requests; with auth enabled, including in dev mode, it validates the bearer JWT and admin permission.
  • The dashboard polls topology/health/lag endpoints and renders snapshot bar charts for replication and consumer lag.
  • Reliability decisions:
  • The SPA is built into the Go binary, so the UI is always version-locked to the server.
  • Background refetches keep existing data visible to avoid scroll jumps.
  • Read-only accessors in internal/schema and internal/tenant limit the admin surface while reusing existing registries.

docs.title: 7.1 Operational Feedback Loops
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    WAL[WAL segments] --> Compaction["Compaction: segments whose events are<br/>finished by every group and exported"]
    WAL --> Retention["Retention by age and size<br/>through PruneWAL; leader-only in a cluster"]
    WAL --> Backup[Backup scheduler snapshots]
    Disk[Disk monitor threshold] --> Compaction
    Metrics[SLO and Prometheus metrics] --> Alerts["Alerting; autoscaler logs threshold warnings"]
    Traces[OpenTelemetry traces] --> Metrics
    Audit[Audit logs] --> Compliance[Compliance reviews]
    Retention --> Compliance

docs.title: 7.2 Reliability Matrix
docs.text:
• Durability:
  • WAL v2 (term + trailing checksum) + CRC32 + fsync modes + backup scheduler (cronos-admin restore) + atomic metadata writes.
  • Correctness:
  • Dedup, schema validation, epoch checks, current-term commitment and lifecycle recovery. Transactions remain experimental and unsupported in production.
  • Backpressure:
  • Credits, admission control, memory guard (--max-memory-percent), rate limiters and backpressure metrics. Per-tenant quotas are not configurable.
  • A restart schedules only future timers; due events are read from the log at consumer pace.
  • Events held back by flow control are redelivered from the WAL when credits return; redrive needs a connected subscriber (delivery.md, ARCHITECTURE known limitations).
  • Fault isolation:
  • Circuit breaker, retry queue, DLQ, service-level error boundaries.
  • Operability:
  • Health endpoints, metrics, tracing, audit logs, periodic stats, admin dashboard; topology ISR from each partition's leader (LeaderReport); cronos-admin cluster remove-node; certificate hot reload; HTTP TLS.
  • Gap (documented): TriggerRebalance admin RPC is a soft stub; membership-driven rebalance works (cluster.md).
  • Replication catch-up:
  • Join bulk snapshot + incremental follower catch-up.
  • Gap (documented): no mid-flight auto InstallSnapshot when lag exceeds threshold (replication.md).

docs.title: 8.1 "Publish succeeded but not delivered"
docs.text:
1. Check API validation and dedup path in internal/api/handlers.go.
  2. Confirm WAL append and offsets in internal/storage/wal.go.
  3. Check schedule timestamp and wheel placement in internal/scheduler/scheduler.go.
  4. Inspect worker/dispatcher flow in internal/delivery/worker.go and internal/delivery/dispatcher.go.
  5. Verify subscriber credits and ack behavior.

docs.title: 8.2 "Node ownership or routing looks wrong"
docs.text:
1. Inspect router assignments in internal/cluster/router.go.
  2. Check cluster member health in internal/cluster/membership.go.
  3. Verify raft metadata state in internal/cluster/raft.go and manager sync in internal/cluster/manager.go.
  4. Confirm virtual-nodes and replication settings in config.

docs.title: 8.3 "High duplicate rates or dedup false positives"
docs.text:
1. Review bloom capacity and TTL in config.
  2. Inspect dedup backend behavior in internal/dedup/bloom_store.go and internal/dedup/pebble_store.go.
  3. Validate message_id generation quality from producers.

docs.title: 8.4 "Replay inconsistent between nodes"
docs.text:
1. Check follower-read flag and ownership checks in replay path.
  2. Verify replication lag and ISR status.
  3. Compare partition high-watermarks and local WAL state.

docs.title: 9. Extension Points for Future Development
docs.text:
• New external sinks:
  • Add implementation under internal/cdc and register via startup wiring.
  • New auth policy backend:
  • Extend internal/auth policy layer and interceptor path.
  • New storage policy:
  • Extend WAL compaction/retention rules and backup integration.
  • New tenant controls:
  • Add policy dimensions in internal/tenant and enforce in handlers.
  • New cluster balancing strategy:
  • Extend hash ring weighting and move planner in internal/cluster.

docs.title: 10. Suggested Reading Order
docs.text:
For a developer new to the codebase:

  1. cmd/api/main.go (composition and lifecycle).
  2. internal/api/grpc_server.go (public API listener, interceptors), internal/api/internal_grpc_server.go (internal replication + Raft listener), and internal/api/handlers.go (entry points).
  3. internal/partition/manager.go (system core assembly).
  4. internal/storage/wal.go and internal/scheduler/scheduler.go (data and time model).
  5. internal/delivery/dispatcher.go and internal/consumer/group.go (delivery and ack semantics).
  6. internal/cluster/manager.go, router.go, raft.go (distributed control plane).
  7. internal/replication/* (leader/follower/mTLS/region) and internal/api/replication_server.go (advanced reliability paths).
  8. internal/compliance, internal/schema, internal/slo, internal/tracing (operational hardening).

If you keep this document open while stepping through cmd/api/main.go and the API handlers, every major production flow in CronosDB becomes straightforward to trace and reason about.

docs.title: Documentation review — 2026-10-21
docs.text: Reviewed the 47 Markdown documents tracked at release source ed7910fa85150d7e6701cf17bdcf37b3388a4883, plus the documentation build, release workflows, Helm settings and referenced source paths. This review aligns descriptions and examples with v0.8.0; it is not a new runtime security audit, fault campaign or capacity measurement. This report is the 48th Markdown document.

docs.title: Main corrections
docs.text:
• Replaced branch-only lifecycle status with the released, opt-in contract: stable references, revision/request-ID retries, majority acceptance, one-way capability agreement and recovery of matching WAL/progress/DLQ state.
  • Corrected replica-count-only commitment descriptions. Term-start proof is required before an older prefix becomes committed; mixed clusters retain the legacy limitation until all required nodes are capable.
  • Updated retention for accepted terminal records, prefix pruning and optional byte-bounded relocation. Unfinished due work and unresolved mutations remain blockers; relocation does not imply unconditional disk reclamation.
  • Updated Docker examples to 0.8.0 and its immutable manifest. Distinguished public image identity, the latest index, config digests and signed provenance. The image was published locally without a signed workflow attestation.
  • Corrected stale scheduler-memory descriptions, quota-enforcement claims, transaction state diagrams, append-error claim rollback, client endpoint advertisement and misleading data-directory upgrade instructions.
  • Preserved dated performance results and probe evidence. Added qualifications where an old result could be mistaken for current release validation.

docs.title: Per-document disposition
docs.text:
“Retained” means reviewed without a content change because the document is already qualified or has no release-specific claim to update. Historical findings and raw evidence retain their original results; closure notes describe subsequent fixes.

Document Disposition README Updated current image, lifecycle scope, timing/retention claims, flags and upgrade examples. Architecture Updated commitment, replication RPCs, retention, recovery, diagrams and limits. Developer guide Updated lifecycle/recovery flows, transaction states, auth and unwired tenant quotas. System-design guide Updated current-term proof, lifecycle qualification, physical identity, timer costs and snapshot triggers. Docker guide Updated image/digest, runnable image references, advertised endpoint, memory limits and upgrade options. Contributing Added strict docs build, protocol documentation expectations and current reading links. Security policy Retained latest-release support policy and private reporting route. PR template Added documentation-only category and strict build check. Code of conduct Retained community policy; no runtime/version claims. Release requirements Updated published artifacts, fixes versus gaps, scheduler memory, backup PVC and build prerequisites. v0.8.0 notes Recorded publication, image/config/index identity and absence of signed provenance. Lifecycle contract Updated released status, standalone development scope and durable activation. Term-start protocol Added release status and mixed-version activation qualification. v0.7.0 hardening Preserved results; qualified historical workflow and legacy snapshot behavior. September audit Updated closure date and later leadership, snapshot, DLQ, retention, memory, scan and release status. October audit Distinguished shipped runtime fixes from remaining release/capacity evidence. September publish measurements Preserved numbers and added explicit pre-v0.8.0 qualification. October throughput measurements Preserved matched v0.6.0/v0.7.0 results; no v0.8.0 extrapolation. Maintenance validation Qualified the historical recovery/retention path against lifecycle generations. July performance baseline Retained existing historical/invalid-result qualifications and comparison method. Throughput harness Distinguished available tooling from an executed release measurement. September probes Retained archived-probe versus ordinary-regression distinction and toolchain prerequisites. October probes Removed obsolete open-DLQ statement; distinguished historical overlays from current tests. Historical remediation plan Updated superseding references; retained historical checkboxes. Historical technical deep dive Added protocol references and qualified illustrative old code. Feature index Updated current hardening, lifecycle links, retention and deferred-feature claims. API Updated lifecycle RPCs, authorization, control visibility and append-error diagram. Audit logging Retained request-interceptor/auth-gated behavior and non-fatal initialization scope. Auth Added lifecycle query/mutation publish-permission requirement. CDC Updated committed/control cursors and lifecycle incompatibility. Cluster Added durable capability requirements for replicas, handoffs and voters. Compliance Added terminal-state and bounded relocation rules. Config Added missing flags, activation constraints, advertised endpoint and unused join setting. Consumer groups Added physical successor ACK and matching recovery-generation semantics. Dashboard Corrected quota availability and identified gRPC-only lifecycle operations. Dedup Distinguished publish TTL/claims from lifecycle identity and request recovery. Delivery Added staged/accepted-state gate, stale-timer suppression and recall limits. Partition Added lifecycle index, term-start and recovery-state ownership. Replay Added committed-boundary and active logical-view semantics. Replication Updated format-specific RPCs, commitment proof, snapshots and relocation. Scheduler Added lifecycle delivery gate and internal-record suppression. Schema Retained registry, compatibility and optional publish-validation flow. SLO/metrics Retained bounded recording and external operational feedback scope. Storage Updated terminal records, prefix pruning, relocation, backup cuts and logical identity. Tenant accounting Retained explicit absence of runtime quota configuration and zero-usage behavior. Tracing Retained startup/shutdown and disabled/sampled exporter behavior. Transactions Added lifecycle incompatibility; retained experimental status and actual state names.

Raw audit .txt evidence, archived .go.txt probes and benchmark output were not rewritten. The embed-placeholder README was checked against the build flow; it remains build guidance, not a rendered dashboard asset. MkDocs navigation now exposes the lifecycle contract, commitment protocol and this review.

docs.title: Verification scope
docs.text:
Validation of this documentation change:

  • python -m mkdocs build --strict --site-dir build/docs-audit-v080-site.
  • 826 relative documentation/source/asset targets checked; none missing.
  • Both flag tables cover all 95 flags registered by the server, with no unknown table entries.
  • All 67 embedded Mermaid diagrams parsed with Mermaid 11.17.2; the 10 changed diagrams also rendered successfully.
  • Anonymous registry checks confirmed the documented v0.8.0 manifest and the single Linux amd64 entry selected by latest on 2026-10-21.
  • git diff --check; historical finding bodies and raw evidence preserved.

The review checks documentation, examples, source-path references, flag coverage and diagram syntax against the release source. The strict site build validates the generated documentation and cross-page anchors. These checks do not rerun the runtime suites or refresh the dated vulnerability scan. Required runtime CI still applies to the pull request.

Remaining product and validation gaps are maintained in release requirements. This review does not assert that all major issues are fixed.

docs.title: Merge-gate follow-up
docs.text:
The PR's current dependency scans found a Go standard-library certificate advisory, Vite's bundled launch-editor advisories, and CVE-2026-63209 in github.com/klauspost/compress after the documentation review. The merge follow-up raises Go to 1.26.10 in the module and image builder, Vite's minimum to 7.3.7, the compression dependency to v1.18.7, and the active build prerequisites accordingly. The image scan failed before container and chart startup tests ran; those tests must still pass on the patched source. Dated measurements and released artifact identities remain historical. A new patch release is needed to distribute the updated build; see v0.8.0 publication record and the v0.8.1 patch notes.

The Go race job also reported an intermittent first-delivery acknowledgement failure. Investigation found that a live subscription could be exposed before its consumer group was created. The follow-up initializes group membership before publishing the subscription to the dispatcher, while rejecting duplicate subscription IDs before changing membership. Controlled regression tests cover an event becoming due during group initialization, rejected initialization, and duplicate registration. A public API test also checks server-assigned partition membership and its first acknowledgement. The isolation test now includes the client's last acknowledgement refusal in its failure diagnostics.

A later non-cgo CI failure exposed a deduplication lookup gap during background flush. The store now keeps pending IDs visible until the Pebble commit succeeds, using the same flush path for timer, single-write and batch-write flushes. A paused-write regression checks existence, offset and timestamp lookups during successful and failed commits; the concurrent-access test now checks write errors and every accepted ID instead of one sample.

docs.title: v0.7.0 hardening
docs.text:
These changes implement the remaining findings of the October audit. They were released as v0.7.0 on 2026-10-17.

This is the dated v0.7.0 record; its measurements are not v0.8.0 results. The v0.8.0 notes describe current-term commitment, opt-in event mutations/relocation, and lifecycle snapshots that bind progress and dead letters to a WAL generation. Those supplement the legacy snapshot path described here. The original release automation command below refers to the v0.7.0 workflow; current manual runs stage an archive unless publish_image=true is explicit.

docs.title: Resource and recovery behavior
docs.text:
The scheduler shares a 64 MiB payload budget across partitions, configurable with --scheduler-memory / CRONOS_SCHEDULER_MEMORY. Overflow is stored as timestamp/offset references and reloaded in bounded pages. This is a scheduler allocation estimate, not a process RSS limit. Worker queues, Pebble, in-flight requests and a transient record read use additional memory.

Dedup recovery uses dedup/recovery.json as a durable replay boundary, validated against the WAL entry's term and message ID. It is written after pending IDs and Pebble tables are flushed. An absent or mismatched checkpoint causes a scan of the retained log, without the old 500,000-event cutoff. Unreadable checkpoints or recovery failures stop admission/startup/promotion rather than serving incomplete dedup state.

Batch quota reservations exclude duplicate retries. Both publish methods return reservations on a definite failure before append. Appended operations retain their reservation and dedup claim while their original publish completes.

docs.title: Completion and dead-letter replication
docs.text:
Sparse consumer completions transfer in pages of at most 4,096 offsets. Each follower has its own cursor and retries failed pages. Version changes and periodic refreshes catch additions behind a cursor. A follower that catches up with the event log receives progress again.

Dead letters transfer from the durable journal, including payloads evicted from the in-memory queue and removal tombstones. Pages contain at most 256 records, normally around 512 KiB; a single larger record can exceed that byte target. Replicas sync records before acknowledging, apply retries idempotently, and encrypt the local copy with their configured key. Completion pages are withheld until the follower has the corresponding dead-letter journal. Retention waits for every assigned follower to acknowledge it. Replicas missing dead-letter state are excluded from the leader's in-sync report. A new replica cannot skip the retained log boundary until its journal is durable. Bulk snapshots transfer journal pages before installing the WAL; a failed journal write leaves the existing WAL in place.

The journal is retained, including removal history. Replay and idempotence metadata grow with its history; journal compaction is not added by this change. Corruption blocks transfer and consequently retention until repaired. Backups remain necessary.

During a rolling upgrade, an older follower cannot provide the new durable acknowledgement. Once dead letters exist, the new leader holds completion transfer and retention for that follower until it is upgraded or removed from the replica assignment. Event replication continues within the follower's existing log coverage. A follower missing the discarded prefix cannot advance past it, and bulk snapshots with dead-letter history require an upgraded receiver. An older leader cannot supply the new guarantee; finish upgrading the cluster before relying on replicated dead-letter recovery.

docs.title: Discovery and disk operations
docs.text:
A node started with --advertise-grpc-addr (CRONOS_ADVERTISE_GRPC_ADDR) gives clients that address in partition metadata; the Helm chart sets it to each pod's DNS name with service.advertisePodAddress=true. Clients learn added nodes, retire obsolete discovered connections and retain explicit NodeIDToAddress overrides. Responses from older servers preserve endpoints already learned. A node started without the flag advertises nothing, and clients reach it through the addresses they were configured with, as before. Advertise addresses reachable from clients, and covered by the client port's certificate when TLS is on, or configure overrides when using proxies.

Before the release, metadata named each node's cluster gRPC address (--cluster-grpc-addr), where replication and Raft are served. A client sent there was refused with "unknown service cronos_db.EventService", or at the TLS handshake when the nodes use mutual TLS. The acceptance tests did not notice: in containers they configure NodeIDToAddress, and as processes a refused handshake made the client try another node. The image check of the release found it, and TestClientsFindTheOtherNodesThroughPartitionMetadata now publishes to every partition through a client given one node.

Full followers reject new log growth while still handling retries of matching entries already on disk. cronos_retention_blocking_offset and cronos_retention_blocking_age_seconds expose the oldest observed retention blocker by partition and reason: unaccepted, change_feed, future_schedule, consumer_completion, or dead_letter_replication. An offset of -1 means no blocker was observed in the last pass.

Set Helm backupPersistence.enabled=true for a separate per-pod backup PVC mounted at /backups; size, mount path, access mode and storage class are configurable. Choose storage in a separate failure domain and preserve the claims during recovery. A second PVC alone does not protect against loss of its storage backend.

docs.title: Release automation
docs.text:
The release workflow needs GitHub repository secrets DOCKERHUB_USERNAME and DOCKERHUB_TOKEN, with push access to johnny711dock/cronos-db. It runs when a GitHub release is published, or with:

gh workflow run release.yml --ref v0.7.0 -f tag=v0.7.0

The image job requires the tag's commit on main and the workflow's source commit to match it. It builds one linux/amd64 image, scans for fixable HIGH/CRITICAL vulnerabilities, and runs both container acceptance tests. It then pushes a run-specific candidate tag, records the registry digest, creates signed provenance with GitHub's attestation action, and publishes the release tag from the same image. IMAGE_DIGEST, scan results and test logs preserve the evidence. It does not move latest.

For v0.7.0 the repository did not have the two secrets, so the image job could build, scan and test the image but not push it. The v0.7.0 image was built from the tagged commit, scanned and started as three nodes by hand, and pushed by hand as 0.7.0 and latest, as for v0.6.0. It has no signed provenance.

CI also audits the locked Rust dependencies. The publication job performs container acceptance and image scanning in Linux CI before registry publication and signing. Local workflow lint alone does not establish those results.

docs.title: Validation and release gates
docs.text:
Local validation on 2026-10-16 includes all 33 Go test packages (Windows amd64, cgo disabled), focused race checks for the changed scheduler, completion, dedup, discovery, quota and dead-letter paths, workflow lint, strict documentation build, and chart assertions for persistent/ephemeral data with and without a separate backup PVC. The dead-letter regression covers loss of the original leader after WAL retention, replacement catch-up through a snapshot, failed journal writes and mixed-version acknowledgement.

These local results come from separate runs. The required GitHub production checks passed on the pull request that took the release to main.

The process acceptance runs passed node faults, certificate/CA rotation, overload refusal, lost-node removal, first-node replacement, backlog recovery and topology convergence after a node was killed and restarted. The overload run delivered all 6,315 acknowledged events. Process backlog recovery delivered all 11,365 acknowledged events with peak observed memory of 111 MiB against a 142 MiB configured limit.

The Linux image passed the container network-partition test with all 2,742 acknowledged events delivered. Its memory-limited restart test accepted 16,371 events of 64 KiB (about 1 GiB), restarted every node, and delivered every acknowledged event. Peak observed memory from restart through delivery was 208 MiB per node against the kernel-enforced 384 MiB limit, with no OOM kill. Thirteen initial publishes failed during cluster formation and are excluded from the acknowledged-event guarantee.

Backup restore passed after every node and data directory was lost. All events acknowledged before the selected backup cut were present in the restored logs, and the cluster accepted new work and rejected an earlier ID as a duplicate. Forty-five of the 60 previously delivered events were redelivered, which is permitted by the at-least-once backup contract.

The local Linux image also passed Trivy 0.75.0 with no fixable HIGH/CRITICAL findings at scan time; this is a thresholded scan, not a claim that the image has no vulnerabilities. The scan report identifies local image sha256:fc47a6380e8f5355825f98f2fc5f9e22a18cb89d8a33cb7bff5ca21e74b4d76b.

The process overload test intentionally raises the scheduler budget so it reaches the process memory guard. With the default budget, this workload spills to disk and need not reject publishes merely because the accepted backlog exceeds RAM.

The initial single-node Windows publish benchmark was slower after the change: three-sample medians were about 21.7k versus 40.8k events/s on the first-batch baseline. These short runs overlapped other validation, varied substantially, and accumulate a backlog without a consumer; the bounded scheduler starts spilling while the baseline keeps payloads in memory. This is a performance concern to investigate, not evidence that the audit's RF=3/minISR=2 durable-capacity comparison passed. Three-node runs with production TLS, authentication and encryption were later matched against v0.6.0 on the same Windows host, with every accepted event checked as delivered: the rates were level, within the variance of that host (record). Matched Linux runs, multi-host runs and real power loss are not established; v0.7.0 was released without them.

The GitHub repository secrets DOCKERHUB_USERNAME and DOCKERHUB_TOKEN were still absent at release. Configure them before relying on the image publication job; no signed v0.7.0 image exists.

docs.title: WAL maintenance and pipeline validation — 2026-09-29
docs.text:
This is a dated record of the pre-lifecycle maintenance path, with its noted October follow-ups. Current v0.8.0 lifecycle backups/snapshots additionally bind consumer progress, dead letters, epoch and accepted boundary to the WAL cut; optional bounded relocation changes which future copies can be pruned. See the lifecycle contract and release requirements. The measurements below are not new v0.8.0 validation results.

This change fixes the backup path, unsafe live-file retention, and a WAL rotation offset defect exposed while testing retention. Existing unrelated working-tree hardening changes were preserved.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
• Scheduled backups capture every loaded partition into backups/backup-*/partitions/<id>, laid out like the partition's data directory: the WAL including its active segment, consumer groups with their offsets and completion records, the dedup store, the dead-letter queue, and the fencing epoch (updated 2026-10-06; earlier generations hold the WAL only). backup.json lists the partitions, their last offsets, and the size and CRC-32 of every file. A generation becomes visible only when every partition succeeds. Failed attempts do not expire previous backups. Shutdown waits for active backup and retention work before closing the WAL.
  • A partition is captured while it serves traffic, in an order that makes the result safe to restore: the log is copied last, so the other stores describe a slightly older moment than the log and never a newer one. A restored node may deliver again what was completed just before the backup. It cannot hold a completion or dedup record for an offset its log does not contain, which would silently drop the next event given that offset.
  • Each generation is independent. With the node stopped, cronos-admin restore --from <backup-dir> --data-dir <dir> checks every file against the manifest and restores all partitions or none; it refuses a data directory that already holds one of them. Start the node on the restored directory and provide the original key for encrypted data; timers are rebuilt from the log. Tests restore plaintext and encrypted logs after later source writes, a whole partition's state into a fresh node, and damaged, incomplete and misplaced backups.
  • Since 2026-10-07 the logs of all partitions on a node are cut at one instant, recorded as cut_at in the manifest, and scheduled backups start at wall-clock multiples of the interval, so the nodes of a cluster take theirs at the same moment as far as their clocks agree. For an encrypted log the manifest carries a value that identifies the key without containing it; cronos-admin restore --encryption-key-file checks the key against it before anything is written, and a wrong key leaves the data directory untouched.
  • A backup holds no key material, credentials or Raft metadata. It does not need the last: when a restored cluster forms, placement is recomputed, each partition is first led by the replica with the most complete log, and epochs continue above those stored with the data. The backups of different nodes remain separate copies that agree only as closely as the schedule and the clocks do, which is why the most complete replica leads.
  • A whole cluster has been restored from its backups (TestClusterRestoredFromBackups in tests/acceptance, run in CI). Three server processes take their backups while publishes keep arriving, so the three copies of a partition do not end at the same entry. Every node is then killed and its data directory removed, each node is restored from its own backup with cronos-admin restore, and the nodes are started. The test checks that every publish acknowledged before the earliest of the three backups is in the restored logs, that the three replicas of every partition hold the same log, that events which were waiting for their time are delivered at that time and not before, that an ID accepted before the backup is still refused as a duplicate, and that the cluster accepts and delivers new events. In the runs so far none of the events that had been finished before the backup was delivered again. Publishes acknowledged after a node's backup are lost with the cluster; that is what a backup means.
  • --backup-interval, --backup-retention and --backup-dir set how often backups are taken, how long they are kept and where they go. The default location is on the data volume, which protects against mistakes and damage, not against the loss of that volume: point --backup-dir at another volume or copy the backups away.
  • Automatic compaction and both admin APIs use the live WAL's deletion lock. Every event must be past due and have a per-event completion record in every matching assigned consumer group. No matching group means keep the event. Cursor overrides and Force do not override this protection. Corrupt or incomplete segments fail verification; the active segment is always retained.
  • Clustered/replicated pruning was refused when this was written. Since 2026-10-07 the leader of a replicated partition removes finished segments from the start of its log and the other replicas follow it; see the storage and replication notes. A replica that does not lead still refuses to prune by its own decision. Size limits remain best-effort: protected data can exceed them; admission/disk-pressure controls remain responsible for rejecting more writes.
  • WAL rotation now derives the next segment's first offset from the last record actually written. Reservations by concurrent writers and speculative creation previously produced incorrect segment boundaries. Speculative segment creation was removed; rotation may incur synchronous creation latency.

docs.title: Correctness checks
docs.text:
Regression tests cover complete independent backups, active tails, encryption, concurrent checkpoint/appends, failed backup publication, shutdown waiting, retention accounting, topic/group isolation, future/unacknowledged events, nonzero partition IDs, and cancellation/corruption protection.

TestMaintenanceConcurrentRotationPreservesEveryAcceptedOffset failed before the rotation fix (offset gap: got 4 want 7) and passes after it, including a WAL reopen and a ledger of all accepted IDs. The gRPC pipeline regression publishes, delivers and ACKs 64 unique events, checks durable completion, takes a checkpoint, prunes completed records, and verifies that a future timer remains readable.

The CDC tests were rewritten on 2026-10-07 for ordered, retryable delivery: order across sinks, a failing sink resuming without the others receiving anything twice, and refusal after shutdown.

docs.title: Throughput method
docs.text:
The publish benchmark now creates routable partitions, uses unique message IDs, applies its concurrency parameter, rejects partial/duplicate/failed batches, and excludes shutdown from timing. Both before and after binaries use this identical harness with real partition deduplication. The original harness could benchmark rejected or duplicate requests as apparent throughput.

Comparison uses Windows/amd64, Go 1.26.7, CGO disabled, four Go execution threads, four publisher goroutines, 256-byte payloads, batches of 1,000, and five samples of two seconds each for batch and periodic fsync. This measures single-node SDK/gRPC publish acceptance through dedup, WAL and scheduling; delivery correctness is checked separately. It does not establish replicated cluster capacity or production tail latency during large checkpoint copies.

Capture matching logs with:

$env:GOARCH = 'amd64'
$env:CGO_ENABLED = '0'
go test ./internal/api -run '^$' -bench '^BenchmarkPublishBatch_EndToEnd_Matrix/fsync=(periodic|batch)$/payload=256B$/batch=1000$/par=1$' -benchtime=2s -count=5 -cpu=4 -benchmem -timeout 180s
python scripts/check-publish-throughput.py before.txt after.txt --max-regression-percent 10

The comparison script checks matching configurations and successful benchmark runs, then compares medians. Raw local logs and compiled before/after binaries are under build/maintenance-validation/ (ignored build artifacts).

docs.title: Follow-up: dedup completion batching
docs.text:
Accepted publish batches now finalize their dedup offsets with one Pebble batch commit instead of one Put per event. Pending claims remain visible until the commit succeeds; the completion test checks offsets after closing and reopening the store. The offline retention test now expects a deleted WAL segment's matching sparse index to be removed while unrelated index and system metadata survive.

GOARCH=amd64 CGO_ENABLED=0 go test ./... -timeout 180s passed. Five paired two-second samples on this machine yielded median accepted-event rates:

Mode Before batching After batching Change batch 124,577 events/s 121,630 events/s -2.37% periodic 191,507 events/s 206,497 events/s +7.83%

The 10% regression gate passed. A saved pre-maintenance binary rerun in the same session measured 119,166 and 186,364 events/s, respectively. Earlier pre-maintenance logs were considerably faster than both paired runs; the machine's absolute rate varied, so this is evidence for the paired local check, not a precise capacity estimate. Logs are current-before.txt, current-after.txt, and current-old-binary.txt in the build directory above. The dedup completion and gRPC publish/deliver/ACK maintenance regressions also passed with the race detector after placing the staged Rust DLL on Windows PATH.

docs.title: CronosDB Performance Baseline
docs.text:
This document records the write-path throughput baseline used to validate the Tier 3 optimizations in July 2026, before v0.3.0.

Historical numbers. They were measured on one Windows laptop with Go 1.25.0 at commit bbf37d7, and the code has changed a great deal since (group commit in batch mode, per-entry terms, encryption v2, quorum replication). Use them to see the shape of the costs, not as current figures. A change to the write path is compared with benchstat against the same benchmarks run on its own base commit, as described under How to Compare a Change. Later dated measurements are in the three-node throughput validation of 2026-10-16, the three-node validation of 2026-09-29 and the maintenance validation. No throughput or latency figure is promised for a release (release requirements).

docs.title: Environment
docs.text: Item Value Date 2026-07-10 Git SHA bbf37d7fda3c728b697e536d88b395da49ebe438 (Tier 3 patches applied on top) Go version go1.25.0 windows/amd64 OS Windows 11 (win32 10.0.26200) CPU AMD Ryzen 7 6800H Disk Local NVMe SSD

docs.title: Benchmark Commands
docs.text:
Run the benchmarks with the same flags used to generate the baseline:

# WAL plaintext, focused matrix
$ go test ./internal/storage/ \
  -bench='BenchmarkWAL_AppendBatch_Matrix/(fsync=every_event|fsync=batch|fsync=periodic)/payload=4KB/(batch=1|batch=10|batch=100|batch=1000)/par=1$' \
  -benchtime=100ms -count=3 -run=^$

# WAL encrypted
$ go test ./internal/storage/ \
  -bench='BenchmarkWAL_AppendBatch_Encrypted_Matrix/(fsync=every_event|fsync=batch)/payload=4KB/(batch=100|batch=1000)/par=1$' \
  -benchtime=100ms -count=3 -run=^$

# End-to-end gRPC PublishBatch
$ go test ./internal/api/ \
  -bench='BenchmarkPublishBatch_EndToEnd_Matrix/(fsync=every_event|fsync=batch)/(payload=64B|payload=4KB)/(batch=1|batch=100|batch=1000)/par=1$' \
  -benchtime=100ms -count=3 -run=^$

Note: the $ suffix in the parallelism part of the regex is required to anchor the end of the sub-benchmark name (before the -GOMAXPROCS display suffix). Without it, par=1 would also match par=16 because the latter starts with par=1.

docs.title: 1. FsyncBatch is now a true per-request group commit
docs.text:
The old implementation treated batch and periodic identically: both relied on the background flush loop. After Tier 3 #12, batch syncs on every append. Since 2026-10-06 the flush and the fsync both happen after the WAL lock is released, and writers that append while a sync is in flight share the next one; the numbers below predate that change. This means:

  • batch=1 is now event-level durable (like every_event) and is much slower than the old batch=1 number, which was not actually syncing.
  • batch and periodic are no longer comparable; periodic remains the highest-throughput mode with a small loss window, while batch is the recommended durable-high-throughput mode and is now the default.
  • Use every_event for maximum durability; periodic gives the most throughput, and production mode refuses it: an acknowledged event is only in memory on the replicas until the next flush.

docs.title: 2. Encrypted writes use record cipher v2 (random nonce)
docs.text:
AES-256-GCM AEAD is cached per partition. WAL record encryption v2 embeds a fresh random 12-byte GCM nonce per record ([version=2][nonce][ciphertext]). This removes the historical v1 counter-nonce collision class (same key reused at the same position across rotated segments). Legacy v1 records remain decryptable with the partition+position-derived nonce for backward read compatibility.

Random nonces cost a small amount of entropy and header bytes per record; fsync still dominates single-threaded throughput. The win of caching AEAD is most visible under concurrent writers (lower allocs/op and GC pressure).

docs.title: 3. Index fsync is out of the write hot path
docs.text: The segment index Sync() every 100 entries was moved to the background flush loop. The index is reconstructable from the segment, so this is a safe durability/performance trade-off. Single-threaded numbers are unchanged; the benefit is lower p99 under concurrent writers.

docs.title: 4. gRPC PublishBatch dedup is batched
docs.text: PublishBatch now calls IsDuplicateBatch per partition instead of IsDuplicate per event, and the partitionEvents grouping map is recycled via sync.Pool. End-to-end throughput improved by roughly 10–15% on the publish path.

docs.title: 5. CRC implementation unchanged
docs.text: A benchmark of klauspost/crc32 versus the standard library showed no consistent win; Go's hash/crc32 is already hardware-accelerated on amd64. The mmap growth policy (1 GiB pre-allocation, doubling on remap) was also left unchanged after verification.

docs.title: 6. Production hardening overhead is off the hot path
docs.text:
Recent production-hardening changes add durability and correctness metadata but do not materially reduce throughput:

  • WAL v2 stores an 8-byte Raft term and a 4-byte trailing checksum per record. The extra bytes are appended outside the fsync lock and checksum verification happens on recovery and replication, not on the append fast path.
  • The retention enforcer runs as a background loop and reads only the 64-byte segment header to decide eligibility; it does not scan record contents.
  • CDC and cross-region replication read a per-partition change feed behind the accepted watermark; nothing runs on the append path. A slow sink makes its feed lag; it neither drops events nor slows publishes. With no sink and no region configured, publishes are not tracked for the feed at all.

docs.title: How to Compare a Change
docs.text:
1. Capture the current baseline: 
    go test ./internal/storage/ -bench=... -benchtime=100ms -count=3 -run=^$ > before.txt
  2. Apply the change and capture again: 
    go test ./internal/storage/ -bench=... -benchtime=100ms -count=3 -run=^$ > after.txt
  3. Use benchstat (golang.org/x/perf/cmd/benchstat): 
    benchstat before.txt after.txt
  4. Include the benchstat output in the commit/PR description.

docs.text: # Optimization Expected delta Measured delta Primary benchmark 12 Real FsyncBatch group commit True per-request durability; batch≡periodic removed batch now durable per request; large batches faster than every_event BenchmarkWAL_AppendBatch_Matrix/fsync=batch/... 13 Cache AES-GCM AEAD + random 12-byte nonce per record (cipher v2) Fewer allocs, lower CPU per record Allocs reduced; throughput neutral-to-slightly-better at par=1. Note: v2 uses a fresh random nonce per record, not a counter nonce — the counter nonce survives only for legacy v1 decryption (see §2) BenchmarkWAL_AppendBatch_Encrypted_Matrix/... 14 Decouple index fsync from WAL lock Lower p99, higher par=16 throughput par=1 unchanged; high-concurrency p99 expected to improve BenchmarkWAL_AppendBatch_Matrix/.../par=16 15 PublishBatch pooling + batched dedup Lower allocs/op in gRPC path ~11% geomean latency reduction, ~13% geomean throughput gain (count=3) BenchmarkPublishBatch_EndToEnd_Matrix/... 16 Vectorized CRC + mmap growth tuning TBD; only swap if benchstat wins No change; stdlib already hardware-accelerated; mmap policy unchanged BenchmarkWAL_AppendBatch_Matrix/...

docs.title: CronosDB production readiness audit
docs.text: Date: 2026-09-27. Audited commit: 2d87a133dff7fa863a2210a8be3e6345b8a82f08.

docs.title: Status of the findings — reviewed for v0.8.0 on 2026-10-21
docs.text: The audit itself (from "Verdict" on) describes commit 2d87a13 and is kept as it was. The closure table tracks v0.8.0; the nine hardening batches that follow record earlier work through v0.6.0. Current release scope and remaining gaps are in the release requirements.

docs.title: Finding closure review
docs.text:
The remediation program is incomplete. The table distinguishes released fixes from remaining product and validation gaps as of v0.8.0. The original v0.6.0 closure assessment has been updated where later releases changed it. It compares the code with each finding's full required outcome. "Core fix implemented" means the specific code defect has been addressed; it does not mean its production release validation is complete. "Partial" means material requirements remain. The evidence is the test suite, and since the third batch also fault injection: the acceptance fault campaign against three server processes and the partition tests between containers, both in CI, and the production chart in a disposable Kubernetes cluster. What a release promises, and what v0.6.0 was released without, is in the release requirements.

Follow-up in v0.9.0: version-2 closed segments have durable boundary evidence in their successor's header, and recovery fails closed on a mismatch, including a zeroed tail with no index. A verified later indexed record also detects some damage in the active tail. Version-1 WALs are rejected rather than migrated. See closed segment boundaries for the clean-start requirement, backup behavior and recovery limits.

Finding Status Implemented work and remaining requirement F01: topic isolation Partial Replay and recipient topic filters, group topic checks, and ACK principal validation added. Two principals are now tested through the public API with authentication on, each with one topic and both topics in one partition: neither can publish to, subscribe to or replay the other's topic, a replay of one's own topic over the shared log returns only its events, both consume at once and receive exactly their own, one cannot join the other's consumer group, and one cannot acknowledge a delivery made to the other. Remaining: consumer groups are named in one space shared by all principals, so a principal can take a group name before another does; there is no tenant scope beyond topics. F02: policy loading Fixed with startup regressions Invalid/missing policy and public-key loading fail before data stores/listeners are initialized. Subprocess tests cover missing, empty, malformed, empty-subject, and null-subject policies. F03: ACK correctness Partial Tracked-delivery validation, per-event completion, and partition-local manager use added. Acks on a stream are recorded in batches with one durable write, outside the group lock. A group's completed work is a durable floor plus the completions above it, and the partition leader sends that progress to its followers, so a follower that takes over does not redeliver finished work, including work finished out of order (tested end to end over the replication channel). Progress reaches followers on the leader's maintenance tick, so what completed in the last moments before a failover can be delivered again; a replication-factor-1 handoff does not move it; an ACK concurrency test through the public RPC remains. F04: delivery/backpressure Partial Worker and scheduler ready-slice ownership, worker count/64 MiB estimated-byte budget, WAL redrive, and unsent-group reservation cleanup added. Held-back, dropped, and abandoned deliveries are queued for redrive by offset range and follow acks; a connecting consumer drains its backlog at credit pace instead of a fixed 512 events/s; dead-lettered events are recorded complete. Regressions cover exhausted credits, worker overflow, disconnect, and backlog. Publishes are now refused while the process holds 80% of its own memory limit (the container's, when there is one), and the Go client reports that as overloaded instead of opening its circuit breaker. The guard that was there compared the whole machine's memory use with a percentage, which says nothing inside a container, and was off by default. Byte bounds on the queues themselves and an accepted-ID conservation ledger remain. Recovery no longer reads the undelivered backlog into memory at a start, the reads of the log are bounded by bytes, and a test restarts three nodes with a backlog larger than their memory limit (eighth batch). F05: timer recovery Partial WAL reconstruction, overdue cold hydration, and promotion scheduling added. Pending-timer preservation now tested through three consecutive snapshot/restart cycles; complete recovery/completion behavior remains to be validated. F06: replication retries Core fix implemented A replica accepts one leader per epoch and records it durably before applying any of its entries; entries carry their term on the wire; an existing entry is replaced only when its term differs from the leader's, never within a term; a superseded leader steps down. Tests cover two leaders claiming one term, replacement of a divergent tail, same-term conflicts, step-down, and a leader change concurrent with appends. A same-term content conflict is rejected and needs a snapshot to reconcile. Every append now names the entry it follows and that entry's term; a replica that holds a different entry there refuses the append and says where its log stops agreeing, and the leader resends from that point.
