docs.title: F20 — Medium, release gate: existing tests and release automation miss the failure boundaries
docs.text:
Evidence: repository inspection and test results.

Only documentation publishing is configured under .github/workflows. A local Makefile target is not an enforced release gate. Existing tests frequently check individual components without verifying accepted-event conservation through restart or failover. A DLQ test expecting an empty result after removal can pass even if all entries fail to load. Snapshot metadata tests do not establish restoration of pending timers. Rust currently has no executed tests.

The chaos material does not establish an end-to-end ledger of accepted IDs and consumed/expired/dropped IDs. Applying a fake clock to a helper command does not demonstrate skew in the running database process. Existing performance results cannot substitute for throughput measured with the intended auth, encryption, replication, consumers and recovery behavior enabled.

Sources: .github/workflows, Makefile, tests, dedup Rust, audit probe results.

Required: CI for Go checks, cgo/race on Linux, dashboard tests/build, actual chart startup, dependency scans, and deterministic failure tests. Gate releases on recovery of identified accepted records, bounded resource use and a successful independent restore.

docs.title: Hardening order
docs.text:
1. Constrain the first supported product. Fixed partitions, one defined telemetry delivery policy, explicit loss/retention limits. Keep transactions, online split, and optional CDC/cross-region paths disabled until separately verified. Decide whether scheduled delivery is essential; if enabled, all F05 paths are mandatory fixes.
  2. Fix isolation and local correctness. F01–F05, F10–F13, and F02's startup behavior. This includes ACK ownership, queue ownership, consumer replay/reconnect, timer recovery, DLQ persistence and unordered time queries. Convert each reproduction into a normal regression test as its fix lands.
  3. Establish a coherent replication protocol. Address F06–F09 together: durable terms, idempotent append, truthful retry results, authoritative leadership, staged handoff and verified snapshot generations. Do not optimize replication before these invariants have executable tests.
  4. Make the shipped deployment and operations real. F14–F15, dependency updates, CI, backup/restore and the accounting metrics in F18. Exercise the actual image/chart, not an alternative developer invocation.
  5. Measure and optimize the complete telemetry path. Address F17 using profiles and controlled saturation only after correctness tests pass. Compare configurations by accepted-and-accounted-for events per second, not just append calls per second.

This is a hardening program across several subsystems, not a configuration-only production promotion. It does not require implementing financial-grade exactly-once transactions for the selected workload.

docs.title: Suggested release acceptance contract
docs.text:
Numerical targets cannot be chosen from the current prompt alone. Set an explicit sustained rate, burst rate/duration, payload distribution, partition count, retention period, maximum tolerable delay, and crash-loss window before capacity testing. The following behaviors should hold regardless of those numbers:

Scenario Required observable result Two tenants/topics share a partition Neither principal can read or ACK the other's records Policy/key configuration is wrong Startup fails without granting permissions or rewriting data Consumers disconnect or run out of credits Retained work resumes, or an explicit configured drop counter accounts for it Quorum times out and producer retries Stable idempotent result; no success for an unfinished operation Process restarts twice with pending timers Retained pending work is reconstructed both times Leader fails / old leader returns One valid append authority per epoch; no truncation from duplicate RPCs Snapshot is interrupted or exceeds 1 GiB Resume/retry safely; last good generation stays recoverable Disk fills or a segment is corrupt Bounded failure, truthful API response, preserved evidence and an explicit repair path Out-of-order timestamps are ingested Replay returns every retained matching record Retention runs with delayed events and slow replicas Documented expiry policy; no unexplained deletion Sustained overload / slow CDC sink Memory and disk stay bounded; backpressure or measured shedding occurs Production pod rolls or node is replaced Correct effective configuration, catch-up and readiness before serving Backup is restored into a fresh environment Event inventory and group/scheduling state meet the documented RPO/RTO

For a first performance campaign, use realistic payload percentiles, skewed keys, multiple consumer groups, a slow consumer, delayed/out-of-order events and one lagging replica. Run long enough to include segment rotation, retention, snapshots and resource steady state; include a separate burst phase. Collect p50/p95/p99 publish and delivery latency, unique accepted IDs, unique delivered IDs, duplicates, explicit drops/expiry, queue bytes, RSS/cgroup usage, disk growth and recovery time.

For each bounded test run after pending work has settled, reconcile accepted IDs against delivered, intentionally expired/dropped and still-retained pending IDs. Loss within a stated crash window can be accepted for telemetry; unexplained missing IDs outside that contract remain release blockers.

docs.title: October Production Audit
docs.text:
CronosDB production hardening audit — 2026-10-16

Audited developement at babee9c2d76743666fb732d8c96580d255e60687. The working tree was clean when the audit began. git diff v0.6.0 HEAD -- internal pkg cmd is empty: the audited runtime source matches the local v0.6.0 tag. This does not verify the provenance of a published container or binary.

The next work should close correctness and bounded-resource gaps before adding features. Much of the prior hardening is present: durable batch fsync, quorum completion, epoch fencing, log matching, restart/redrive, consumer-progress replication, authenticated internal traffic, and CI fault/restore/overload campaigns. They should be preserved. The findings below distinguish reproduced defects, code-traced limits, and missing validation; the September audit's historical defects are not being treated as still open without checking the current code.

Status of the findings

The runtime fixes below shipped in v0.7.0 and remain in v0.8.0. Closure notes were reviewed on 2026-10-21; the original findings and measurements later in this document describe the audited v0.6.0 source.

Finding Status 1. Unreadable records Fixed. One record limit for writers, readers and recovery; publishes check it before claiming an ID. 2. Producer-chosen terms Fixed. A log stores its own term for every entry it appends for itself; followers store the leader's. 3. Append errors and dedup Fixed. Appends report whether their events reached the log, and publishes hold those for the retry instead of releasing the ID. A failed write or fsync stops the log and the node; a failed rotation no longer fails the append. 4. Dead-letter copy not replicated Implemented. Bounded journal pages include payloads and tombstones; followers fsync before acknowledging. Completion transfer and retention wait for the copy. 5. Whole-segment startup verification Fixed. The second, whole-segment read was removed; opening a segment already checks every record one at a time. 6. Scheduler memory Implemented. A shared node payload budget spills overflow to WAL references; hydration is paged and can evict later timers for earlier work. 7. Dedup recovery cutoff Implemented. Durable checkpoints replace the count cutoff; startup and promotion fail closed on recovery errors. 8. Pinned log and disk admission Implemented. Disk admission covers new follower appends; retries of already stored entries remain possible. Retention exports the blocking offset, age and reason. An optional separate backup PVC is available. Retention remains conservative; unfinished events are not discarded to reclaim space. 9. Sparse completion transfer Implemented. Per-follower cursors send 4,096 completions per page, across all groups, with versioned retry rounds. 10. Client discovery of new nodes Implemented. Metadata advertises public endpoints; clients refresh routing and preserve explicit overrides and mixed-version discoveries. 11. Quota refusal strands an ID Implemented. Both publish paths release refused claims, charge after deduplication, and refund reservations on definite pre-append failure. 12. Release evidence Workflow implemented. The release image is built once, scanned, tested, pushed and attested by digest. Publishing requires repository credentials and a successful CI run. The repository had no Docker Hub credentials at release, so the v0.7.0 image was built, scanned and pushed by hand, without provenance.

The probes of findings 1, 2, 3 and 11 are now ordinary tests (internal/api/publish_integrity_test.go, internal/storage/append_outcome_test.go). The probe of finding 3 changed with the fix: the publish that fills a segment now succeeds, and the test checks that its retry does not append the event again.

The second batch implementation and upgrade behavior are described in v0.7.0 hardening. v0.8.0 additionally fixes old-term commitment after capability agreement and adds opt-in lifecycle mutations, bounded relocation and consistent recovery snapshots. These do not close all of finding 12: the image was published locally from the CI-tested archive without signed workflow provenance; multi-host validation, real power loss and release-specific capacity remain unproven. Lifecycle v1 excludes CDC and experimental features; relocation cannot discard unfinished due work. See v0.8.0 notes and remaining limits.

The checks below describe the original audit, not a new run against v0.8.0.

What was checked

  • Followed the public publish handlers through dedup, WAL append, replication, scheduling, and retry; reviewed completion/DLQ transfer, recovery, retention, client discovery, and release workflows.
  • GOARCH=amd64 CGO_ENABLED=0 go test -count=1 ./internal/... ./pkg/... ./cmd/... -timeout 300s: passed on Windows with Go 1.26.9.
  • GOARCH=amd64 CGO_ENABLED=0 go vet ./internal/... ./pkg/... ./cmd/...: passed.
  • Six isolated audit test functions, with nine leaf cases, failed on the expected invariant assertions and reproduce five distinct defects. Runner and scope, probe source, captured output.
  • No runtime source was changed. Probes are installed through a Go overlay and do not make ordinary CI fail.

This session did not run Linux/cgo/race, the tagged acceptance campaigns, a new dependency scan, a production load benchmark, or a real power-loss test. Existing CI definitions and archived measurements are evidence of coverage and prior work, not new executions. Expected performance costs below are engineering estimates, not measured results.

1. Critical — a successful publish can create an unreadable WAL record. Reproduced.

Both public publish methods restrict payloads to 4 MiB but do not restrict total encoded event size. The public gRPC limit is 16 MiB. PrepareRecord checks field widths and the uint32 record length, while WAL readers and recovery reject records larger than 10 MiB. A small payload plus 180 metadata values of 60 KiB passes admission and encoding, is acknowledged, and cannot immediately be read back at its assigned offset. The reproduced event is 11,062,302 protobuf bytes, below the transport limit. Both single and batch requests exhibit this.

On recovery, the oversized record is classified as an invalid tail. Depending on whether populated segments follow, that can discard the tail or refuse to reopen the partition. This recovery consequence follows from the code; the recorded probe demonstrates immediate unreadability, not a cluster crash.

Evidence: public validation, batch validation, transport limit, record size calculation, read limit, recovery limit, tail handling.

Fix: establish one maximum physical record size shared by encoder, reader, recovery, and replication. Validate before reserving offsets or claiming IDs, including metadata and encryption overhead. Bound metadata count/key/value sizes as well. Test just below/at/above the boundary, encrypted and plaintext, single and batch, and reopen all accepted records.

Expected cost: a size check in the metadata traversal already performed by encoding; no additional disk sync or network round trip. Rejecting formerly accepted unreadable inputs is an intentional compatibility change.

2. High — public producers can choose the term stored in the replicated log. Reproduced locally and on a follower.

Event.Term is part of the public event object. The public handlers pass it through; termForEvent and PrepareRecord prefer a nonzero supplied term over the local WAL term. The probes store term 999999 while the local current term is 7, and separately propagate term 999999 through real follower gRPC replication while the leader epoch is 1.

Terms are protocol authority, not application data. Election ordering prefers a higher last-entry term before comparing offsets, and log matching/truncation assumes terms reflect actual leadership. Thus a producer can violate a prerequisite for recovery correctness. The probes prove the authority violation; they do not demonstrate acknowledged-data loss in a full election campaign.

Evidence: term selection, termForEvent, election comparison, follower log matching.

Fix: reject or overwrite server-owned fields at public ingress, and make local append derive its term from the current fenced leader. Preserve historical terms only in the explicitly internal replication path. Test forged positive/negative terms, leadership changes, and a retry using an event object previously returned to a caller.

Expected cost: constant-time field normalization; no new I/O. Correct epoch assignment must stay within the existing leadership/append synchronization boundary.

3. High — append errors are treated as if nothing reached the log. Reproduced with rotation failure.

The WAL can append an event, advance its watermark, and then return an error from flush, fsync, or rotation. Both public handlers unconditionally roll back the dedup claim on any append error. The probe makes the next segment filename unavailable, gets the expected rotation failure, removes that obstacle, and retries the same message ID. The retry succeeds with two entries for that ID. Both public methods exhibit this.

This is distinct from the already repaired replication-timeout retry path. At-least-once delivery allows repeated delivery attempts; it does not make the advertised publish deduplication correct when a failed operation is appended twice.

Evidence: append mutation and late errors, batch path, single rollback, batch rollback, existing held-publish mechanism.

Fix: return a structured append outcome distinguishing no mutation, appended range, durability established, and indeterminate/partial failure. Release an ID only for a definite no-append result. Reconcile an appended operation through its original offsets; fence an indeterminate writer until its prefix is established. Review follower retries too: an existing matching record alone must not stand in for a durable sync after a failed append. Test rotation, short write, ENOSPC, and fsync failure, followed by retry and restart.

Expected cost: outcome bookkeeping on success and additional work on failure. Keep batched/group durability; this does not require a second fsync on every healthy publish.

4. High — completed dead-letter work is replicated without its DLQ copy. Reproduced at the disposition/progress boundary.

sendToDLQ durably writes the local DLQ and invokes OnDeadLettered, which records ordinary consumer completion. Consumer progress is replicated, but that protocol contains no DLQ entry or dead-letter disposition. The probe follows this actual persistence order and invokes the replication handler: the follower reports the event completed while its DLQ is empty.

If the leader's disk is then lost, the replacement has neither an accessible DLQ copy nor an automatic redelivery obligation for that group. The original event may initially remain in its WAL, but completion makes it eligible for retention; keeping the event temporarily is not a recoverable DLQ disposition. A temporary leader failure with its disk intact is a weaker scenario: the copy still exists on that old disk.

Evidence: DLQ transition, completion hook, progress export, progress installation, retention predicate.

Fix: replicate a durable dead-letter disposition and its recoverable payload/reference before completion allows the source event to be pruned. Include DLQ retry/removal state in that ownership model. Gate this with leader-volume loss after dead-lettering, follower promotion, retention, and subsequent DLQ inspection/redrive.

Expected cost: quorum work on the dead-letter transition, which can be batched; ordinary successful publishing need not gain an additional round trip.

5. High — startup verification still materializes a whole segment. Code trace.

loadSegments invokes verifySegment; that calls the unlimited ReadEventsByOffsetRange over the whole segment and retains the returned event slice. Parsing allocates each payload. Consequently startup needs memory proportional to a populated segment, before the later byte-bounded timer/dedup replay loops help. Default segments are 512 MiB. Both backlog restart tests explicitly use 8 MiB segments, so their successful 384 MiB container scenario does not cover restarting a large default segment under that limit.

Evidence: load and verification, whole-segment read, unlimited range wrapper, payload allocation, default segment size, test segment sizes.

Fix: validate incrementally with a streaming scanner or bounded chunks, checking record CRC and continuity without retaining all payloads. Avoid duplicating the startup scan where possible. Add a restart test whose single populated segment exceeds the container's heap allowance, with production encryption settings. No OOM was induced in this session.

Expected cost: no publish-path cost; lower recovery memory, and potentially less repeated decode work.

6. High — scheduling can exceed the memory budget without any new publish. Code trace; extends a documented limit.

Hot timers retain complete events. The cold hydrator obtains every matching offset for its time window, reads each payload, and inserts all of them into the wheel/ready queue. It has no byte budget or bounded page. Publish admission checks do not govern hydration or timer recovery. Many far-future events can therefore be accepted while cheap, then enter the hot window together and exhaust memory even after publishers have stopped. Restart also schedules every future event in the hot window. Count limits and sampled RSS rejection are not reservations against these allocations; concurrent requests can pass the same count check.

Evidence: hot scheduling, unbounded cold scan, hydration, recovery, admission. The worker already has a 64 MiB cap per partition; that is useful but is neither a node-wide cap nor a cap on the timing wheel.

Fix: add a node-wide retained-byte budget with explicit reservations and per-partition fairness. Keep offset/schedule references for overflow, page cold-store reads, and hydrate only within the reserved budget. Consider replacing payload-bearing hot timers with references plus a bounded payload cache; benchmark the extra WAL reads and due-event latency before selecting that representation. Test synchronized due times, no consumers, large metadata, concurrent ingress, and promotion/restart under a cgroup limit.

Expected cost: cheap batched accounting can have low overhead; reference-based scheduling trades retained memory for reads. This is a real design tradeoff that requires measurement, not a promised zero-cost fix.

7. High — dedup recovery has an event-count cutoff, not a durable recovery boundary. Code trace; known open limit.

The dedup Pebble database disables its WAL, uses 64 MiB memtables, and recovery scans only the last 500,000 log entries. The cutoff is justified by an assumption that older IDs were flushed or expired, not a persisted frontier proving it. Follower append does not maintain the producer's dedup store; a promoted follower relies on this bounded reconstruction too. Retained, still-in-window IDs before the cutoff can be absent from the promoted node's dedup state. A larger configured TTL does not repair that.

Evidence: dedup storage options, cutoff and recovery, promotion, follower append. The production values configure a 168-hour TTL.

Fix: persist a crash-consistent dedup checkpoint frontier and replay the required suffix, or maintain dedup state on replicas in bounded background batches. Define how the promised ID window survives WAL pruning and node replacement; rebuilding a retained tail cannot reconstruct already pruned IDs. Fail readiness or disable writes if required recovery fails, instead of logging and continuing with incomplete dedup state. Test over 500,000 IDs, a fresh follower promotion, crash before a dedup flush, pruning, and retries within the promised window.

Expected cost: amortized checkpoint/replica maintenance, not necessarily per-event dedup fsync. Benchmark recovery time and write amplification separately.

8. High for sustained operation — one unfinished event can pin the replicated log; disk pressure does not reject ingress. Code trace; known retention limit.

Replicated pruning deliberately removes only a contiguous prefix. One far-future event, a group that never completes, or a stalled change feed can retain every later segment. DiskMonitor requests compaction at its threshold, but CanAcceptBatch has no disk-headroom gate. Compaction cannot free a pinned prefix, so continued traffic can reach disk-write errors precisely where finding 3 is unsafe.

Evidence: prefix-only rationale and enforcement, disk monitor, admission checks, completion eligibility.

Fix first: cached disk-headroom admission with hysteresis and emergency reserved space for metadata/recovery, plus oldest blocking offset/reason/age metrics. Keep draining existing work when ingress is refused. Establish schedule-horizon and inactive-group policies. Separating long-horizon scheduling from the delivery log is a later storage/protocol change, not permission to delete arbitrary middle segments: election and replication currently depend on a contiguous log.

Expected cost: periodic filesystem measurement and a cheap cached admission check. No filesystem stat per event is needed.

9. Medium — completion replication truncates sparse progress. Code trace; known limit.

Only the first 100,000 completed offsets above a group's floor are exported. In a partition shared by topics, or with one old delayed offset, the floor can remain pinned while completions accumulate beyond that limit. Exporting the same prefix again is not pagination, so the omitted completions need not reach a follower even after the system has been idle. Failover can cause a large replay of completed work, beyond the normal short maintenance-tick duplicate window.

Evidence: cap and exporter, full-state shipping.

Fix: versioned, bounded progress chunks with per-follower continuation, or compact intervals/bitmaps plus topic-aware safe cursor advancement. Preserve the rule that an unrelated topic's offset is not an acknowledged event. Test more than 100,000 sparse completions, mixed topics, an old future event, and failover after all progress has supposedly converged.

Expected cost: background replication; compact deltas can reduce repeated scanning, bytes, and lock occupancy compared with repeatedly exporting full lists.

10. Medium — connected clients cannot discover newly added node addresses. Code trace; documented operational restriction.

Metadata refresh gets leader IDs but resolves addresses from a static map or IDs that already look like addresses. Candidate fallbacks are the existing connection pool. Leadership can move to a new node that none of those addresses names, leaving existing producers and consumers unable to route there.

Evidence: metadata refresh, candidate addresses, release restriction.

Fix: return authenticated, advertised client endpoints with versioned topology metadata; update the pool and retire obsolete endpoints safely. Test adding a node and moving leadership while original clients remain connected, including certificate SAN validation. Preserve the existing static mapping as a compatibility fallback.

Expected cost: metadata-refresh/control-path work; negligible expected steady-state publish cost.

11. Medium, currently latent in the shipped entry point — quota refusal can strand a message ID. Reproduced.

Single publish claims the ID before ReservePublishBatch. A quota refusal returns without releasing the claim. Raising the quota then leaves the retry rejected as an earlier publish still in progress, with WAL next-offset still zero. Batch publish performs quota reservation before dedup instead, so the ordering is inconsistent; reservation accounting on later failures/duplicates also deserves coverage.

Evidence: single publish ordering, quota refusal, batch ordering.

Qualification: the production entry point constructs an accountant, but a repository search finds no non-test caller of SetLimits. This is a defect when quota configuration is exercised, not a claim that the default server is currently rejecting users this way.

Fix: one reservation/claim lifecycle for both APIs; undo a claim on every pre-append rejection and reconcile quota reservations with actual accepted work. Test quota rejection/retry, duplicate-only batches, validation failure, and append failures. Expected throughput cost is bookkeeping and can be negligible when quotas are disabled.

12. Release and capacity evidence remains incomplete. Confirmed workflow/documentation gaps, not reproduced runtime failures.

CI already includes meaningful fault and container tests; adding another generic unit-test target is not the missing work. Prior cluster throughput measurements use periodic fsync and are not a production durable-capacity baseline. Other archived end-to-end benchmark rows are explicitly marked invalid. The release workflow builds binaries, but states that the image is built and pushed manually; the CI image scan does not automatically establish the identity/security of the exact published digest. Backups default to the data volume and the chart provides no separate backup mount. Multi-host load/fault tests and large bootstrap validation remain unshown.

Evidence: release workflow, CI, nightly coverage, performance qualifications, invalid historical benchmark rows, release limitations.

Close this with a digest-bound release pipeline that builds, scans, tests, and publishes the same artifact, with provenance and checksums; add Rust dependency auditing. Add off-volume backup configuration and restore drills that destroy the original volumes. These have no serving-path throughput cost. No current dependency vulnerability count is asserted by this audit.

Recommended implementation order and throughput guardrails

  1. Land small invariant fixes for findings 1–3; move the corresponding probes into normal CI tests and extend them to encrypted records and durable replicated faults. Fix the latent quota lifecycle while consolidating admission only if that scope remains small.
  2. Fix DLQ disposition durability and streaming startup verification. Establish regression coverage for leader-volume loss and large individual segments.
  3. Add scheduler byte reservations/bounded hydration, a real dedup recovery frontier, and disk-headroom rejection. Keep format/protocol changes explicit and test rolling compatibility.
  4. Address sparse completion transfer and live client topology discovery; then tackle the larger retention architecture if real workloads need long schedule horizons mixed with high-rate near-term work.
  5. Gate the resulting production claim on measured durable throughput and fault recovery, and automate publication/backup evidence.

For the performance comparison, use the same machines, payload distributions, partition count, TLS/auth/encryption settings, RF=3/minISR=2, dedup enabled, and fsync=batch before and after each change. Exercise batches of 1, 100, and 1,000; small and large payloads; one and several groups; immediate and future schedules; a skewed hot partition; and a lagging follower. Keep offered IDs, unique accepted IDs, and terminal/pending outcomes separate: rejected requests and successful duplicate responses are not newly persisted throughput.

Record sustainable accepted-and-accounted-for events/s, publish p50/p95/p99, delivery lateness, duplicate rate, fsync latency, queue/cache bytes, process/cgroup memory, disk growth, recovery time, and follower catch-up lag. Fault tests must also reconcile DLQ and explicit expiry outcomes. Run enough to include rotation, checkpointing, hydration, pruning, and steady-state resource behavior; follow a shorter controlled comparison with a multi-hour soak on multiple hosts.

Suggested initial change budget, subject to the workload's requirements: investigate a repeatable drop greater than 5% in durable sustainable throughput or a rise greater than 10% in p99 publish latency across matched runs. These are proposed regression budgets, not measured guarantees or release capacity promises. Correctness remains mandatory; a faster path that acknowledges unreadable or unsafe data is not a valid baseline to preserve.

Retain group fsync, parallel follower sends, quorum completion without the slowest unnecessary replica, batched dedup/ACK writes, and work outside the WAL append lock. If profiles show replicated partitions bottlenecking on ReplicateMu spanning local sync and replication, consider a bounded per-partition batch combiner with an explicit latency budget. Pipelining the replication protocol is a separate, higher-risk optimization; do not mix it into the initial correctness fixes.

docs.title: Production release requirements
docs.text:
v0.10.0 fixes the thirteen defects of the 1.0 readiness review and keeps v0.9.0 data directories. Message IDs are unique per topic and v0.9.0 duplicate records are not carried over; see the v0.10.0 notes. The review's release gates (a multi-host soak, recovery and upgrade drills, machine or power-loss testing) are open.

v0.9.0 changes the WAL segment format to version 2. It requires new data directories on every node; version-1 data and backups are not migrated, older binaries cannot read the new files, and mixed-version clusters are unsupported. The published v0.8.1 and earlier artifacts are unchanged. See the v0.9.0 notes and closed WAL segment boundaries.

The v0.8.0 source line adds the lifecycle and replication changes described in the release notes. Available artifacts and publication status are on the releases page. Hardening goes on: the audit closure table tracks unresolved guarantees, and current release limits are listed below. A green CI run is necessary but does not establish the complete release acceptance contract.

Commit IDs in these notes refer to the history as rewritten on 2026-10-29 to correct commit attribution; no source tree changed. Images and binaries published before that date carry the earlier commit ID, for example in the image's org.opencontainers.image.revision label.

docs.title: v0.10.0 release
docs.text:
The v0.10.0 notes describe the fixes for the thirteen defects of the 1.0 readiness review, among them two ways to lose acknowledged writes (replica placement changes and retried publishes after a change of leader), scheduler drift, duplicate detection that forgot accepted IDs, and an encrypted node that could not restart after a crash. The chart and default image tag are 0.10.0. Publication status, checksums and the exact deployment digest are on the release page. Use its IMAGE_DIGEST and publication evidence to identify the tested image. v0.9.0 data directories are kept; duplicate records are not. This release makes no new capacity claim.

Published on 2026-10-28 from 359e5ba0efd169e6c723bf576f8aa7c24b57f78f. The fixes passed the required checks on PR #17, and the release revision on PR #18. The run on main passed on its second attempt; the first failed the discovery test, which published before leadership had settled after start-up, while the fault campaign in the same attempt passed. The release staging run built the binaries, started the Linux binary, and scanned and fault-tested the exact image archived on the release, including container network faults and a restart with a backlog larger than memory. The scan reported no findings.

The Linux amd64 image is johnny711dock/cronos-db:0.10.0, manifest digest sha256:9e21824133d9dd76aabe00d4dbb96b1fa2219014cd3fdc8ba11d19b58c575011. It was loaded from the staged archive and pushed locally; its configuration and all nine filesystem layers match the scanned image, and anonymous registry requests select the same manifest for 0.10.0 and latest. Pin the manifest for deployments. This publication has no signed GitHub workflow provenance. latest previously selected v0.9.0 (sha256:b597796916f59408801e37577ea591e38bac312828d7bbc6bf06b15e07b3abf4); a node started from latest on a v0.9.0 data directory keeps it.

docs.title: v0.9.0 release
docs.text:
The v0.9.0 notes describe the version-2 WAL segment format, which detects erased areas of closed segments, and a fix for a node crash when a scheduled backup overlapped the release of a partition. The chart and default image tag are 0.9.0. Publication status, checksums and the exact deployment digest are on the release page. Use its IMAGE_DIGEST and publication evidence to identify the tested image. This release breaks on-disk compatibility and makes no new capacity claim.

Published on 2026-10-27 from 31e809248d850766726c381438c9b2a284f4352b. The required source checks passed on PR #15 (second attempt of the run; the first failed a cluster start-up timing test and passed when re-run on the same revision). The release staging run built the binaries, started the Linux binary, and scanned and fault-tested the exact image archived on the release, including container network faults and a restart with a backlog larger than memory.

The Linux amd64 image is johnny711dock/cronos-db:0.9.0, manifest digest sha256:b597796916f59408801e37577ea591e38bac312828d7bbc6bf06b15e07b3abf4. It was loaded from the staged archive and pushed locally; its configuration and all nine filesystem layers match the scanned image, and anonymous registry requests select the same manifest for 0.9.0 and latest. Pin the manifest for deployments. This publication has no signed GitHub workflow provenance. latest previously selected v0.8.1 (sha256:f2839385386b2f44b6a07669fcb001dcab31273a3e7ba14f1f0510f6a9594883); a node started from latest on a v0.8.1 data directory now refuses it, because the WAL segment format changed.

docs.title: v0.8.1 patch release
docs.text: The v0.8.1 notes describe the security, subscription registration and deduplication lookup fixes. The chart and default image tag are 0.8.1. Publication status, checksums and the exact deployment digest are on the release page. Use its IMAGE_DIGEST and publication evidence to identify the tested image. This patch adds no WAL format and makes no new capacity claim.

docs.title: v0.8.0 publication record
docs.text:
Published on 2026-10-19 from ed7910fa85150d7e6701cf17bdcf37b3388a4883. The required source checks passed before promotion to main; the release staging run also built the binaries, started the Linux binary, and scanned and fault-tested the exact image archived on the release.

The Linux amd64 image is johnny711dock/cronos-db:0.8.0, manifest digest sha256:428690215148b97eb9b6aaed5a3afb7c7a3227613c8fee731ab922e2276d4928. It was loaded from that archive and pushed locally, then verified through anonymous registry requests. At publication, latest was an OCI index selecting that same manifest; an index digest need not equal the image manifest digest. Pin the manifest for deployments. This publication has no signed GitHub workflow provenance. Evidence and binary checksums are attached to the published release.

Development follow-up on 2026-10-21 raises the build toolchain to Go 1.26.10, the dashboard's Vite floor to 7.3.7, and github.com/klauspost/compress to v1.18.7 after current CI found GO-2026-6809 in crypto/x509, the bundled launch-editor advisories in Vite 7.3.6, and CVE-2026-63209 in the image's compression dependency. See the Go patch release, Vite advisory, and compression advisory. These source updates are included in v0.8.1; the v0.8.0 binaries and image above retain their original contents and scan date.

The same development follow-up initializes consumer-group membership before a new subscription can receive live events. This closes a registration window in which the first acknowledgement could be refused because its group did not yet exist. This change is included in v0.8.1.

Deduplication lookups also keep buffered IDs visible until their Pebble batch has committed. Previously, a lookup during the handoff from the buffer to Pebble could briefly report an existing ID as missing. Failed flushes now leave those buffered IDs visible while they wait for another attempt. These fixes are included in v0.8.1.

The major correctness work in this release is current-term commitment after leader changes, opt-in future-event cancellation/rescheduling, bounded relocation, and consistent lifecycle recovery snapshots/backups. See the lifecycle contract and term-start protocol. Current-term activation waits for every assigned replica, handoff target and Raft voter to be capable. Mixed clusters retain legacy accounting and its old-term defect until then. Lifecycle operations additionally require explicit opt-in and majority acknowledgements. Once formats activate, incompatible downgrade is unsupported.

docs.title: What v0.7.0 adds
docs.text: v0.7.0 implemented fixes for the runtime findings of the October audit: records that could not be read back, terms chosen by producers, append and fsync errors that released message IDs, quota refusals that stranded them, scheduler memory, the dedup recovery cutoff, completion and dead-letter replication, disk admission on followers and client discovery of new nodes. The workflow for building, scanning, testing, pushing and attesting one image was also implemented; actual local publications lack that attestation. See hardening and upgrade behavior, including what a rolling upgrade from v0.6.0 holds back, the Docker Hub secret names and the optional separate backup PVC.

docs.title: Supported scope under validation
docs.text:
The first release targets fixed partitions and telemetry with explicit loss, retention, and duplicate-delivery limits. Transactions and online partition splitting are disabled by default. Both require --dev --experimental-features; production configuration rejects that flag. Production also rejects --exactly-once-commits: commit-ID storage is not an end-to-end delivery guarantee.

Change data capture to Kafka and webhooks is supported: it exports accepted events in log order from each partition's leader, and a partition keeps its log entries until they have been exported. Replication to other regions is experimental and part of the same opt-in: a node with CRONOS_REGIONS set refuses to start without --dev --experimental-features.

Production mode accepts --fsync-mode=batch and every_event. In both, a replica has an entry on disk before it acknowledges it, so a publish acknowledged with min-insync-replicas=2 is on two disks. periodic is refused: it acknowledges first and syncs later, and loses acknowledged publishes when the machines of a quorum lose power together.

docs.title: Configuration and installation
docs.text:
Settings are applied in this order: defaults, matching CRONOS_* environment variables, explicit command-line flags. Invalid environment values fail loading. An explicit empty --cluster-seeds= clears environment-provided seeds. Startup logs effective partition, replication, durability, and address settings without logging secret values. Invalid authorization files fail before data directories or listeners are initialized.

The production chart requires these existing secrets:

Default secret Required keys cronos-db-auth jwt-secret, policy.json cronos-db-tls tls.crt, tls.key, ca.crt cronos-db-replication-tls tls.crt, tls.key, ca.crt cronos-db-encryption master.key

The policy file is a JSON object keyed directly by JWT subject, for example {"operator":{"admin":true}}. Supply topic-specific permissions for application subjects. The encryption key must meet LoadMasterKey's 32-byte requirement. The chart's non-root init container copies the projected key into a memory volume with mode 0600; the application reads that private copy. Keep the default user/group/fsGroup relationship or adapt key staging to your security policy.

Use certificates whose SANs cover the advertised pod DNS addresses, including <pod>.<headless-service>.<namespace>.svc. Replication certificates must support client and server authentication. Public client certificates depend on the configured public TLS policy.

The cronos-db-replication-tls secret secures all traffic between nodes: replication, membership and Raft. Each of the three ports reads nothing from a caller that has not presented a certificate signed by the CA in ca.crt, and a node checks that the certificate of the node it calls is valid for the address it called. ca.crt may hold more than one CA certificate.

Certificates are replaced without a restart (since v0.6.0-rc.4; earlier releases read them once, at a start). A node reads a certificate, its key and its CA file again when they change, and uses what they hold for the next connection it makes or accepts, on every port: the client port, the HTTP port, replication, membership and Raft. It looks at the files when a connection is made, at most every two seconds, so nothing has to be signalled. Connections that are open keep the certificate they were made with. A certificate whose key has not arrived yet, or a file that cannot be read, leaves the one read before in use and is reported in the log once.

To replace the CA that issues the nodes' certificates: put the old and the new CA in every node's ca.crt; then give each node a certificate of the new CA; then take the old CA out of ca.crt. Every step can be made on running nodes and in any order of nodes. TestCertificatesAndTheirCAReplacedWhileRunning does it to three running nodes that producers and a consumer group are using, and then restarts one of them. That node comes back with the new files only, and has to be let in by the two that were never restarted, and let them in, on the membership, Raft and replication ports; the cluster is then made to depend on it by killing one of the two.

A cluster that runs 0.6.0-rc.2 or earlier with replication TLS cannot be upgraded one pod at a time: those versions speak plain TCP on the membership and Raft ports, and a node of this version does not talk to them. Stop all its nodes and start them on the new version together. The data stays.

The chart starts pods in parallel, and every pod names every pod as a seed. Ordinal zero is the one that creates the cluster (--cluster-bootstrap), and it does so only when it has no Raft state and no other pod belongs to a cluster. Raft state is on the data volume under raft/.

A pod whose volume is replaced comes back empty, finds the cluster through the other pods and is filled from it; that holds for ordinal zero too. Replace one volume at a time and wait for the pod to be ready: with two of three volumes gone, events that were acknowledged by two replicas can be on neither of the two that are left. Production mode refuses to start a node without --cluster-seeds, because such a node creates a cluster whenever it has no state.

A node that is lost for good is removed from the cluster by hand (since v0.6.0-rc.4). Until then it stays a member, which is what lets a node come back, and it keeps counting towards what a majority is in Raft: a cluster of four with one node lost needs three of four, which is every node that still runs. Once the node is certain not to return, from a machine that has the cluster's certificates:

cronos-admin cluster remove-node <node-id> --server <any-node>:<cluster-grpc-port> \
  --tls --tls-ca ca.crt --tls-cert tls.crt --tls-key tls.key

Any node can be asked; one that does not coordinate the cluster passes the request on. A node that is running is refused: it would join again at once. cronos-admin cluster voters lists the nodes that count. A removed node that is started again with its data joins as a member again. In TestLostNodeIsRemoved one of four nodes is lost and removed, and the cluster then loses a second node and carries on with two of three.

In v0.6.0 and before, a node cannot be added to a running cluster for applications that are already connected. Partition metadata names a leader by its node ID, and a client turns that into an address only for the nodes it was started with or was given in NodeIDToAddress. A node that joins later takes over leadership of some partitions, and clients that do not know its address cannot publish to those. Replace a node under the name and address of the one it replaces, as a StatefulSet does, and restart or reconfigure clients before growing a cluster.

Since v0.7.0 a node started with --advertise-grpc-addr gives clients that address in partition metadata, and updated clients refresh their address map when membership changes; the Helm chart advertises each pod's DNS name with service.advertisePodAddress=true. Explicit NodeIDToAddress overrides still take precedence. Upgrade clients as well as servers to use discovery, and advertise addresses reachable from those clients, which the client port's certificate covers when TLS is on. A node started without the flag advertises nothing.

The HTTP port (health, metrics, dashboard and the admin API) is served over TLS with --http-tls-enabled, with the certificate of the client port (--tls-cert-file, --tls-key-file). The production values of the chart turn it on (tls.http), and the probes and the ServiceMonitor then use HTTPS. Callers are not asked for a certificate on that port: the admin API checks the bearer token. Prometheus does not verify the pods' certificate unless metrics.serviceMonitor.tlsConfig names the CA and the server name. Without the setting the port is plain HTTP, and the token and the answers cross the network unencrypted; leave it off only when something in front of the pods ends TLS for that port. The setting is there since v0.6.0-rc.4.

The image builds dashboard assets from the npm lockfile and the Rust library from the Cargo lockfile. Its Go builder matches the module's minimum version. Pin the resulting application image digest for a release deployment.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
.github/workflows/ci.yml defines Linux cgo/race tests, Go vet/build/formatting, Rust tests, dashboard tests/build, Go/npm vulnerability checks, Helm assertions, a scan of the built image for known vulnerabilities, a fault campaign against three server processes, and a disposable kind cluster running the production chart with security enabled. It runs for pull requests and for pushes to main. Work on the development branch is not checked as it is pushed; a commit there can be checked on request with gh workflow run ci.yml --ref developement. The five jobs (go, fault-campaign, dashboard-and-chart, go-security, production-chart-startup) are required checks on main since 2026-10-13, for administrators as well: main moves only to a commit on which all five have passed in a run for a pull request or a push. A run on request does not count for this, because GitHub does not hold its results against the commit. A release therefore goes through a pull request from the development branch to main, which runs the five jobs, and main moves when they are green. A vulnerability finding fails its job; it is not silently waived.

Run chart assertions locally with python scripts/check-production-chart.py (Helm and PyYAML required). scripts/production-chart-smoke.sh requires the disposable kind-cronos-ci context and an already-loaded cronos-db:ci image. It creates ephemeral test credentials, installs three production-mode pods, and checks readiness, embedded dashboard assets, key permissions, and rejection of unauthenticated HTTP admin requests. It then restarts the pods one at a time, and starts the cluster again with the volume of ordinal zero emptied, checking that the pod joins the cluster instead of creating one. It sends no events: it is not a proof of quorum acceptance, failover, or restore. Tooling follows the kind quick-start workflow.

The fault-campaign job runs tests/acceptance: three server processes on the runner, producers and a two-member consumer group working through the client library, and a sequence of faults (a leader killed, a follower killed, a leader frozen and released, each node restarted, a replica replaced with an empty one and killed while it is refilled, the whole cluster killed). It fails if an acknowledged event was not delivered, if one arrived before its time, or if the replicas of a partition do not end with the same log. Its nodes speak mutual TLS with each other, as production nodes do. Run it locally with go test -tags acceptance -count=1 -timeout 25m ./tests/acceptance/; it needs about 500 MB of memory. It stops and kills processes, and it publishes about 60 events a second, so it says nothing about behavior under load.

Processes on one machine cannot be cut off from one another, so the network is failed in a test of its own. TestNetworkPartitions runs three containers of the image on a network of their own and drops what chosen nodes send each other, without a word, as a failed link does, while all three keep running and applications still reach every one of them: the leader of a partition on its own, one link down between two nodes that both still reach the third, each node on its own in turn, and every link down. The same checks apply as for the other faults. It runs in the production-chart-startup job, which has built the image, and locally with CRONOS_IMAGE=<image> go test -tags acceptance -run TestNetworkPartitions ./tests/acceptance/.

The fault-campaign job also restores a whole cluster from backups (TestClusterRestoredFromBackups, on processes): three nodes back up while publishes arrive, all three are destroyed, each is restored from its own backup, and what was acknowledged before the backups is there and is delivered at its time. Backups go to backups under the data directory unless --backup-dir names another place. A backup on the volume it copies does not survive the loss of that volume. The chart can provision a separate per-pod backup PVC with backupPersistence.enabled=true, mounted at /backups by default. Choose a separate failure domain and preserve the claims during recovery; another PVC on the same storage backend does not protect against that backend's loss.

cronos-admin is in the image at /app/cronos-admin. restore and check-log work on the files of a stopped node: scale the StatefulSet down and run them from a pod of the same image that mounts the node's volume.

The acceptance tests make faults that show once in a few runs, and a change gets one run. .github/workflows/nightly.yml runs them three times over every night on main, on processes and on containers, and keeps the node logs of a failure for two weeks. It runs on request for any branch: gh workflow run nightly.yml --ref developement.

docs.title: Binaries
docs.text:
A release carries the server and cronos-admin for Linux and macOS (amd64 and arm64) and Windows (amd64), one archive for each, with SHA256SUMS. .github/workflows/release.yml builds them from the tag when the release is published, starts the Linux server it built and waits for it to say it is ready, and attaches them. Manual staging can attach them to a draft before publication. To build equivalent binaries locally, build and stage the dashboard first (make dashboard, requires npm), then run bash scripts/build-release-binaries.sh <version> <output-directory> with Go, Bash, tar and zip available. Running the script alone from an unstaged checkout leaves the dashboard placeholder embedded.

They are built without cgo, which is what lets one machine build all five and lets each run without a library beside it. A build without cgo uses the bloom filter written in Go; the image is built with cgo and uses the one in Rust, which is faster. Neither keeps anything on disk, so a data directory can go from one to the other. The go job of CI runs the suite once without cgo and builds the five archives, so that a release is not the first to find out that one of them does not build. The first release with binaries is v0.6.0-rc.4: before it the server did not build for macOS, and needed cgo and the Rust library everywhere but on Windows.

docs.title: Memory and overload
docs.text:
The scheduler shares a node-wide payload/accounting budget, 64 MiB by default (--scheduler-memory, minimum 32 MiB). Far-future work and overflow within the hot window (--hot-window-minutes, 60 by default) remain WAL references in the cold store. Hydration reads bounded pages and can evict later timers for earlier ones. This is an allocation budget, not an RSS cap: worker queues, Pebble caches, in-flight requests and temporary WAL reads consume additional memory.

Publishes are refused, with ResourceExhausted, while the process holds --max-memory-percent (80) of its memory limit. The limit is the container's when there is one, otherwise the machine's memory, or --memory-limit. The Go client reports the refusal as an error of kind overloaded and does not retry it: the application should send less. A node at that point keeps delivering, and takes publishes again when consumers have worked the backlog off. cronos_memory_held_bytes and cronos_memory_limit_bytes show where a node stands, and the chart alerts when a node has been refusing for two minutes. The fault-campaign job tests this (TestOverloadIsRefusedAndSurvived): producers flood a cluster that has a small limit and no consumer; the nodes refuse, none dies, and everything that was acknowledged is delivered once a consumer starts.

A node that restarts leaves on disk what is due and not delivered: a subscription reads it from the log at the pace its consumers take it, a few megabytes at a time. Two tests hold it to that. In TestRestartWithABacklogLargerThanMemory three processes take in a backlog a quarter larger than the memory limit they are restarted with, and must stay below it until a consumer has received everything. In TestRestartInContainersWithABacklogLargerThanTheirMemory three containers of the image, which the kernel kills above 384 MiB, take in a gigabyte, are killed, come back and deliver it. Recorded peaks are specific to each run; see v0.7.0 validation for its measured results. This holds since v0.6.0-rc.4. v0.6.0-rc.3 and everything before it reads the backlog into memory at a start, and a node there whose backlog exceeds its memory is killed on every start.

Queue admission also has event-count caps (--max-ready-queue, --max-timing-wheel-size, --max-in-flight). These and sampled process memory admission do not prove that all workloads avoid an OOM kill. A replay/redrive page can exceed its byte target by one valid record. Backlogs beyond the tested gigabyte, large future schedules and sustained production-size loads remain unmeasured. The harness must not override a node's memory policy with the test runner's GOMEMLIMIT.

docs.title: What a release promises, and what that rests on
docs.text:
Each promise below is checked by the test named with it, in CI: for every pull request, for every push to main, and for the commit of a release. The tests run three server processes on one machine at about 60 small events a second; the last column says what they do not show.

Promise Checked by Not shown A publish that was acknowledged survives the loss of any one node (replication factor 3, two in-sync replicas, fsync batch or every_event) TestFaultCampaign: a leader killed, a follower killed, a leader frozen and released, every node restarted, a node replaced with an empty one and killed while it is refilled, the whole cluster killed Two nodes' disks lost together; loss of power on a real machine (the tests kill processes) The same holds when the network between the nodes fails while all of them keep running, and a node that is cut off acknowledges nothing TestNetworkPartitions: links cut between three containers of the image: a leader alone, one link down, each node alone in turn, every link down Slow or lossy links, as opposed to dead ones; outages longer than a minute; more than one machine Every acknowledged event is delivered at least once, and never before its time The ledger of the same test, and of the restore and overload tests Exactly once: after a failover some events are delivered again The replicas of a partition hold the same log TestFaultCampaign compares them entry for entry A partition takes publishes again within 90 seconds of its leader's death The bound the campaign enforces Typical times; behavior under load Any node, the first included, can be replaced with an empty one TestFaultCampaign, TestFirstNodeReplaced, the kind job on the chart Two at once A node that is lost for good is removed, and no longer counts towards a majority (since v0.6.0-rc.4) TestLostNodeIsRemoved: one of four nodes lost and removed through cronos-admin, then a second node killed Growing the cluster with connected clients is not covered by this test; TestClientsFindTheOtherNodesThroughPartitionMetadata shows a client given one node publishing to the leaders of every partition through the addresses metadata gives it A cluster that is lost entirely comes back from its nodes' backups with everything acknowledged before the earliest of them TestClusterRestoredFromBackups Restore to a point between backups; getting backups off the node, which is the operator's to arrange Producers that outrun the cluster are refused, and no node dies of it TestOverloadIsRefusedAndSurvived Load at production sizes A node comes back with more waiting for consumers than it has memory, and delivers it (since v0.6.0-rc.4) TestRestartWithABacklogLargerThanMemory; TestRestartInContainersWithABacklogLargerThanTheirMemory, with a limit of 384 MiB that the kernel enforces and a backlog of 1 GiB Backlogs beyond a gigabyte; future events under production load. v0.7.0 adds a separate scheduler payload budget for future events Traffic between nodes is encrypted and only nodes that hold the cluster's certificate take part TestTransportTLS_*, the kind job Certificates and their CA are replaced without a restart, and the HTTP port is served over TLS (since v0.6.0-rc.4) TestCertificatesAndTheirCAReplacedWhileRunning on three running nodes; TestNodes_ReplaceCertificatesAndTheirCAWhileRunning, TestCredentials_VerifyAgainstTheCAOfTheMoment, TestBuildHTTPTLSConfig_ServesTheHTTPPortOverTLS; the kind job asks the HTTP port over TLS and checks that it does not answer without The certificate of the client port and of the HTTP port replaced under load; a certificate that expires while a connection is open One tenant cannot read, replay or acknowledge another's events TestIsolation_*

No throughput, payload-size or latency figure is promised. None has been measured on production hardware.

docs.title: What v0.7.0 was released without
docs.text:
Releases are cut from the development branch when CI is green on the commit. v0.7.0 was published as the latest release and as the latest image; the five CI jobs are required checks on main (see Checks).

v0.7.0 was released without the following. These are limits of what has been shown, not defects that are known; a deployment that depends on one of them has to show it for itself first:

  • A run on more than one machine. Everything above was shown on one host, with processes or with containers; links were cut between containers.
  • A replica refilled from a partition larger than 1 GiB. The transfer has no size limit and resumes file by file, and has a ten minute deadline; it has only been run on megabytes.
  • Throughput and latency measured on the hardware a deployment will use, with the memory that the backlog it allows needs. The measurements of 2026-10-16 ran three processes on one Windows laptop; none was made on Linux.
  • A cut of power. Recovery is tested after processes are killed, not after the machine loses power with writes in flight.
  • An image published by the release workflow. Its image job needs the repository secrets DOCKERHUB_USERNAME and DOCKERHUB_TOKEN, which the repository did not have. The image of v0.7.0 was built from the tagged commit, scanned with the settings of CI (Trivy, HIGH and CRITICAL vulnerabilities that have a fix), started as three nodes and pushed, by hand, as for v0.6.0. It has no signed provenance; its digest is in the release notes.

docs.title: What v0.8.0 was released without
docs.text:
The runtime fixes do not close every product or validation gap:

  • Multi-host fault/load validation, real machine power cuts, deployment-specific capacity, replica refills beyond the tested size, and a new v0.8.0 throughput measurement are not established. Older dated benchmarks are not measurements of this release.
  • Lifecycle v1 excludes CDC, cross-region replication, transactions and online splitting. Cancellation only affects future work; it cannot recall a sent event. Delivery remains at least once. Mixed-version commitment and one-way format activation have the limits above.
  • Relocation is opt-in and bounded. Unfinished due work, unresolved mutations, lagging dead-letter replication and other retention gates can still pin a log. Dead-letter journal/tombstone history is not compacted.
  • Distribution has one Linux amd64 image and five non-cgo binary targets. The image has no signed workflow provenance; automated publishing requires the Docker Hub repository secrets. The thresholded image scan found no fixable HIGH/CRITICAL findings at scan time; it is not a claim of zero vulnerabilities.
  • Lag-driven automatic snapshots remain unwired, TriggerRebalance remains a soft stub, and tenant quota configuration remains unavailable in the shipped server. See the architecture limitations.

Known limits of what is released are in the audit: log entries are removed from the start of a replicated log only, so without eligible relocation one pinned event keeps later segments; a partition shared by several topics keeps a completion record per finished event until the start of its log passes it. Up to v0.6.0 a leader sent its followers at most 100,000 of those per group, so after a failover a group could be given events again that it had finished; since v0.7.0 they go in pages, all of them.

docs.title: 1.0.0 readiness review — 2026-10-28
docs.text:
Reviewed source: 77a9d49 on main (v0.9.0 source line). This is an assessment, not a release approval or an implementation of the fixes.

The earlier nine findings are not the complete work list. This follow-up reproduced them and confirmed four additional defects, for at least thirteen known issues. Passing the existing tests does not establish completeness: the three new Go probes and the new chart assertion fail while the corresponding ordinary SDK, backup and chart tests pass.

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
All thirteen are fixed on branch fix/1.0-readiness. Each probe became a regression test that fails on 77a9d49 and passes with the fix; the opt-in releaseaudit probes and the zz_audit_* files are gone. The release gates below are not covered by these fixes and remain open.

# Fix Regression tests 1 A replica that placement drops goes on the partition's Retiring list: elections ask it and count it, and it keeps its copy. A leader drops former followers before it reports the new epoch, and the list is cleared once that epoch is reported and minISR−1 remaining replicas hold the leader's log from that point. The leader used to keep replicating to dropped nodes and counting their acknowledgements. internal/cluster/retiring_replicas_test.go 2 The wheel advances to the tick the clock has reached, at most 1000 ticks per fire, never past it. internal/scheduler/wheel_clock_test.go 3 A filter rebuild reloads Pebble's IDs, with every check going to Pebble until it has; claims pause only for the snapshot. The rebuild trigger is the false-positive rate over checks of absent IDs. internal/dedup/bloom_refresh_test.go 4 A record that does not decrypt, with nothing written after it and unwritten trailing bytes, is a torn write, judged like a plaintext checksum failure. The first record of a segment needs its whole tag unwritten, so a wrong key still fails closed. internal/storage/torn_encrypted_tail_test.go 5 Leader.Replicate replicates an entry below the current term's start record through that record. internal/replication/term_start_retry_test.go 6 The index buffer holds whole entries; opening an index cuts it after its last valid entry; a read the index points to the wrong place rescans the segment. internal/storage/index_alignment_test.go 7 Dedup records are kept per topic and message ID (dedup.Key). Records written before 1.0 are not carried over. internal/api/client_limits_test.go 8 Group names and subscription IDs are at most 255 bytes; a partition holds at most --max-consumer-groups groups (default 10000). Existing groups are kept and can be joined. internal/api/client_limits_test.go 9 Cancellation ends a replay's pause; speed must be 0 or at least 0.001. internal/api/client_limits_test.go 10 The SDK saves only the completion floor the server reports, 0 included, and in async mode from the server's answers rather than at send time. pkg/client/ack_commit_test.go 11 With CommitStrategySync, Ack waits for the server's answer and returns refusals, stream failures and cancellation. pkg/client/ack_commit_test.go 12 A partition backup includes changefeed.json, taken before the log is cut. internal/partition/changefeed_backup_test.go 13 The disruption budget allows one pod at a time (podDisruptionBudget.maxUnavailable), and the production values require one pod per node (podAntiAffinity: hard). scripts/check-production-chart.py asserts both. scripts/check-production-chart.py (check_disruption)

Corrections to the findings below: #6 is reachable in ordinary operation, not only after a partial write such as a full disk, because production WALs use the shared fsync coalescer, which never flushed the index. #13 costs availability during voluntary disruptions; evicted pods keep their volumes, so "lose all of its replicas" means unavailable, not lost.

The assumed 1.0 scope is the existing supported product: fixed partitions, replicated durable publishing, scheduled at-least-once delivery, replay, the Go SDK, authenticated topic access, backups, and optional Kafka/webhook CDC. Transactions, online splitting and cross-region replication remain experimental. Features deliberately excluded from 1.0 need explicit documentation and runtime gating; they do not need to be completed merely to assign a 1.0 version.

docs.title: 10. SDK resume checkpoints can skip unfinished deliveries — high priority
docs.text:
pkg/client/consumer.go:954 saves the ACK request's next offset in asynchronous mode immediately after sending, without waiting for the server's committed floor. In synchronous mode, lines 946–948 use the same value when the server correctly reports a committed floor of zero. A delivery's highest offset does not prove earlier offsets were processed: scheduling and concurrent handlers allow completion out of order.

Reproduction: the server acknowledges delivery of offset 10 while reporting committed floor 0. With an explicitly configured checkpoint store, both modes save 11 and reconnect with StartOffset=11. The server uses that as the minimum redrive origin (internal/api/handlers.go:1363); queued retries and its safety sweep also respect that minimum (lines 1450 and 1492). Previously due, unfinished records below it can therefore be skipped. They remain in the WAL.

Probe: TestReleaseAudit_CheckpointMustNotSkipUnfinishedOffsets in pkg/client/zz_release_readiness_test.go. Evidence: build/audit-1.0-sdk.log. This needs no malicious client. The default configuration without a checkpoint store avoids this particular path.

Required outcome: persist only a server-confirmed contiguous completion floor; preserve zero as a valid floor. Reconnect after refused/lost ACKs and out-of-order completion must still deliver every unfinished event. Include failover, since server completion replication is asynchronous and a client-side checkpoint must not override a successor's older safe progress.

docs.title: 11. SDK synchronous ACK returns before server confirmation — medium priority
docs.text:
CommitStrategySync promises that ACK waits for the RPC outcome, but Delivery.AckSuccess ultimately returns when worker enqueues an ACK (pkg/client/consumer.go:853). ackSender receives the server response on another goroutine; no result is returned to the original caller.

Reproduction: a test gRPC server withholds every ACK response. AckSuccess with a 150 ms deadline returns nil immediately even with CommitStrategySync. A caller cannot rely on the documented commit boundary or act on a server refusal.

Probe: TestReleaseAudit_SyncAckMustWaitForServer in pkg/client/zz_release_readiness_test.go. Evidence: build/audit-1.0-sdk.log.

Required outcome: synchronous ACK waits for its matching response and returns refusal, stream failure or cancellation to the caller. This does not imply exactly-once delivery or quorum replication of consumer progress.

docs.title: 12. Backup/restore silently drops pending CDC export work — high priority
docs.text:
internal/partition/backup.go:173 checkpoints the dedup, consumer and DLQ stores, and copies epoch/format markers, but omits changefeed.json. On restore, openChangeFeed interprets the missing cursor as a newly enabled feed and starts at the end of the restored log (internal/partition/changefeed.go:114).

Reproduction: accept three records while the CDC sink is down, take a backup, and restore it through storage.RestoreBackup. All three records are present in the restored WAL. The export cursor changes from -1 to 2 without exporting any of them. Recovering the destination therefore does not retry those records. The probe holds the restored sink unavailable while checking the cursor so legitimate fast export cannot be mistaken for the bug. The probe uses fsync-mode=every_event; this is not a periodic-durability artifact.

Probe: TestReleaseAudit_BackupPreservesPendingChangeFeed in internal/partition/zz_release_readiness_test.go. Evidence: build/audit-1.0-backup.log.

Required outcome: include a conservative, durable feed position in the backup manifest and restore it with the log. Test a failing sink, concurrent publishes and exports, and restart after restore. Missing/invalid recovery metadata must not silently certify unexported entries as exported. Define how older backups without a cursor are handled.

docs.title: 13. Production disruption budget permits losing quorum — high priority
docs.text:
charts/cronos-db/templates/poddisruptionbudget.yaml:14 derives global minAvailable from the partition replication factor, not the number of cluster voters or partition placement. Production values render five pods, RF=3 and minISR=2, but minAvailable=2. Thus the PDB permits three simultaneous voluntary evictions from a healthy five-node cluster. Two remaining voters cannot form a five-voter Raft majority, and a three-replica partition can lose all of its replicas. Readiness changes after an eviction do not prevent requests already admitted concurrently under that budget.

Probe: a script that rendered the actual production chart and failed the quorum assertion; it is now check_disruption in scripts/check-production-chart.py. Evidence: build/audit-1.0-chart-probe.log. This is a rendered-configuration proof, not a live Kubernetes drain experiment. The existing chart assertion script passes.

Required outcome: protect both Raft and partition availability. For the default RF=3/minISR=2 configuration, permitting at most one concurrent voluntary eviction is the conservative starting point; verify recovery/readiness before the next. Also provide/test failure-domain placement: the production values currently inherit empty affinity, so distinct pods are not guaranteed distinct hosts. PDBs alone do not protect against host failure or controller-driven updates.

docs.title: Earlier findings rechecked
docs.text:
All nine reproduced on Linux amd64 with Go 1.26.10 and CGO_ENABLED=0. The existing internal/*/zz_audit_*_test.go files were preserved unchanged.

  1. Unsafe replica replacement on node join. Both the one-join/lagging-replica and two-join/empty-replica election probes fail. Outgoing nodes still have data, but are excluded from the committed election set. Fixing this requires a quorum-safe membership transition, including writes and elections during catch-up; simply adding a copy step is not sufficient evidence of safety.
  2. Permanent scheduler drift after missed ticks. Both hydration and repeated short-stall probes fail. Clock catch-up must also remain bounded and preserve the no-early-delivery guarantee.
  3. Bloom maintenance forgets accepted IDs. The existing-ID retry is accepted again after maintenance. Rebuild/reset must preserve correctness while concurrent claims, expiry and buffered writes occur.
  4. Encrypted damaged tail prevents recovery and repair. Both reopen and check-log --repair probes fail. The previous suggested fix was too broad: a decryption failure after a good record is not automatically a torn final append. Keep wrong-key, interior-corruption and sealed-segment checks; prove which tail can safely be discarded before truncating anything.
  5. Old-term publish retry acknowledged without current-term commitment. The replication probe succeeds below the current-term commit barrier. The retry path needs the same commitment proof as a new publish.
  6. Partial index entry corrupts later reads after another restart. The 24-byte entries and 64 KiB write buffer can create a partial on-disk entry during ordinary buffering; this is not limited to a full disk. Align or rebuild the advisory index and verify reads against the WAL.
  7. Cross-topic/principal message-ID collision. A publisher to beta can block an ID on alpha. Decide and enforce the namespace/idempotency contract before making a stable multi-tenant promise. Accidental cross-topic ID reuse can trigger this with trusted publishers too.
  8. Unbounded permanent consumer-group creation through Subscribe. Eight subscriptions retain 16 MiB of names in the probe. Bound names and group creation/storage. Do not fix it by deleting durable consumer progress on every disconnect.
  9. Replay cancellation does not interrupt pacing sleep. All ten cancelled handlers remain alive in the probe. This is a cancellation/resource bug for ordinary clients too, not exclusively a multi-tenant security issue.

Findings 1–6 and 10–13 should be addressed for the assumed supported scope. Findings 7–9 should also be fixed before a broad stable release; a restricted trusted-client deployment can reduce some exposure but does not remove these bugs. CDC can instead be explicitly excluded and disabled in a narrower release, but the current product documents it as supported.

docs.title: Validation performed
docs.text:
• Full pure-Go Linux suite: CGO_ENABLED=0 go test -count=1 -json -timeout 300s ./internal/... ./pkg/... ./cmd/.... 29 packages passed, 6 failed, 3 had no tests; 1,171 passing test/subtest records. Every failed test was one of the previously supplied audit probes; no additional ordinary-suite test failed in this run. Evidence: build/audit-1.0-linux-tests.jsonl.
  • The new SDK and CDC probes ran separately with -tags releaseaudit; all three top-level probes failed in the expected way. They are opt-in and do not add failures to ordinary test runs.
  • One real three-process cluster backup/restore acceptance run passed: go test -tags acceptance -count=1 -timeout 10m -v ./tests/acceptance -run TestClusterRestoredFromBackups. It took 155.5 seconds. This does not establish that a previously reported intermittent failure is fixed, and does not cover the pending-CDC scenario. Evidence: build/audit-1.0-restore-acceptance.log.
  • Dashboard: 21 tests in 6 files passed; production build passed. npm audit reported zero vulnerabilities in its response on this date.
  • scripts/check-production-chart.py passed, as did all 8 publication-tooling unit tests. The additional disruption-budget assertion failed.
  • govulncheck on the pure-Go server/client/command packages reported no called-symbol vulnerabilities. It reported two findings in required modules outside the imported/called code. This is a dated scan, not a zero-risk claim.
  • Targeted Rust/cgo probes under -race completed across all eight selected packages. All nine earlier issue categories and all three new Go probes reproduced; no data race or test timeout was reported. These are failing correctness assertions, not a passing race suite. Evidence: build/audit-1.0-race-probes.jsonl and its stderr log.

An earlier native Windows suite run was stopped before its overall completion; the complete suite result above is the Linux run. This review did not rebuild or rescan the shipped container, run the entire acceptance campaign, perform a live Kubernetes drain, or run real multi-host/power-loss tests.

docs.title: Release gates beyond fixing individual defects
docs.text:
These are proposed 1.0 acceptance requirements, not additional confirmed bugs.

  1. Data-conservation fault campaign. Exercise 3-to-5 node growth, staged replacement, drains/removal and leader failures at every reconfiguration step. Track every acknowledged event through recovery and eventual delivery, with out-of-order ACKs, retries, duplicate detection maintenance and encrypted logs. Allow only the documented at-least-once duplicates, and no early delivery.
  2. Representative sustained load on separate hosts. Establish supported payload sizes, event rates, backlog, p99 lateness, memory and disk envelopes. Include slow consumers, failing CDC, repeated restarts and disk pressure. A suggested starting gate is a 24–72 hour soak; duration alone is not proof. The current release docs explicitly lack multi-host/capacity evidence.
  3. Recovery and compatibility drills. Restore pending CDC, scheduled work, consumer progress and DLQ state; refill a replica beyond the previously tested size; measure recovery point/time. Test v0.9-to-1.0 upgrade and supported rollback/format boundaries. Test machine/power-loss durability before claiming that guarantee; a killed process is a different failure.
  4. Bounded operation and honest stable contracts. Choose tested limits and runbooks for pinned WAL segments, DLQ journal growth, group creation and overload. Automatic snapshot catch-up, manual rebalance and tenant quota configuration are documented gaps; they may remain excluded or constrained, but exposed APIs/flags must not imply unsupported behavior. Publish explicit topic/idempotency, ACK, replay, compatibility and supported-platform contracts.
