  5. Release-candidate evidence. Run required CI, race and pure-Go suites, complete acceptance/container/Helm tests, fresh dependency and image scans on the final candidate. Fix or explain intermittent failures without treating a lucky rerun as closure. Publish the tested digest and recovery documentation; close the documented signed-provenance gap or explicitly record that limitation.

No production files were changed by this review. The deliverables are this assessment and the three opt-in probe files. The known-issue list is a lower bound supported by the evidence above, not a proof that other defects do not exist.

docs.title: CronosDB v0.10.0
docs.text: This release fixes the thirteen defects confirmed by the 1.0 readiness review. Two could lose acknowledged writes: a change of replica placement, and a retried publish after a change of leader. Others delayed scheduled events, accepted duplicates, stopped an encrypted node from starting, or made reads come back empty. It keeps the version-2 WAL format of v0.9.0: v0.9.0 data directories are used as they are. It is not 1.0: the release gates the review lists are still open.

docs.title: Changes
docs.text:
• A replica that placement drops stays in elections until it is no longer needed. Placement used to drop a replica at once, before its replacement had copied anything. The leader went on replicating to the dropped node and counting its acknowledgements, while elections no longer asked it. A leader failure in that window could elect a replica without writes acknowledged with its help; growing a cluster by two nodes could elect an empty replica. A dropped replica is now retiring: elections ask it and count it, and it keeps its copy. A leader stops replicating to it before taking up the new assignment. The retiring list is cleared once the leader has done so and enough remaining replicas hold its log. If the leader and a retiring replica both fail before then, the partition waits for one of them rather than elect a replica that may lack acknowledged writes.
  • A retried publish is acknowledged only once it is committed. A retry can concern an entry an earlier leadership term wrote. Replication now goes on through the current term's start record, which is what commits it.
  • Scheduled events no longer drift later over time. The scheduler's wheel advanced one tick per timer fire, so every pause of its worker (a pass loading events from disk, garbage collection, CPU throttling) delayed every later event for good. It now advances to the time the clock shows, and never past it.
  • Duplicate detection keeps accepted IDs. Hourly maintenance emptied the bloom filter without reloading the stored IDs, and judged it full under ordinary traffic; retries of accepted IDs were then accepted again. The filter is rebuilt from the store, with checks going to the store meanwhile, and only when it really is too full.
  • Message IDs are unique per topic. The same ID on two topics used to be refused the second time, and a client allowed to publish to one topic could block, or detect, IDs used on another.
  • An encrypted node starts after a crash during a write. An encrypted record that was not completely written stopped the log from opening, and cronos-admin check-log --repair could not fix it. It is now cut off like a torn plaintext record. A wrong key, or a complete record that does not decrypt, still stops the log.
  • Reads no longer come back empty after a crash. The sparse index could hold a partial entry after a crash, and after the next two restarts reads of the events behind it returned nothing, without an error. The index is now written in whole entries, cut back to its last valid entry when opened, and a read it points to the wrong place reads the segment from its start.
  • Backups keep the change feed's position. A restored partition started its Kafka/webhook export at the end of its log, and events not yet exported when the backup was taken were never exported.
  • Go SDK. With a CheckpointStore, the SDK saves only the completion floor the server reports: every offset below it is complete. It used to save the offset after the last acknowledged delivery, and since events are delivered in schedule order, a consumer that resumed from it skipped unfinished events. With CommitStrategySync, Ack now returns the server's answer, including refusals; it used to return once the acknowledgement was queued.
  • Limits on what clients create. Consumer group names and subscription IDs are at most 255 bytes, and a partition holds at most --max-consumer-groups groups (default 10000). A replay's speed must be 0 or at least 0.001, and cancelling a replay ends its pause.
  • Helm chart. The disruption budget allows one pod down at a time (podDisruptionBudget.maxUnavailable). It used to keep floor(RF/2)+1 pods, which let a drain take 3 of 5 production pods at once. Pods are spread across Kubernetes nodes (podAntiAffinity, soft by default); the production values require it (hard), so they need one node per pod.

docs.title: Upgrade and compatibility
docs.text:
v0.9.0 data directories are kept. The WAL format is unchanged. Stop every node, upgrade, and start them again: mixed-version clusters remain unsupported, and cluster metadata gains a field that v0.9.0 nodes drop.

  • Duplicate-detection records written by v0.9.0 are not carried over. Until dedup TTL (--dedup-ttl, 168 hours by default) has passed since the upgrade, a retry of a message ID first accepted by v0.9.0 is accepted again.
  • A local SDK checkpoint saved by an earlier SDK may be past unfinished events. Clear checkpoint stores when upgrading the SDK; the server's own progress is kept.
  • Subscriptions to a consumer group whose name is longer than 255 bytes are refused.
  • The production Helm values need at least as many Kubernetes nodes as replicaCount. Set podAntiAffinity: soft to run them on fewer.

The chart's version and default image tag are 0.10.0. A downgrade to v0.9.0 has not been tested. The v0.8.0 capability and v0.9.0 format constraints still apply. Delivery remains at least once.

docs.title: Validation and artifacts
docs.text:
Every defect has a regression test that failed on v0.9.0's source (77a9d49) and passes here. The full Go suite passes, the changed packages pass under the race detector, and the process acceptance suite passes on three-node clusters. Node logs from its node-replacement and node-removal runs show the retiring path: a leader removes the former follower, and the former replica is released once the remaining replicas hold the log. The required CI checks passed on PR #17.

The release gates in the readiness review remain open: a sustained multi-host soak, recovery and upgrade drills, and machine or power-loss testing. No new throughput or capacity claim is made. The remaining release limits continue to apply.

Publication status, binary checksums, the image scan and exact image identity are recorded on the v0.10.0 release. The binaries cover Linux and macOS amd64/arm64 and Windows amd64 and use the Go bloom filter. The container is Linux amd64 and uses the Rust implementation. release.yml stages the scanned and fault-tested image archive on a draft release; local publication loads that exact archive, verifies its config and layers, pushes johnny711dock/cronos-db:0.10.0 and moves latest. Pin the IMAGE_DIGEST recorded on the release for deployments. Local publication has no signed GitHub workflow provenance.

docs.title: CronosDB v0.8.0
docs.text: This release line adds opt-in future-event cancellation, rescheduling and bounded WAL relocation. It also fixes commitment of old-term entries after leader changes. Implementation and regression coverage were merged in PR #8.

docs.title: Changes
docs.text:
• --event-lifecycle enables cancellation and rescheduling through GetEventState, CancelEvent and RescheduleEvent. Save the publish receipt's partition, offset, term, message ID and topic. Mutations require the expected revision and a request ID; retry an ambiguous result unchanged.
  • --wal-relocation-bytes bounds how much future work a retention pass may move from the oldest closed segment. Zero disables copying. A retained replacement preserves the original logical identity after its root is pruned.
  • New leaders commit older entries only after a durable current-term term-start record reaches the required replicas. Idle partitions receive the same proof. Internal records consume physical offsets and stay out of user delivery, public replay and change-feed output.
  • Recovery handles lost mutation replies, promotion, restart, suffix replacement and offset reuse. Staged mutations freeze their predecessor without releasing its retention obligations. Relocation reaches quorum before the predecessor can be pruned.
  • Lifecycle snapshots and full backups carry a recovery manifest tying the WAL cut to its epoch, accepted boundary, consumer progress and dead letters. Recovery pages are bounded, checksummed and encrypted with the WAL key when encryption is enabled. A crash after WAL publication resumes import before the partition serves work.
  • Acceptance nodes use their own memory policy instead of inheriting a runner's GOMEMLIMIT. With that correction, the process backlog campaign delivered all 9,389 acknowledged events at 81 MiB peak against a 117 MiB limit.

docs.title: Upgrade and compatibility
docs.text:
Lifecycle operations remain off by default. Standalone use requires RF=1 and --min-insync-replicas=1. Replicated lifecycle operations require majority acknowledgements and every assigned replica, handoff target and Raft voter to advertise the required formats before the coordinator activates them.

Term-start activation also waits for all assigned replicas and voters. A mixed-version cluster retains legacy commit accounting until agreement, including its old-term limitation. Complete the upgrade before relying on the new guarantee. Once activated, format requirements persist through placement and elections; downgrade to a build that ignores them is unsupported.

Version 1 rejects lifecycle operations combined with CDC, cross-region replication, experimental transactions or online partition splitting. Cancellation applies only to future work, not to events already delivered. Delivery remains at least once. Existing performance measurements are for v0.7.0; no new throughput claim is made for v0.8.0.

The Helm chart's version and default application image tag are 0.8.0. The release and Linux amd64 image were published on 2026-10-19; pin the image manifest digest below for deployments.

docs.title: Validation and artifacts
docs.text:
All six checks passed on the implementation revision 8bb7e2b, including Linux cgo/race and non-cgo suites, the process fault campaign, Docker network partitions and memory-limited restart, security scans, and production chart startup with TLS, authentication and encryption. The required source checks also passed on the release preparation revision ed7910f before promotion to main (successful check run).

The GitHub release carries server and cronos-admin binaries for Linux and macOS (amd64 and arm64) and Windows (amd64), with SHA256SUMS. These binaries use the Go bloom filter; the Linux amd64 container uses the Rust implementation.

A manual preparation run of release.yml stages the tested image as cronos-db_v0.8.0_linux_amd64_image.tar.gz, plus IMAGE_ID, IMAGE_ARCHIVE_SHA256 and release-image-scan.json, on a draft release. The gzip archive can be loaded directly with docker load --input <archive>. IMAGE_ID identifies its config digest; a local engine may display a manifest digest instead. Neither is a signed provenance statement.

johnny711dock/cronos-db:0.8.0 (Linux amd64) was published from local Docker on 2026-10-19 using the exact staged image archive above. Its config digest and all nine filesystem layers match the scanned image. Local admin and server readiness checks passed, and the published image was verified through anonymous Docker Hub registry requests.

Pin the published image for deployments:

docker pull johnny711dock/cronos-db@sha256:428690215148b97eb9b6aaed5a3afb7c7a3227613c8fee731ab922e2276d4928

IMAGE_DIGEST and LOCAL_PUBLICATION_EVIDENCE.json record the registry digest, source revision and verification. This local publication has no signed GitHub workflow provenance. Docker Hub's latest was moved to this image on 2026-10-19 as an OCI index (sha256:a17853491e12898cfa22fa8b698c7c41d7f70ac3773da74c499226ad3efec176) whose only entry, linux/amd64, is the manifest above, so both tags run the same image. Pin the digest above for deployments.

Automated publication through release.yml requires repository secrets DOCKERHUB_USERNAME and DOCKERHUB_TOKEN. That workflow builds, scans and fault-tests an image, pushes it and attests its registry digest. Local Docker publication uses the workstation's saved Docker Hub login instead.

The existing limits in the release requirements still apply: validation uses one host, has not simulated a machine power cut, and does not establish deployment-specific throughput or very large refill performance. Dead-letter journal history is not compacted. Relocation is opt-in and does not make unfinished due events removable.

See the lifecycle contract and current-term commitment protocol for details.

docs.title: CronosDB v0.8.1
docs.text: This patch contains security dependency updates and two concurrency fixes found while validating the v0.8.0 documentation audit. It retains the v0.8.0 lifecycle and current-term commitment protocols.

docs.title: Changes
docs.text:
• Go 1.26.10 replaces 1.26.9 in the module and container builder, addressing GO-2026-6809 in crypto/x509.
  • Vite 7.3.7 replaces 7.3.6, including fixes for the bundled launch-editor advisories. github.com/klauspost/compress v1.18.7 replaces v1.18.2 to fix CVE-2026-63209 in dictionary processing.
  • Consumer-group initialization finishes before a live subscription is exposed to delivery, so its first acknowledgement can record completion. Duplicate subscription IDs are rejected before changing membership, and server-assigned subscriptions join their resolved partition.
  • Deduplication IDs remain visible to existence, offset and timestamp lookups while their pending buffer is being committed to Pebble. Failed flushes keep the buffered entries available for retry.
  • The documentation audit corrects release status, lifecycle and retention behavior, recovery guarantees, configuration flags and unsupported features. Its per-document report is available here.

docs.title: Upgrade and compatibility
docs.text:
The Helm chart's version and default image tag are 0.8.1. There is no new WAL or replication format in this patch. The v0.8.0 capability activation and downgrade constraints still apply; see the v0.8.0 notes. Lifecycle operations remain opt-in, and delivery remains at least once.

Existing v0.8.0 binaries and images retain their original contents. Use the v0.8.1 artifacts to obtain these fixes. No new throughput or multi-host capacity claim is made. The remaining release limits continue to apply.

docs.title: Validation and artifacts
docs.text:
The implementation passed all required source checks before PR #10 merged: Linux cgo/race and non-cgo suites, the process fault campaign, security scans, dashboard/chart checks, container network faults, memory-limited restart and production chart startup. The paused-flush regression and strengthened dedup concurrency test also passed 100 local non-cgo repetitions; the dedup package passed 20 local cgo/race repetitions. Release preparation runs the required checks again on the final release revision.

Publication status, binary checksums, the image scan and exact image identity are recorded on the v0.8.1 release. The binaries cover Linux and macOS amd64/arm64 and Windows amd64. They use the Go bloom filter. The container is Linux amd64 and uses the Rust implementation.

release.yml stages the scanned and fault-tested image archive on a draft release. Local Docker publication loads that exact archive and verifies its config and filesystem layers before pushing johnny711dock/cronos-db:0.8.1 and promoting latest. IMAGE_DIGEST and LOCAL_PUBLICATION_EVIDENCE.json on the release record the registry identity and verification. Pin that digest for deployments; latest is a mutable convenience tag. Local publication has no signed GitHub workflow provenance.

After local publication and evidence upload, dispatch publish-staged-release.yml with --ref main -f tag=v0.8.1. It verifies the successful staging run, uploaded checksums and registry tags before publishing the draft as the latest GitHub release. It does not rebuild the image or need Docker Hub write credentials in GitHub.

docs.title: CronosDB v0.9.0
docs.text: This release changes the on-disk WAL segment format and requires new data directories. It detects erased areas of closed log segments that earlier versions could not tell from unused space, and it fixes a node crash that a scheduled backup could cause while a partition was being moved away. The lifecycle and current-term commitment protocols of v0.8.0 are unchanged.

docs.title: Changes
docs.text:
• WAL segment format version 2. A new segment's header records the closed predecessor's first offset, last offset and byte end, covered by the header checksum. A segment is preallocated, so zero bytes after its last readable record look the same whether they are unused space or erased data; record checksums cannot tell the two apart once every record beyond that point is gone, and the sparse index can be missing or stale. Startup and cronos-admin check-log now compare each recorded boundary with the prefix they recover and refuse to open a log that does not match, including a zeroed tail with no index. A verified indexed record beyond the point where reading stops also marks damage in the active tail. See closed WAL segment boundaries.
  • Repair stays explicit. check-log --repair cuts a damaged segment after its last readable record and updates the successor's boundary. It discards every later record in that segment, and reports that the last discarded offset is unknown when no segment follows. It refuses to change a segment whose recovered records extend past the recorded boundary; restore a backup or rebuild the replica from its leader instead. For a replicated partition, rebuilding from a healthy leader is preferred.
  • Backups and restore check the format first. cronos-admin restore and the WAL restore path reject a backup holding version-1 segments before anything is published, so an incompatible backup cannot appear to restore and then fail at the next start. The legacy incremental backup keeps the last closed segment's boundary by copying the active segment's header as an empty successor.
  • A scheduled backup can no longer crash a node. A backup that overlapped the release of a partition, or a shutdown, could use that partition's stores after they were closed. The storage engine panics on that instead of returning an error, which ended the whole process. A partition is now kept open until a running backup has finished with it, and a backup that begins after a partition was stopped leaves it out. A partition is also stopped only once, however many callers reach it.
  • The Go 1.26.10 toolchain of v0.8.1 is kept. The dashboard's test tooling moves to undici 7.30.1 and vitest 4.1.12 to clear new advisories; these are development dependencies and do not ship in the dashboard bundle.

docs.title: Upgrade and compatibility
docs.text:
Start with new, empty data directories on every node. This version reads and writes only version-2 segments. It rejects version-1 logs and backups with an error that names the version it found, and it does not migrate them. Older binaries reject version-2 segments. Rolling upgrades and mixed-version clusters are unsupported, and a version-1 backup must not be restored into a version-2 cluster. Keep existing data directories separately if their contents might be needed.

The Helm chart's version and default image tag are 0.9.0. There is no new replication format, and the v0.8.0 capability activation and downgrade constraints still apply; see the v0.8.0 notes. Lifecycle operations remain opt-in, and delivery remains at least once.

Existing v0.8.1 binaries and images retain their original contents. Boundary evidence protects closed segments created by this version. The currently active segment has no closed boundary, deleting whole files together with their evidence is outside what it can detect, and records are checked when a log is opened, not continuously. No new throughput or multi-host capacity claim is made. The remaining release limits continue to apply.

docs.title: Validation and artifacts
docs.text:
The storage, partition, replication and compliance suites pass, and so does the process acceptance suite on three-node clusters, including backup and restore, node replacement, certificate rotation and a restart with a backlog larger than memory. The container tests (network faults and memory-limited restart) run against the exact image when it is staged. The backup crash has two regression tests: one reproduced the failure's stack trace before the change, and the other shows a release waiting for a backup that is using the partition. Release preparation runs the required checks again on the final release revision.

Publication status, binary checksums, the image scan and exact image identity are recorded on the v0.9.0 release. The binaries cover Linux and macOS amd64/arm64 and Windows amd64. They use the Go bloom filter. The container is Linux amd64 and uses the Rust implementation.

docs.title: Current-term commitment and term-start records
docs.text:
Released in v0.8.0. The coordinator activates this protocol after capability agreement; it does not require --event-lifecycle. A mixed cluster retains legacy commitment accounting, including the old-term defect, until agreement. Complete the upgrade before relying on this guarantee.

An entry written by an earlier leader is not committed just because a later leader copies it to enough replicas. A conflicting replica whose last log term is newer can still win the next election and replace it. The regression in internal/api/old_term_quorum_test.go reproduces this with three real WALs: term 2 leaves y only on A, term 3 leaves conflicting z only on B, and A leads again in term 4 and copies y to C. Replica counting alone previously delivered y, although B could then lead and remove it.

The fix follows the current-term commitment restriction in the Raft paper, section 5.4.2: confirming an entry of the leader's current term also commits the prefix before it.

docs.title: Commitment boundary
docs.text:
A partition in term-start mode appends an internal record when a local leader activates a term, including after a restart. The marker has no message ID, topic, payload or schedule; its only metadata is cronos.internal.term_start=1. The WAL assigns its physical offset and term. The leader fsyncs it before publishes can follow, and a follower fsyncs any replicated batch containing it before acknowledging. Catch-up transfers it on an idle partition too.

The replication leader remembers the offset of that durable local marker. A replica-count watermark below the marker proves no new commitment. Once enough replicas acknowledge the marker or a later entry, the confirmed prefix is committed. This proof stays valid when a follower disconnects or is removed; delivery, held-write resolution, retention and export use the same boundary. A new epoch installs a fresh commit generation so a delayed calculation or cached acknowledgement cannot act as its predecessor's proof. Quorum checks use memory and add no per-event disk reads or fsyncs.

Repeated reconciliation of one running leader writes no extra marker. A new epoch, or a restart that reactivates leadership, writes one. The record consumes a physical WAL offset but does not represent a user publish or consumer ACK.

A retried publish can concern an entry of an earlier term, before the marker: the earlier attempt reached this leader's log and then failed. Replication of an entry below the marker continues through the marker (Leader.Replicate), so the retry is acknowledged only once the entry is committed. Before 1.0 the retry replicated the entry alone and was acknowledged once a quorum held it, which proves nothing for an older-term entry.

docs.title: Rolling upgrades and durable format requirements
docs.text:
This build advertises term-start/1. The coordinator adds that requirement to a replicated partition only when every assigned replica, handoff target and Raft voter is alive and advertises support. Requirements are one-way Raft metadata: placement, elections and replacement voters must continue honoring them. A membership advertisement alone is not permission to change a log.

Before agreement, the partition uses the legacy format and commit accounting, including its old-term limitation. Mixed clusters do not receive new records. After agreement, reconciliation switches the leader and persists term-start.version before its first control append. Downgrading a required partition or a voter to a build that ignores requirements is unsupported. Replicated lifecycle mutations additionally require this commit protocol. Lifecycle activation is opt-in, and also waits for every assigned replica and Raft voter to advertise the lifecycle append and recovery snapshot protocol.

Every append, catch-up request and empty probe of a term-start log uses the dedicated AppendTermStart RPC. It names the term-start format and, independently, the lifecycle format when required. An older server returns Unimplemented; the sender never falls back to ordinary append. Updated receivers also reject plain/lifecycle-only appends once the partition requires term-start support. Malformed control records and unsupported versions are rejected before appending.

Snapshots advertise and verify the term-start format before installing files. The source captures the format and WAL checkpoint under the replication lock, so a concurrent format switch cannot put controls in a legacy snapshot. The receiver persists its marker before installing the WAL. Full backups retain the marker, while recovery recognizes retained controls when rebuilding stores.

docs.title: Reader behavior
docs.text:
• Delivery and scheduling discard term-start records. Public replay also waits behind the committed boundary and never emits a control record.
  • Dedup recovery does not claim their empty message IDs. Consumer progress continues to refer to the physical offsets of actual delivered events.
  • Retention treats an accepted control as terminal without requiring a matching consumer group. An uncommitted control cannot release a segment.
  • Change feeds skip controls but advance through their physical offsets. Remote fetch reads the committed prefix and returns next_offset so even a page containing only controls can advance its cursor. Older clients can ignore this additive response field and still receive no internal events.
  • Partition splitting skips controls; a leadership proof belongs to its source log and is not a publish to copy into another partition.

The regression tests cover old-prefix catch-up without its term-start record, idle commitment once the record arrives, epoch changes, quorum loss, incompatible receivers, capability agreement, election preference, malformed records, snapshot refusal/install/restart, interrupted snapshot retries, lost success replies followed by leader death, change-feed cursors, retention and backup recovery.

The three-node acceptance campaign compares authenticated physical WAL snapshots, including control records, for contiguous offsets and identical events on every replica. Public replay cannot establish that invariant because it omits controls and serves only a leader's committed prefix. Restoring the old replica-count-only rule makes the old-term regression fail even with the new versioned transport still enabled.

docs.title: WAL retention, cancellation, and rescheduling
docs.text: Status: released in v0.8.0, off by default. Standalone nodes use RF=1 and --min-insync-replicas=1 in development mode; production requires a replicated cluster. Replicated clusters activate only after every assigned replica, handoff target and Raft voter advertises the required protocols. Activation persists a one-way format requirement.

docs.title: Contract
docs.text:
--event-lifecycle enables future-event cancellation and rescheduling. A replicated cluster requires majority acknowledgements. Standalone RF=1 uses --min-insync-replicas=1. --wal-relocation-bytes optionally sets a byte budget for moving future work out of the oldest closed WAL segment; zero disables copying. The matching environment variables are CRONOS_EVENT_LIFECYCLE and CRONOS_WAL_RELOCATION_BYTES.

The WAL remains authoritative. A change appends a self-contained successor; it never edits the original record. A payload-free index is rebuilt from the retained WAL before readers run. Consumer acknowledgements always refer to the physical offsets actually delivered, so moving work never inherits an old copy's completion.

Save the publish receipt's partition, offset and term together with message ID and topic as an EventReference. The Go producer exposes the term in SendResult. GetEventState returns the current revision. CancelEvent and RescheduleEvent require that revision and a unique request ID. Retry an ambiguous request unchanged; a completed retry does not append another record. Aborted means the revision changed, NotFound means the reference expired or never matched, and Unavailable means its outcome is unresolved or this node cannot serve it. Only future events can be changed; cancellation is terminal. Rescheduling also requires a future timestamp. This is not a recall protocol for events already sent to consumers.

docs.title: Identity and staged state
docs.text:
A logical identity is (partition, original offset, original term, message ID, topic). Its term prevents an offset reused after recovery from selecting a different event. Rescheduling and relocation preserve that identity. User mutations create a new revision; relocation preserves the last user revision and request history. The reference remains valid after its original physical record is pruned while a retained successor represents it. Deduplication TTL is never the recovery frontier.

A staged successor freezes delivery of its predecessor immediately. It does not make that predecessor removable. Only an accepted successor proves that an old copy is terminal for retention; an accepted cancellation is itself terminal. An unresolved mutation cannot release a prefix, report success, reach public replay, or cause repeated evacuation of a pinned segment.

The delivery gate excludes a mutation through durable local append and index update. In a cluster, the append lock preserves WAL order while replication runs. Success requires durable acknowledgement by the configured replicas. Timeout after append has an unknown outcome: the record is held until catch-up proves its acceptance or another leader's suffix replaces it. A later retry resolves that outcome using the original request ID and revision.

The current-term commitment protocol establishes the accepted boundary after promotion. Counting old-term replicas alone cannot release work. A new leader's durable term-start record must reach the required replicas before its preceding log is committed, including on idle partitions.

docs.title: Format and recovery
docs.text:
Version 1 uses CRC-protected WAL records with reserved cronos.internal.* metadata. Public publish and batch publish reject that namespace. Cancel records have no payload; reschedule and relocate records contain the complete event. Public delivery and replay remove the lifecycle envelope and skip term-start records entirely.

The disk-backed index stores the local head, mutation offsets and terms, and cleanup keys without payloads. Accepted-state queries seek directly to the newest retained mutation at or below the supplied boundary. Rebuild uses at most 1,024 offsets with a 4 MiB target per chunk; a chunk may exceed the byte target by one valid record. Readers see a complete generation. A failed rebuild or conflicting observation fails delivery and retention closed.

A suffix cut forgets invalid consumer completions and rebuilds the index under the delivery gate before offsets can be reused. Cached records removed by that cut stay inactive. Promotion reconstructs timers from the surviving log and uses a fresh current-term proof before allowing delivery. A successful cancellation does not resurrect after failover. A retained reschedule or relocation represents one pending event after recovery.

Standalone lifecycle nodes persist a new generation term on open, protecting receipts from periodic-fsync offset reuse. Cluster nodes preserve the epoch assigned by the coordinator on reopen; they do not invent an unassigned epoch. They accept election fences and replicated progress, while standalone lifecycle partitions refuse those requests.

docs.title: Replication and rolling upgrades
docs.text:
Nodes advertise lifecycle-records/1, lifecycle-replication/1 and term-start/1 when their configuration supports lifecycle data. Enabling --event-lifecycle on cluster nodes asks the coordinator to commit that one-way requirement. Every assigned replica, handoff target and Raft voter must be alive and capable first. Before agreement, mutations are refused. Placement, elections, handoffs and replacement voter admission continue to honor the durable requirement afterwards. Downgrading a required partition or voter to a build that ignores capabilities is unsupported.

Every request of a term-start log, including empty probes and catch-up, uses AppendTermStart, independently naming both record formats. Older servers answer Unimplemented; there is no fallback to ordinary append. Receivers validate versions, requirements and envelopes before storing records. The lifecycle-only AppendLifecycle transport remains for format compatibility; it cannot carry term-start records.

docs.title: Retention and relocation
docs.text:
Pruning removes a contiguous prefix of closed segments. A pass may move active, never-due work out of the oldest selected segment within its encoded byte budget. It does not bypass disk admission, unresolved mutations, unfinished due work, change-feed progress or durable dead-letter replication. The active segment is not evacuated.

A replicated evacuation uses the append lock and replicates its durable replacement in WAL order. It cannot prune the predecessor until quorum acceptance. An interrupted pass stages at most the budget it was given; catch-up resolves that state, and a later pass does not duplicate the copy. The leader advertises the new log start only after proving retention safe. A follower behind that start resets there and receives the retained successor. Raising its consumer floor must not complete that successor's newer offset.

An accepted cancellation or superseded record has no remaining consumer obligation. The active replacement still does. An unaccepted control cannot release a segment. Index cleanup is bounded and advances the retained floor, so old cached references cannot become active after their heads are collected.

docs.title: Consistent recovery snapshots and backups
docs.text:
A lifecycle snapshot requires recovery format 1 in addition to the record formats. Its manifest names partition, epoch, physical first/last offsets and accepted boundary. Consumer progress is captured before dead letters while appends and suffix replacement are excluded. Progress beyond the captured accepted boundary is omitted. Recovery pages are bounded, checksummed and written with an explicit footer. Payload-bearing pages use the WAL's encryption key when encryption at rest is enabled.

The receiver validates the complete transfer and manifest before switching WAL generations. Recovery pages move with the segments through the existing journaled install. An interrupted transfer leaves the old live state intact. After publication, stale local completion records are cleared, dead letters are made durable, and then matching consumer progress is imported and synced. The recovery file remains until import completes. A crash after WAL publication therefore resumes import on startup before the partition serves work. It cannot combine old mutation heads or completions with newly reused offsets.

Full backups retain lifecycle and term-start markers and include the same recovery manifest/pages alongside their WAL cut. Restore validates files, selects a complete WAL generation and reconstructs the index. An encrypted backup requires the matching master key. Credentials and key material are not included in backups.

docs.title: Change feeds and migration
docs.text:
Version 1 supports lifecycle operations without CDC, cross-region replication, transactions or online partition splitting. Those combinations are rejected explicitly before enabling the format; nodes configured for them do not advertise lifecycle replication support. A raw publish sink has no cancellation or reschedule contract, so controls must never be presented to it as new publishes. Adding logical-operation sinks or migration identity mappings is a separate feature, not a fallback in this protocol.

Ordinary term-start clusters can continue using change feeds. Feeds skip term-start records while advancing physical cursors; cross-region fetch also returns next_offset for a control-only page. It exports only the committed prefix. Partition splitting skips term-start records because a leadership proof belongs to its original log.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Focused tests cover revisions, exact retries, forged envelopes, due-event rejection, delivery/mutation exclusion, staged versus accepted history, periodic fsync, encryption, bounded relocation, pruning and backup restore. Replication tests cover current-term proof, lost success replies, leader death, restart, election fences, consumer progress, suffix replacement and offset reuse, retained replacements whose roots were pruned, incompatible receivers, and interrupted snapshot installation. Snapshot tests include a crash after WAL publication but before recovery-state import.

Three-node acceptance tests compare authenticated physical WAL snapshots for contiguous offsets and identical events, including internal records. The lifecycle campaign activates through committed capabilities, cancels and reschedules future work, loses its leader, restarts the entire cluster, and checks delivery after the original schedule has passed. The general campaign also exercises node replacement, retention and whole-cluster loss.

Use low Go concurrency on the development laptop; do not substitute a throughput benchmark for invariant and fault tests. Acceptance node processes must use their own memory policy rather than inherit a test runner's GOMEMLIMIT. Run both native race tests and the non-cgo release suite, plus the Docker network-partition and container-memory checks in CI before release.

docs.title: Closed WAL segment boundaries
docs.text: A segment is preallocated, so zero bytes after the last readable record can be either unused space or erased data. Record checksums alone cannot distinguish the two if all records beyond that point are gone. A sparse index is also not an authoritative boundary: it can be absent, incomplete or stale.

docs.title: Boundary evidence
docs.text:
For a newly rotated segment, the header of its successor records the closed segment's first and last offsets and logical byte end. The successor header's existing CRC covers these fields. The predecessor is flushed and synced before the successor header is created and synced; its directory entry is synced on platforms that support directory fsync. A failure while publishing the header fences the WAL if publication is uncertain. Version 2 uses the same header size and places the boundary in bytes previously reserved by version 1. The layout is BND1 at bytes 32–35, followed by three big-endian 64-bit values at bytes 36–59: predecessor first offset, last offset, and logical byte end. The existing CRC covers bytes 0–59. Every successor must contain BND1; the first retained segment may omit it.

At startup and during cronos-admin check-log, recovery compares each recorded boundary to the prefix recovered from the preceding segment. A mismatch is reported as log damage, including when the successor is empty, and startup fails closed. This does not rely on an index. Explicit offline repair cuts the damaged segment at its last readable record and updates the successor boundary; it discards all later records in that segment, even if some could still be read. If readable records extend beyond the recorded boundary, offline repair refuses to change the segment; restore a backup or rebuild the replica instead. For a replicated partition, prefer rebuilding the replica from a healthy leader or restoring a backup over cutting out data.

WAL checkpoints and full backups copy the successor header along with the log. The legacy incremental backup excludes active records but copies the active header as an empty successor when it carries the last closed segment's boundary; a later incremental backup replaces that placeholder with the full segment. Snapshot copies of an active segment are cuts, so events appended after the cut are not included. The legacy incremental BackupWAL helper is not a coordinated live checkpoint; do not use it concurrently with truncation or retention. Production full backups use coordinated checkpoint cuts.

docs.title: Interrupted operations
docs.text: A successor's original boundary stays in place until that successor is deleted during follower truncation. A crash after its predecessor was shortened but before the successor was deleted may therefore cause startup to fail closed; rebuild that replica from its leader. Repair writes and syncs the discarded tail before updating the successor's header. A torn header update fails the header CRC and requires recovery from a healthy replica or backup.

docs.title: Clean-start requirement and limits
docs.text:
From v0.9.0 the server reads and writes only version-2 WAL segments. It rejects version-1 data and backups without modifying or migrating their WAL segments. Older binaries reject version-2 segments. Start with new, empty data directories and use the updated binary on every node; rolling upgrades and mixed-version clusters are unsupported. Keep existing directories separately if their data might be needed. Do not restore a version-1 backup into a version-2 cluster.

The currently active segment has no closed boundary; a zeroed active tail can still resemble an interrupted write. Removing a successor (including by retention) also removes the evidence it contains, and deletion of whole files, simultaneous loss of data and its evidence, maliciously recomputed checksums, and continuous detection while a node is running are outside this mechanism. The sparse-index check can identify some additional damage but is not a proof that the rest of a log is intact.

docs.title: CronosDB Architecture By Feature
docs.text: This folder contains the architecture split by feature so developers can read subsystem docs independently.

docs.title: Production-Hardening Highlights (current code)
docs.text:
• WAL v2 record format with Raft term and payload checksum; pre-v2 layouts have no automatic migration. The v0.7.0 to v0.8.0 upgrade uses capability agreement.
  • Encryption at rest v2 uses a random 12-byte GCM nonce per record; legacy v1 counter nonces remain decrypt-only.
  • Persistent consumer group metadata in OffsetStore. Exactly-once commit IDs exist in OffsetStore, but --exactly-once-commits is refused in production and the Ack path does not read it.
  • DLQ wired per partition at create time (NewDispatcherWithDLQ).
  • Dedup crash recovery reseeds claims from the WAL tail on partition start.
  • Restart does not load the backlog: timer replay schedules only events whose time has not come; events already due stay in the log and each subscription reads them at its consumers' pace (redriveRetained).
  • Change feed for CDC (and experimental cross-region replication): accepted events only, in log order, from the partition's leader, with a position that survives restarts and failovers. A failing sink makes its feed lag; nothing is dropped.
  • Log-start pruning: compaction and retention remove segments only through Partition.PruneWAL. Active events must be due, completed and exported; accepted terminal controls and superseded copies have no consumer obligation. Replicated and standalone lifecycle partitions prune a contiguous prefix; followers follow their leader's log start. Optional bounded relocation moves never-due work only after the replacement is accepted.
  • Backups and restore: scheduled checkpoints of every partition at wall-clock multiples of --backup-interval; cronos-admin restore, and cronos-admin check-log to report or cut a damaged segment.
  • Memory guard: publishes are refused while the process holds --max-memory-percent of its memory limit (cgroup limit by default).
  • Listener split:
  • Public gRPC :9000 — Event, Partition, ConsumerGroup, Admin (Transaction only with --dev --experimental-features)
  • Internal gRPC :7947 — Replication, Raft (mTLS in production; CrossRegion only with --dev --experimental-features)
  • HTTP :8080 — health, metrics, /ui/ dashboard, /api/admin/*; TLS with --http-tls-enabled
  • Certificate hot reload: public TLS, HTTP TLS and node-to-node mTLS certificates, keys and CAs are re-read when their files change.
  • Bulk snapshot install (ReplicationService.Snapshot) for join/wipe recovery.
  • Raft-authoritative leadership for local promote/demote reconcile (not gossip-only); the hash ring only proposes placement.
  • Fenced elections and staged handoff: an election first commits that the partition has no leader, fences the replicas at that epoch, then picks the most complete one; a planned leader move waits until the target's log ends at the same entry.
  • Current-term commitment: after capability agreement, a new leader must replicate a durable term-start record before committing an older prefix. Mixed clusters retain legacy behavior until agreement; activation is one-way.
  • Lifecycle (off by default): future-event cancellation/rescheduling uses stable references and idempotent revision checks. Replicated operations require majority acknowledgements and capable replicas/voters. Recovery snapshots bind consumer progress and dead letters to the matching WAL generation. See the lifecycle contract and term-start protocol.
  • Topology from leaders: the admin topology reads each partition's in-sync replicas from its leader (ReplicationService.LeaderReport).
  • Node removal: cronos-admin cluster remove-node <node-id> takes a lost node out of Raft and off every node's member list.
  • Experimental gate: transactions (2PC), online partition splitting and cross-region replication run only with --dev --experimental-features.
  • Production security gate (unless --dev): TLS, JWT auth and policy file, encryption at rest, replication mTLS, RF≥3, minISR≥2, fsync mode batch or every_event, --cluster-seeds in cluster mode; refuses --experimental-features, --exactly-once-commits and a non-loopback --pprof-addr.

docs.text:
These are known product gaps. The release requirements also distinguish unvalidated operating conditions from implemented guarantees. Details and mermaid: ARCHITECTURE.md § Known Limitations.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The API layer is the system entrypoint for all client and internal RPC traffic. It translates contracts into partition-aware operations and enforces security, guardrails, and observability through interceptors.

docs.title: Key Files
docs.text:
• internal/api/grpc_server.go — public listener on :9000; registers EventService, PartitionService, ConsumerGroupService, and AdminService; TransactionService only with --experimental-features (which requires --dev).
  • internal/api/internal_grpc_server.go — dedicated internal listener (InternalGRPCServer, default :7947); registers ReplicationService and, in cluster mode, RaftService; CrossRegionService only with --experimental-features (cmd/api/main.go). Peer traffic never shares the public client port.
  • internal/api/handlers.go — EventService handlers (Publish, PublishBatch, Subscribe, Ack, Replay) with dedup claims and append-outcome reconciliation.
  • internal/api/event_lifecycle.go — GetEventState, CancelEvent, RescheduleEvent; leader routing, publish authorization and disk admission for opt-in lifecycle operations.
  • internal/api/admin_handler.go — operator AdminService (topology, health, lag, retention, compaction, schemas, tenants; TriggerRebalance soft-stub — see Known Limitations). Every RPC requires the global policy flag "admin": true when auth is enabled.
  • internal/api/web_handler.go — embedded SPA + /api/admin/* JSON proxy on HTTP :8080.
  • internal/api/consumer_handler.go — ConsumerGroupService (create, get, list, rebalance) over the consumer-group state of the first local partition (partition 0); requires global "admin": true when auth is enabled.
  • internal/api/partition_handler.go — partition metadata (a valid token is enough) + compact/retention/split (global "admin": true when auth is enabled). See authorization by RPC.
  • internal/api/replication_server.go — Append, versioned AppendLifecycle / AppendTermStart, Sync, Snapshot, Position, LeaderReport, SyncConsumerProgress on the internal listener.
  • internal/api/raft_server.go — Raft join/leave/status and node removal (cronos-admin cluster remove-node) (internal).
  • internal/api/crossregion_server.go — CrossRegion inject/fetch with LWW (internal only).
  • internal/api/audit_interceptor.go — request-level audit interceptor.
  • internal/api/health.go — HTTP health endpoints.
  • internal/api/metrics.go — Prometheus collectors.
  • internal/api/ratelimit.go, internal/api/topic_ratelimit.go — IP and per-topic rate limiters.
  • internal/api/stream_interceptors.go — stream interceptor wiring.
  • internal/api/tls.go — public gRPC TLS / mTLS configuration.
  • internal/api/version.go — wire version gate / rolling upgrade helpers.
  • proto/events.proto, proto/admin.proto — wire contracts.

docs.title: Listener matrix
docs.text: Listener Default Services Public gRPC :9000 Event, Partition, ConsumerGroup, Admin; Transaction (experimental only) Internal gRPC :7947 Replication, Raft (cluster mode); CrossRegion (experimental only) HTTP :8080 /health*, /metrics, /ui/, /api/admin/*; TLS with --http-tls-enabled (certificate from --tls-cert-file / --tls-key-file, no client certificate) pprof off /debug/pprof/* on --pprof-addr when set; a separate listener, loopback-only in production (cmd/api/pprof.go)

docs.title: Main Request Flow
docs.text:
1. cmd/api/main.go starts public and internal gRPC servers plus HTTP.
  2. Public unary/stream interceptors apply tracing, SLO, version, authentication, topic limits, audit, metrics, and IP rate limiting (SLO, metrics and IP rate limiting are skipped when auth is disabled, whether or not --dev is set).
  3. Handlers validate, authorize, and route via partition manager / cluster router.
  4. Internal replication/cross-region RPCs use optional cluster mTLS credentials.

docs.title: Production Decisions
docs.text:
• Start() exposes ServeError() so server startup failures are observable.
  • GracefulStopWithTimeout(ctx) falls back to forced Stop if the deadline expires.
  • Health-server startup errors are propagated rather than swallowed.
  • Message size and keepalive limits are configured in server options to avoid unbounded payload and idle-connection risk.
  • Partition ownership checks in handlers prevent writes on non-owner nodes and fence stale leaders.
  • Replay path respects follower-read policy flags for consistency control.
  • Acks on one stream are read ahead and recorded in batches (up to 256): each partition's completions in a batch are written with one durable commit (processAcks in handlers.go).
  • --exactly-once-commits is refused in production; the Ack path records per-event completions and does not read the flag.
  • Lifecycle RPCs require topic publish permission, including GetEventState, and run on the partition leader. Save the publish receipt's partition, offset, term, message ID and topic. Mutations require an expected revision and request ID; retry an ambiguous result unchanged. Only future events can be changed. Standalone RF=1 and capable replicated clusters are supported with --event-lifecycle; replicated operations require majority acknowledgements. See the lifecycle contract.
  • Public publishes reject reserved cronos.internal.* metadata. Delivery and replay expose active logical events, strip lifecycle envelopes and omit term-start records. Physical offsets can therefore have gaps in public output.

docs.title: Known Limitations (API surface)
docs.text: RPC / path Status Detail AdminService.TriggerRebalance Soft stub Membership-driven rebalance works; on-demand trigger does not move partitions. cluster.md, ARCHITECTURE Cross-region on public port Not exposed Only on internal :7947, and only with --dev --experimental-features TransactionService Experimental Registered only with --dev --experimental-features Subscribe control-stream Recv Not used for credits Flow control via credits/Ack path; control Recv is unused

docs.title: Publish flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Producer
    participant API as EventService.Publish
    participant Auth as Auth / RBAC / schema
    participant PM as PartitionManager
    participant Dedup
    participant WAL
    participant Repl as Replication Leader optional
    participant Scheduler
    participant Worker
    participant Dispatcher
    participant Consumer
    participant Group as ConsumerGroup

    Producer->>API: Publish / PublishBatch
    API->>Auth: JWT topic perms + schema validation optional
    API->>PM: Resolve partition for message_id or meta partition_key
    API->>API: Cluster writability: ownership + leadership + epoch fence
    API->>API: Admission control: ready queue / wheel / in-flight caps
    API->>Dedup: Claim message_id batch
    alt duplicate
      Dedup-->>API: duplicate
      API-->>Producer: duplicate / already exists
    else new
      Dedup-->>API: claimed
      API->>API: Tenant quota reservation
      API->>WAL: Append WAL v2 term + payload checksum
      alt WAL error
        API->>API: Inspect append outcome and fence a failed log
        Note over API,Dedup: Release IDs only if nothing appended, retain appended claims for reconciliation
        API-->>Producer: error
      else appended
        WAL-->>API: offsets
        opt replication leader present
          API->>Repl: Replicate until minISR incl. leader with current-term commitment proof
          Note over API,Repl: On replication failure the dedup claim is KEPT
        end
        opt cronos.durable_ack meta set
          API->>WAL: fsync active segment before ack
        end
        API->>Scheduler: Schedule by schedule_ts
        API-->>Producer: success offsets
      end
    end

    Scheduler->>Worker: ready events
    Worker->>Dispatcher: dispatch
    Dispatcher->>Consumer: Subscribe delivery stream
    Consumer->>API: Ack stream
    API->>Group: CommitDeliveries: completions of a batch of acks, one durable write per partition

docs.text: The audit module records important actions and security-relevant requests for compliance and post-incident analysis.

docs.title: Main Flow
docs.text:
1. Audit logger is created during startup.
  2. The unary and stream audit interceptors write request-level audit events, but only when authentication is on (--auth-enabled). Without it every subject is anonymous and the interceptors record nothing (internal/api/grpc_server.go).
  3. Records are appended to audit files with structured payloads.

docs.title: Production Decisions
docs.text:
• Audit initialization is non-fatal so data plane stays available even if audit path is degraded.
  • Write path is guarded for concurrent access.
  • Output is structured and parse-friendly for tooling.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The auth module handles authentication and authorization policy enforcement before business handlers execute.

docs.title: Key Files
docs.text:
• internal/auth/auth.go
  • internal/api/grpc_server.go
  • cmd/api/main.go

docs.title: Main Flow
docs.text:
1. Startup builds auth config from flags and environment.
  2. Unary and stream auth interceptors validate credentials and claims on every public RPC.
  3. Requests without a valid token never reach a handler. The interceptor only authenticates.
  4. Each handler checks the policy for its own RPC (see authorization by RPC).

docs.title: Production Decisions
docs.text:
• Authentication is off by default (--auth-enabled=false). Production mode (no --dev) refuses to start without --auth-enabled, a JWT secret or public key, and --auth-policy-file. --dev only lifts these production requirements; it does not switch auth off. With --dev --auth-enabled, every request is authenticated and authorized as in production.
  • Supports HMAC (--auth-jwt-secret) and Ed25519, RSA or ECDSA public-key (--auth-jwt-public-key) JWT verification, and an RBAC policy loaded from a JSON file.
  • Fails closed: with --auth-enabled, the server exits at start if the policy file is missing or cannot be loaded, or if the public key cannot be loaded.
  • Runs early in interceptor chain to minimize wasted work for rejected requests.
  • GetEventState, CancelEvent and RescheduleEvent also require topic publish permission in the lifecycle handler. A state query is a leader operation, not a bypass of topic authorization. See API behavior.

docs.title: Authorization by RPC
docs.text:
The policy file is a JSON object keyed by JWT subject, for example {"ops":{"admin":true},"app":{"topics":{"orders":{"publish":true,"subscribe":true}}}}. With --auth-enabled, the handlers require:

RPCs Requirement Every AdminService RPC, and the dashboard's /api/admin/* Global "admin": true (CheckAdminPermission) PartitionService.Compact, RunRetention, SplitPartition Global "admin": true PartitionService.GetPartition, ListPartitions, GetWALStatus, GetSchedulerStatus A valid token only ConsumerGroupService.CreateConsumerGroup, GetConsumerGroup, ListConsumerGroups, RebalanceConsumerGroup Global "admin": true EventService.Publish, PublishBatch, GetEventState, CancelEvent, RescheduleEvent Topic publish EventService.Subscribe, Ack, Replay Topic subscribe

The global admin flag grants no topic permission. Topic names match exactly. The per-topic admin flag is parsed but no RPC checks it. A subject missing from the policy gets PermissionDenied wherever a policy check applies. The internal listener (ReplicationService, RaftService, and the experimental CrossRegionService) reads no JWT; --replication-tls-enabled protects it with mutual TLS. See the cronos-admin permissions.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Change data capture hands every accepted event to external systems (Kafka, a webhook) without the publish path ever waiting for them.

docs.title: Key Files
docs.text:
• internal/partition/changefeed.go — the per-partition change feed: accepted watermark, feed goroutine, stored position.
  • internal/cdc/sink.go — Manager.Deliver, the Sink and BatchSink interfaces.
  • internal/cdc/kafka_sink.go
  • internal/cdc/webhook_sink.go
  • cmd/api/main.go — registers sinks from the environment and calls PartitionManager.SetChangeFeed.

docs.title: Main Flow
docs.text:
1. Startup registers sinks from the environment (CRONOS_CDC_KAFKA_BROKERS, CRONOS_CDC_KAFKA_TOPIC, CRONOS_CDC_WEBHOOK_URL). If there is a sink, or a region is configured for cross-region replication, the partition manager is given a change feed before any partition exists, so partitions created later have one too.
  2. Each partition runs one feed goroutine. It reads the log behind the accepted watermark and hands the events over in log order, up to 500 at a time.
  3. cdc.Manager.Deliver writes them to every sink, in order, and returns once each sink has taken them or failed. A sink that implements BatchSink (Kafka) gets one call per batch.
  4. On success the feed's position moves forward. On failure it stays, and the same events are offered again after a pause that grows from 100 ms to 5 s.

docs.title: What "accepted" means
docs.text:
Partition.AcceptedThrough is the physical accepted boundary, including internal controls. An entry is not accepted while:

  • its publish is still in flight (BeginPublish … EndPublish);
  • it is held after a publish that failed past the append (no quorum, a failed sync), until a retry or catch-up shows it is replicated;
  • on a replicated partition, it is beyond the committed boundary. In term-start mode this requires a current-term proof, not just copies of old-term entries on min-insync-replicas replicas.

The feed never passes the first such entry, so events leave in log order. The last rule keeps exported entries behind the current-term commitment proof. Mixed-version partitions retain legacy accounting until capability agreement.

docs.title: Production Decisions
docs.text:
• Pulled from the log, not pushed from the append path. The append hook this replaces fired before a publish was accepted, on every replica, and only for the partitions that existed at startup (in a cluster: one).
  • Leader only. In a cluster the feed runs on the partition's leader. Followers hold the same events and export nothing.
  • A position that survives. How far the feed has got is written to changefeed.json in the partition directory at most once a second, and sent to followers with the consumer progress. After a restart or a failover the feed continues from there. Delivery is at least once: the last second or so can be handed over again.
  • Nothing is dropped and nothing queues in memory. A slow or failing sink makes the feed lag; events stay in the log until they are handed over.
  • Sinks do not get the same event once per retry. The manager remembers, per sink and partition, the last offset that sink took.
  • Switching the feed on does not replay history. A partition without a stored position starts at the end of its log.
  • A backup keeps the position. A partition backup includes changefeed.json (component changefeed), taken before the log is cut, so a restored partition exports again whatever the destination had not taken when the backup was made, and possibly a little more. Before 1.0 a backup left it out, and a restored partition started its feed at the end of the restored log: events the destination had not yet taken were never exported. Restoring a backup taken before 1.0 still starts the feed at the end of the log.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Lifecycle v1 rejects CDC and cross-region feeds with --event-lifecycle: these sinks have no cancellation/reschedule contract. Ordinary term-start partitions can use CDC. Feeds omit internal controls while advancing their physical cursors; cross-region fetch returns next_offset for control-only pages. See compatibility.
  • The feed of a partition is one stream for all sinks. While one sink refuses events, the other sinks wait with it for that partition.
  • Retention waits for the feed. Partition.PruneWAL removes an entry only once the feed has exported it, besides every consumer group having finished it, so a sink that is down holds the log on disk. If the feed still finds offsets missing from the log (for example after a failover to a replica whose stored position trails where the old leader's log starts), it logs "Change feed skips offsets" and continues after them.
  • A replica that takes over before it was told the feed's position starts at the end of its log.
  • Cross-region replication is experimental. It is refused unless the server runs with --dev --experimental-features; with CRONOS_REGIONS set otherwise, the server exits at start. It reads the same feed but stays asynchronous and best-effort beyond it: its per-region buffer holds at most 100,000 events and drops the oldest when a remote region is unreachable for long.

docs.title: Debug Pointers
docs.text:
• "Change feed is waiting at offset N": a sink is refusing events; the log line carries the sink's error. "Change feed continues" follows on recovery.

  • Watermark and position: internal/partition/changefeed.go
  • Sink behavior: internal/cdc

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The cluster module provides node membership, partition routing, leader assignment, and metadata consensus.

docs.title: Key Files
docs.text:
• internal/cluster/manager.go — Manager.JoinCluster, the control loop (5 s tick and 500 ms leader tick), updateReplicaOffsets / noteInSync (in-sync replicas of the partitions this node leads).
  • internal/cluster/leadership.go — reconcileLocalLeadership (acts on committed assignments: PromoteToLeader, DemoteFromLeader, AddFollower), fenced elections (electNewLeader, fencedPositions), staged handoff (handoffMayStart, advanceTransfers), syncClusterState, checkPartitionHealth.
  • internal/cluster/router.go
  • internal/cluster/hashring.go
  • internal/cluster/membership.go
  • internal/cluster/transport.go — mutual TLS for the membership and Raft ports.
  • internal/cluster/memberlist_adapter.go — not connected; the server refuses --use-memberlist.
  • internal/cluster/raft.go
  • internal/cluster/capabilities.go — one-way partition format requirements, replica/handoff/voter compatibility and activation.
  • internal/cluster/election.go — ChooseFailoverLeader, the fallback choice used by electNewLeader only when no replica-position source is wired; the normal election asks the replicas for their log positions (see leadership.go).
  • internal/cluster/autoscaler.go — logs warnings when CPU, memory, disk or partition lag cross a threshold; it changes nothing in the cluster.
  • internal/cluster/types.go
  • cmd/api/main.go

docs.title: Main Flow
docs.text:
1. Cluster manager starts Raft and membership services.
  2. Router computes partition placement, and the leader it would prefer, via the consistent hash ring.
  3. The Raft leader commits each partition's assignment. A partition that has never had a leader gets one as soon as --cluster-expected-nodes nodes are up, or once membership has been unchanged for --cluster-formation-wait (5 s), so a cluster whose nodes start one after another is assigned once, across all of them. It first asks the partition's replicas what they already hold: in a new cluster nothing, and the ring's choice stands; after a restore the replica with the most complete log leads, at an epoch above any a replica has accepted.
  4. Each node acts on the committed assignments only: it leads what is committed to it, follows what it is a replica of, and unloads what it no longer holds. A partition with no committed assignment has no leader.
  5. Leader-only tasks elect a replacement for a dead leader and move leadership to the ring's preferred replica by a staged handoff. Both are described in replication.md.

docs.title: Production Decisions
docs.text:
• Production clusters require --replication-factor>=3 and --min-insync-replicas>=2.
  • The coordinator activates term-start/1 only after every assigned replica, handoff target and Raft voter is alive and capable. Lifecycle operations are separately opt-in with --event-lifecycle, require majority acknowledgements and the lifecycle append/recovery formats, and exclude CDC/experimental features. Committed requirements constrain future placement, elections, handoffs and replacement voters. Before agreement, legacy old-term commitment behavior remains; after activation, downgrade to an incompatible build is unsupported. See term-start and lifecycle upgrades.
  • A node skips its own entry in the seed list, introduces itself to every other seed and keeps retrying the ones that do not answer. Nodes that start together therefore find each other in any order; a node that cannot reach its cluster stays not ready.
  • Nodes keep sending heartbeats to the nodes they count as failed, every heartbeat interval while a node is suspected and every fifth once it is counted as dead, and a heartbeat says where its sender is found. Two nodes that lost contact therefore meet again when the network lets them, and a node that restarted with an empty member list, which is the case for the node that names no seeds, learns the others from the heartbeats they still send it. A node that was itself not running for longer than the failure timeout (a frozen process, a suspended machine) gives the others a full timeout to be heard from before it suspects them.
  • A node asked where a partition's log ends answers from disk if the partition is not loaded, which is the state of every partition after a restart. Elections and first assignments would otherwise take a restarted replica for an empty one.
  • All traffic between nodes is mutual TLS in production, with the certificates of --replication-tls-*: replication (see replication.md), membership and Raft. The membership and Raft ports decide who belongs to the cluster and who leads; they used to be plain TCP even with replication TLS on, and a join request from anyone who could reach the membership port made the sender a member, which the Raft leader then added as a voter. Now a caller must present a certificate signed by the cluster's CA before anything it sends is read, and a node checks that the certificate of the node it calls is valid for the address it called (TestTransportTLS_* in transport_test.go). A certificate, its key and the CA file are read again when they change, at the next connection a node makes or accepts, so they are replaced without a restart (tlsfiles). ca.crt may hold more than one CA certificate, which is how a CA is replaced: both, then new certificates, then the new one alone.
  • A node that is lost for good is removed by hand: cronos-admin cluster remove-node <node-id>, asked of any node on the port the nodes use with each other. A dead node stays a member until then, which lets it come back, and keeps counting towards what a majority is in Raft; four nodes with one lost need three of four. The removal takes the node out of the Raft configuration and, through the Raft log, off every node's list of members (Manager.RemoveNode, Manager.forgetNode). A node that runs is refused, since it would be heard from and join again. cronos-admin cluster voters lists the nodes that count.
  • A node that joins a running cluster is found by clients that are already connected (since v0.7.0), when it is started with --advertise-grpc-addr: partition metadata names a leader by node ID and gives the address each node advertised, and a client adds the addresses it learns to its address map. Addresses given in NodeIDToAddress take precedence. The address travels between nodes in membership messages (ClientAddr), which nodes of v0.6.0 ignore. It is not the cluster gRPC address, which serves replication and Raft only. Clients of v0.6.0 and before, and nodes started without the flag, work as before: a client has addresses only for the nodes it was started with or was given.
  • A node of this version does not form a cluster with nodes of 0.6.0-rc.2 or earlier when replication TLS is on, because those speak plain TCP on the membership and Raft ports. Such a cluster is upgraded by stopping all its nodes and starting them on the new version together; a rolling update stalls at the first pod.
  • A cluster is created once, by the node given --cluster-bootstrap, and only when that node has no Raft state and every other node in its seed list has said it belongs to no cluster (bootstrap.go). One node that belongs to a cluster settles it: the node joins that cluster and is filled from it. A node that does not answer leaves the question open, and the node waits, logging whom it waits for. The node that creates a cluster used to be the one that names no seeds, and it created a cluster whenever it started without state: back with an empty disk, it created a second one, added the other nodes to it, and left them with two histories of who leads what. In the chart that was pod 0 with a replaced volume. A node that names no other node still behaves that way and says so in its log; production mode refuses to start one.
  • A leader takes a publish only while it counts enough of the partition's replicas as alive, itself included, to make up --min-insync-replicas. A leader that is cut off from the others is still the committed leader as far as it can tell, because the change that replaces it is committed by the nodes it cannot hear; it could never acknowledge a publish, but it used to take each one and hold its sender until replication timed out. It now answers at once that the publish has to go to another node (seesEnoughReplicas in leadership.go).
  • A heartbeat connection is used again only while the node at its other end is being heard from, and for ten heartbeat intervals at most. A write into a connection that carries nothing succeeds, and after a network failure such a connection stays silent long after the network has returned; two nodes that kept theirs stayed dead to each other.
  • /health/deep reports which node decides who leads the partitions: the check cluster_role reads coordinator on the node that leads the cluster's Raft group and member on the others.
  • A node whose partition has accepted a newer epoch than its own records of the cluster show has been replaced as leader, and has not heard it from the cluster yet. It refuses publishes and subscriptions for that partition with an answer that sends the client to the leader (ensureClusterPartitionLed in handlers.go).
  • A node that the ring gives a partition does not start a bulk copy from a leader it counts as dead: the copy cannot be made, and the attempt held the partition's log locked until the connection timed out.
  • A replica that placement drops is not dropped at once: it is put on the partition's Retiring list. Elections ask retiring replicas too, count them in the replicas they must hear from, and may elect one; a retiring node keeps its copy. A leader replicates only to the replicas of the assignment it has taken up, and it stops replicating to dropped ones before it reports that assignment's epoch. The retiring list is cleared once the leader reports that epoch and --min-insync-replicas − 1 of the remaining replicas hold the log the leader held at that point (releaseRetired in leadership.go). Before 1.0 placement dropped a replica at once, before the replica that replaced it had copied anything; the leader went on replicating to the dropped node and counting its acknowledgements, while elections no longer asked it. A leader failure while the new replicas caught up could then elect a replica without writes acknowledged with the dropped node's help, and adding two nodes at once could elect an empty replica.
  • An election changes who leads a partition and leaves alone where the ring wants its replicas. It used to write the replica list it had started from over the ring's entry. When a node had come back in the meantime, that entry was the only place that said the node belongs to the partition again; with it gone the partition ran on one replica, refusing publishes for want of a second, until another node joined or left. The fault campaign found this in CI.
  • A node that was counted as failed and announces itself again is put back in the ring at once. The router used to hear nothing of the return and went on without the node until its periodic comparison, up to ten seconds later, and a Raft leader elected in that time committed every partition without it.
  • Configurable virtual nodes improve partition leadership balance (default 2048, raised from the older 150 because sparse vnode counts produced severe ownership skew in small clusters).
  • Consensus metadata is persisted with Raft and Bolt-backed storage.
  • Rebalance path uses partition accessor hooks to avoid ownership without data.
  • Explicit epoch usage supports leader fencing behavior.
  • New-node join path: Manager.JoinCluster iterates router.GetLocalPartitions() and calls PartitionManager.SyncPartitionFromLeader(partitionID, leader.Address), which triggers Follower.InstallSnapshot (bulk ReplicationService.Snapshot install) for each partition the joining node owns.
  • In-sync replicas are known only to each partition's leader. Every node, every 5 s, puts the in-sync replicas and replica offsets of the partitions it leads into its router and logs when a partition is under-replicated or back to full (updateReplicaOffsets, noteInSync in manager.go). The ISR in the committed assignment is what it was when placement last changed; the admin topology reads the ISR from each partition's leader (LeaderReport).
  • reconcileLocalLeadership runs whenever a committed assignment changes, and every 5s, and uses Raft-committed assignments only to idempotently PromoteToLeader / demote / AddFollower for local partitions — enabling streaming ReplicationService.Append on a healthy cluster. A node that has just joined leads nothing until it has received the assignments.
  • /health/ready answers 503 while a partition has no committed leader, while this node is still loading a partition committed to it, or while one of its partitions is being handed over. Publishes for those partitions are refused with a retryable error in the meantime.
  • Under replication factor 1 a handoff copies the log to the target by snapshot; consumer progress does not move with it, so the target may redeliver.
  • Partition ID routing for keys uses FNV-1a; node placement on the ring uses SHA-256 virtual nodes (default 2048).

docs.title: Known Limitation: Admin TriggerRebalance soft stub
docs.text:
Automatic rebalance (works) Membership join/leave → router assignment → Raft apply → reconcileLocalLeadership (~5s) promotes/demotes and may SyncPartitionFromLeader. On-demand RPC (stub) AdminService.TriggerRebalance / dashboard POST /api/admin/cluster/rebalance is implemented as a soft stub: RBAC still required; response is Success=true with an explanatory Error string and PartitionsMoved=0. It does not force a full ring reshuffle. Why Prevents unsafe operator thrash until a controlled drain/move API exists. Code internal/api/admin_handler.go (TriggerRebalance) See also ARCHITECTURE.md § Known Limitations, dashboard.md

Operator guidance: To change placement, change membership (add/remove nodes) or wait for failure detection; do not rely on the Rebalance button as a manual “reshuffle now” tool.
