docs.title: Cluster rebalance
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    NodeJoin[Node joins or leaves]
    Membership[Membership service emits event]
    Router[Router updates hash ring placement]
    RaftSync["Raft leader commits placement<br/>(syncClusterState); leader moves by staged handoff"]
    Promote["Each node acts on the committed assignment<br/>(reconcileLocalLeadership)"]
    Follower[Leader adds followers; followers catch up]
    Sync["Joining node: SyncPartitionFromLeader<br/>(bulk snapshot install)"]
    Healthy[Cluster converged]

    AdminBtn[Admin TriggerRebalance / UI button]
    SoftStub["Soft stub: no forced reshuffle<br/>Success + explanatory message"]

    NodeJoin --> Membership --> Router --> RaftSync --> Promote --> Follower --> Healthy
    NodeJoin -.-> Sync -.-> Follower
    AdminBtn --> SoftStub
    SoftStub -.->|does not replace| Membership

Note: the steps above run across different loops in code (router rebalance goroutine, the Raft leader's syncClusterState / advanceTransfers every 500 ms, and reconcileLocalLeadership on every committed change and every 5 s), so the depicted order is logical rather than a single linear sequence. The ring proposes placement; only the Raft-committed assignment makes a node a leader.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The compliance module enforces retention and storage lifecycle constraints while preserving protected runtime data paths.

docs.title: Key Files
docs.text:
• internal/compliance/retention.go
  • internal/api/partition_handler.go
  • cmd/api/main.go

docs.title: Main Flow
docs.text:
1. Startup creates a managed retention enforcer (compliance.NewManagedEnforcer) with pm.RemoveRetainedSegment as its remove function, and runs it once an hour.
  2. The enforcer parses the 64-byte segment header (firstOffset, createdTS), never proposes the active segment of a partition, skips protected system directories, honors context cancellation, and picks segments older than --retention-max-age-hours or the oldest ones while the total is above --retention-max-size-gb.
  3. It does not delete files itself. Each candidate goes to PartitionManager.RemoveRetainedSegment, which calls Partition.PruneWAL for that segment. A segment is removed only when, for every entry in it, at least one consumer group takes the entry and every group that does has finished it, and the change feed (when one runs) has exported it. On a replicated partition only the leader decides, and only the oldest segments go, so the log stays one unbroken range; a follower's call returns without removing anything, and followers drop what their leader has released (FollowLogStart). A segment of a partition not loaded on this node is kept.
  4. The partition admin RPCs RunRetention and Compact go through the same PruneWAL boundary and report reclaimed segments and bytes.

With --event-lifecycle, accepted cancellations and superseded copies can be terminal before their original schedule. The retained active successor still has its own consumer obligation. Accepted term-start records need no consumer completion. Neither an unaccepted mutation nor an uncommitted term-start record can release a segment.

--wal-relocation-bytes optionally moves never-due work out of the oldest selected closed segment. It is off by default, requires lifecycle mode, and replicates the replacement before the predecessor can be pruned. It cannot evacuate unfinished due work or the active segment. See retention and relocation.

docs.title: Production Decisions
docs.text:
• Age and size limits only propose segments; accepted lifecycle state, consumer completion, the committed boundary, change-feed progress and dead-letter replication decide. A pinned segment can keep a log above its size limit.
  • Protected directories and system paths are excluded from destructive cleanup.
  • Context cancellation is honored during enforcement scans.
  • Retention operations are separated from hot request path.
  • Admin operations return explicit status payloads rather than silent actions.

docs.title: Config and reload architecture
docs.text: For every flag, exact environment variable, default and plain-language use, see the server configuration reference. Application connection, publishing and consuming settings are in the SDK guide.

docs.title: Key files
docs.text:
• internal/config/config.go: registers flags, applies environment values and validates startup requirements.
  • internal/config/defaults.go: binary defaults.
  • internal/config/reload.go: limited SIGHUP parsing and the shared config wrapper.
  • cmd/api/main.go: constructs components, registers CDC sinks and starts listeners.
  • internal/partition/manager.go: passes startup settings to each partition and reads admission limits.
  • pkg/types/event.go: typed server config.

docs.title: Main flow
docs.text:
1. LoadConfig applies defaults, nonempty environment values, then explicit flags. Invalid values fail startup.
  2. ValidateConfig checks required values, lifecycle compatibility and production security/durability requirements.
  3. The composition root builds listeners, tracer, partition manager and other components. Partition construction copies delivery settings into a dispatcher.
  4. The Unix SIGHUP listener updates selected fields in the shared config. The composition root registers no component-update callbacks, so most running components keep their startup values. Admission reads load shedding directly. Restart to apply changes consistently; see per-field reload limits.

docs.title: Full Flag Reference
docs.text: The maintained configuration reference lists every flag with its exact environment variable, units, default and intended use. cronos-api --help lists accepted flags in the binary. The test TestEveryFlagIsInTheConfigurationReference checks that no flag is missing or invented and that every environment name matches startup parsing.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text: Every flag reads CRONOS_<FLAG> with the uppercase name and dashes replaced by underscores, except --dedup-ttl (CRONOS_DEDUP_TTL_HOURS) and --min-insync-replicas (CRONOS_MIN_IN_SYNC_REPLICAS). Explicit flags win. Additional CDC, experimental region and reload variables are described in the reference.

docs.title: Production decisions and limitations
docs.text:
• Production requires TLS, JWT auth with an explicit policy, WAL encryption, replication mTLS, at least three replicas, at least two write acknowledgements, durable fsync and seeds in cluster mode. --dev bypasses the requirements; it does not disable security that was explicitly enabled.
  • Event lifecycle mode requires supported persistent formats and, in a cluster, majority acknowledgements and capability agreement. CDC sinks and experimental features cannot be combined with it. Activation is one-way; see the lifecycle contract.
  • --raft-join, --snapshot-catchup-threshold and --clock-skew-threshold-ms are parsed but unused. Join uses seeds; connected followers use incremental catch-up; node clocks must be synchronized operationally.
  • Helm configures the binary through environment variables. Named chart values cover common settings; extraEnv accepts the rest, including secret references. Base values enable dev mode. Use values-production.yaml and the required secrets for production.
  • SIGHUP is not a complete component reload, and Windows has no usable SIGHUP path. The acknowledgement-timeout reload parser uses integer seconds, unlike startup's duration syntax. Restart instead of relying on runtime reload.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The consumer module manages group membership and records, per group and partition, which events consumers have finished, so consumption resumes after a restart or a failover. Delivery is at least once.

docs.title: Key Files
docs.text:
• internal/consumer/group.go
  • internal/consumer/completion.go — per-event completion records and the completion floor.
  • internal/consumer/offset_store.go
  • internal/api/handlers.go
  • internal/api/consumer_handler.go
  • internal/api/replication_server.go — SyncConsumerProgress, where a follower takes its leader's progress.

docs.title: Main Flow
docs.text:
1. Subscribe requests create or join group members.
  2. An Ack names a delivery; the server validates it against the delivery it made (Dispatcher.ValidateAck) and records completion for the events that delivery carried (GroupManager.CommitDeliveries). A client cannot move progress by sending an offset.
  3. Completion is recorded per event, above a completion floor below which every event is complete. The floor advances over the completed prefix, and records it passes are removed. Per-event records are needed because schedule order need not match log order.
  4. Completions, floors and group metadata/assignments are kept in PebbleDB (OffsetStore) and loaded on restart. Acks that arrive together share one durable write.

docs.title: Production Decisions
docs.text:
• Ack parsing extracts the partition from the delivery ID.
  • Completion commits are serialized per group manager (commitMu).
  • On a replicated partition the leader sends each group's floor and completed offsets to its followers (SyncConsumerProgress, from the leader's maintenance loop). A follower takes them only as far as its own log reaches. What finished on the old leader in the last moments before a failover, and had not reached the new leader yet, can be delivered again.
  • A replica keeps no completion at or beyond the end of its own log (ForgetCompletionsFrom), so an offset reused after the log was cut does not count as finished.
  • --exactly-once-commits (commit IDs and strict monotonic commits) is refused in production ("use per-event at-least-once completion"). The commit-ID method in OffsetStore is not called by any server path.
  • Lifecycle rescheduling and relocation preserve logical identity but use a new physical offset. Acks complete the copy actually delivered; an old copy's completion never completes its successor. Lifecycle recovery imports group metadata, floors and sparse progress with the matching WAL generation after clearing stale state. See consistent recovery.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The admin dashboard is the operator-facing web UI for CronosDB AdminService. It surfaces cluster topology, partition health, replication lag, consumer-group lag, retention, compaction, schemas, tenants, and rebalance actions through a React 19 SPA served by the same Go binary that runs the public gRPC API.

The dashboard talks to the process over HTTP JSON (/api/admin/*), which is a thin proxy over the same AdminServiceHandler used by gRPC — no separate business logic path.

docs.title: Key Files
docs.text:
• web/dashboard/src/main.tsx, App.tsx — React 19 entry and nav shell (basename /ui).
  • web/dashboard/src/views/ — views for home, cluster, partitions, replication, consumers, schemas, tenants, operations, login.
  • web/dashboard/src/lib/api.ts — live fetch() client + React hooks; JWT stored in localStorage.
  • web/dashboard/src/components/ — theme, toasts, mobile nav, error boundary, shadcn-style UI primitives.
  • web/dashboard/vite.config.ts — Vite 7 build; emits web/dashboard/dist/ with content-hashed assets.
  • internal/api/web_handler.go — embeds SPA via //go:embed web/dist/*; serves /ui/ with SPA fallback to index.html; exposes JWT-gated /api/admin/* JSON proxy.
  • internal/api/web/dist/README.txt — embed placeholder until make dashboard / make build stages real assets.
  • cmd/api/main.go — mounts WebHandler on the HTTP mux next to health and metrics.
  • pkg/types/admin.pb.go — protobuf JSON tags define the wire field names.
  • internal/auth/auth.go — ParseToken + CheckAdminPermission shared with gRPC admin paths.

docs.text:
Browser (SPA)
   │  GET /ui/…                 (assets + SPA routes → index.html fallback)
   │  GET /api/admin/topology   (Authorization: Bearer <jwt> when auth on)
   ▼
Go binary (cronos-api)  HTTP :8080
   │  /ui/     → embedded dist (spaFileServer)
   │  /api/admin/* → authMiddleware → AdminServiceHandler.<RPC>
   │                 → json.Marshal(proto response)
   ▼
Same handler code as gRPC AdminService

docs.text: HTTP path Admin RPC / action /api/admin/topology GetClusterTopology /api/admin/partition-health GetPartitionHealth /api/admin/replication-lag GetReplicationLag /api/admin/consumer-groups ListConsumerGroups /api/admin/consumer-group-lag GetConsumerGroupLag /api/admin/schemas ListSchemas /api/admin/schema GetSchema /api/admin/tenant-usage GetTenantUsage /api/admin/retention/run RunRetention /api/admin/compaction/run RunCompaction /api/admin/cluster/rebalance TriggerRebalance soft-stub — RPC exists, RBAC applies; returns success + message that rebalance is membership-driven (PartitionsMoved=0). See cluster.md and ARCHITECTURE known limitations.

docs.title: Production Decisions
docs.text:
• Single binary, single HTTP listener. SPA and JSON proxy share :8080 with /health and /metrics.
  • //go:embed keeps the binary self-contained. make build stages web/dashboard/dist → internal/api/web/dist before compile.
  • SPA client-route fallback. Unmatched /ui/* paths return index.html so React Router deep links work.
  • Auth mirrors gRPC. Bearer JWT, same secret/keys/policy; admin requires Subject.Admin=true. In --dev (auth off) middleware is a pass-through.
  • gRPC status → HTTP. NotFound→404, PermissionDenied→403, etc.
  • Schemas are live; tenant limits are not configured by the shipped server. The accountant is initialized, but no runtime configuration calls SetLimits. The tenant usage view therefore reports zero with limits_configured: false; initialization alone does not enable quotas. See tenant.md.
  • The topology asks the leaders. Which replicas of a partition are in sync, and their offsets, are known to the node that leads it alone. GetClusterTopology asks every node that is alive for the partitions it leads (ReplicationService.LeaderReport on the port the nodes use with each other, with the replication certificates) and waits at most two seconds. A partition whose leader did not answer comes with leader_reported: false and no in-sync replicas, and the view says so.
  • Zero values are not in the JSON. json.Marshal of a proto response leaves out empty and zero fields: partition 0 has no partition_id, and an unreported partition has no isr. The SPA's types mark such fields optional.
  • make build depends on dashboard stage so release binaries include UI.
  • Lifecycle state/cancel/reschedule operations are gRPC EventService methods; this dashboard has no controls for them. See api.md.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Deduplication prevents duplicate message processing while keeping publish latency low.

docs.title: Key Files
docs.text:
• internal/dedup/store.go
  • internal/dedup/key.go — Key: what is recorded for a message ID on a topic.
  • internal/dedup/bloom_store.go
  • internal/dedup/pebble_store.go
  • internal/dedup/rust_bloom_unix.go — Unix CGO bindings for the Rust bloom filter.
  • internal/dedup/rust_bloom_windows_cgo.go / internal/dedup/rust_bloom_nocgo.go — Windows CGO and non-CGO bindings (the older rust_bloom_windows.go was split into these two files when the Windows build added a non-CGO fallback path).
  • internal/dedup/rust/src/lib.rs — Rust crate: lock-free AtomicU64 arrays, XxHash64, Rayon parallel batch.

docs.title: Main Flow
docs.text:
1. Handler checks message identifier through dedup manager.
  2. Fast probabilistic path handles common-case duplicate checks.
  3. Persistent fallback confirms and stores dedup state with TTL behavior.
  4. Result controls whether publish continues or exits as duplicate.

docs.title: Production Decisions
docs.text:
• A message ID is unique within its topic. The store records dedup.Key(topic, message ID), so the same ID on two topics names two events. IDs were recorded per partition alone before 1.0; with the default partition key (the message ID) the same ID on two topics met in one partition, and a principal allowed to publish to one topic could block, or detect, IDs used on another. Records written before 1.0 are not carried over.
  • Two-tier design balances speed and correctness (bloom fast-path, Pebble source of truth).
  • The filter's bits are never cleared as IDs expire. Hourly maintenance rebuilds it from Pebble once its false-positive rate over checks of absent IDs exceeds 5%. Until the rebuild has read Pebble, every check goes to Pebble, and a claim made meanwhile adds its ID to the filter itself; claims pause only while the filter is emptied and a snapshot is taken. Before 1.0 maintenance emptied the filter and left it empty, so a retry of an accepted ID was taken for new, and its rate was taken over "maybe" answers alone, which ordinary traffic puts near 100%. A filter that stays full after a rebuild needs a larger --bloom-capacity.
  • The Rust bloom filter is used only in cgo builds. Any build without cgo, on any system, uses the pure-Go bloom filter (rust_bloom_nocgo.go returns nil and callers fall back to GoBloomFilter); the release binaries are built this way. The Docker image is built with cgo and ships libcronos_dedup.so, so it uses the Rust filter.
  • Publish path claims IDs before WAL append and RollbackBatch on definite pre-append failure so retries are not spurious duplicates.
  • Crash recovery: on partition start, recoverDedupFromWAL re-seeds claims from the WAL tail, because the dedup Pebble store writes with DisableWAL + NoSync and can lose recent claims in a crash. Recovery walks the retained log in bounded byte pages from a validated (offset, term, message ID) checkpoint, skipping events older than the dedup TTL. The checkpoint is saved only after pending IDs and Pebble tables are flushed. Without a valid checkpoint every retained entry is examined; a recovery error blocks startup or promotion.
  • TTL pruning bounds store growth (default 7 days).
  • Deduplication concerns publish retries, not end-to-end processing exactly once. Internal term-start records never claim their empty message IDs. Lifecycle successors preserve their logical identity independently of the dedup TTL; cancellation/reschedule request history is reconstructed from the retained WAL by the lifecycle index, not expired with a publish claim.

docs.text:

docs.title: Dedup decision flow
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    Start[Incoming message_id] --> FastCheck[Bloom check]
    FastCheck --> MaybeDup{Possible duplicate?}
    MaybeDup -- no --> StoreFast[Store and continue]
    MaybeDup -- yes --> PersistentCheck[Persistent store lookup]
    PersistentCheck --> Exists{Exists in store?}
    Exists -- yes --> Reject[Reject as duplicate]
    Exists -- no --> StoreConfirmed[Store and continue]
    StoreFast --> Accept[Publish continues]
    StoreConfirmed --> Accept

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The delivery module moves scheduled events to subscribers with backpressure, retry, and dead-letter safety.

docs.title: Key Files
docs.text:
• internal/delivery/worker.go — scheduler-driven worker that drains ready events.
  • internal/delivery/dispatcher.go — 32-shard dispatcher with credit-based flow control.
  • internal/delivery/retry_queue.go — non-blocking min-heap retry queue ordered by retryAt.
  • internal/delivery/circuit_breaker.go — per-subscription circuit breaker (Closed→Open→HalfOpen).
  • internal/delivery/dlq.go, internal/delivery/dlq_segment.go — append-only DLQ segments (binary, CRC32, 64MB rotation).
  • internal/delivery/expiry.go — message expiry handling for time-bounded deliveries.

docs.title: Main Flow
docs.text:
1. Worker is notified by scheduler when events become ready.
  2. Dispatcher sends deliveries through subscription streams.
  3. Ack success commits progress; failures move to retry queue.
  4. Retries use backoff and circuit breaker protections.
  5. Exhausted retries move to DLQ for inspection and replay.

docs.title: Production Decisions
docs.text:
• Lifecycle delivery gate: canceled and superseded copies are suppressed, including stale wheel/ready-queue entries. A staged mutation freezes its predecessor without releasing retention; the successor cannot be delivered until accepted. The active-state check and send share a gate with mutations. Acks always refer to the delivered physical offset. Lifecycle operations only change future work; they cannot recall work already sent to a consumer. See the contract.

  • Circuit breaker isolates unstable subscribers.

  • Retry queue is non-blocking and deadline ordered (no inline sleep in timeout loop).
  • Dispatcher sharding reduces lock contention in high concurrency.
  • DLQ is constructed per partition at create time (NewEncryptedDeadLetterQueue + NewDispatcherWithDLQ in partition.Manager) so poison messages are not silently dropped.
  • DLQ journal replication copies failed payloads and removal tombstones in bounded pages. Followers sync before acknowledging; completion transfer and retention wait for the copies. A retry removes only its event when several entries share a batch delivery ID. See upgrade behavior.
  • DLQ entries are encrypted with the partition's key when encryption at rest is on: a dead-lettered event is stored whole, payload included. Entries written before encryption was switched on are still read. An encrypted entry that cannot be opened, because the key is wrong or missing, stops the partition from starting.
  • A damaged DLQ file loses only the damaged records. Records that fail their checksum are counted and logged with their file, and the counts are part of the queue's stats (CorruptRecords, UnreadableBytes). A file that cannot be read at all is an error.
  • A subscription ends when its node stops leading the partition, with an error that says so, and the consumer reconnects to the node that leads now. The dispatcher of a node that no longer leads delivers nothing.
  • A batch goes out in offset order, and is acknowledged with the offset after its highest event; the server refuses any other. Up to v0.6.0 a batch could go out in the order the scheduler handed its events over, and a client acknowledged the offset after its last event, so every acknowledgement of an out-of-order batch was refused, its redeliveries' too, and the subscription's credits stayed taken until it reconnected. The client also reports refused acknowledgements to its error hook (consumer.ack), and ends a subscription whose ack stream fails, so the reconnect opens both streams again.
  • Credit-based flow control and in-flight limits protect memory under slow consumers.
  • Publish-side admission (ready-queue / wheel / memory) lives in partition/backpressure.go.

docs.title: Redrive under backpressure
docs.text:
Delivery is push-first: the scheduler hands ready events to the worker, and the dispatcher sends them to a subscriber with credits. Anything that path cannot hand over is redelivered from the WAL.

Mechanism Behavior Credits No credit → the event is held back, counted in cronos_dispatcher_backpressure_skips_total{reason="no_credits"}, and its offset is queued for redrive In-flight cap Cap hit → same, with reason="in_flight_cap" Worker queue The worker keeps at most 10,000 ready events (64 MiB); the rest are queued for redrive for every group, reason="worker_capacity" Disconnect / failed send Unacked deliveries of that subscriber are queued for redrive to the rest of its group, including those that timed out and were waiting to be sent to it again. A delivery that cannot be sent again goes back to the group the same way; neither counts as an attempt Not replicated yet An entry beyond the offset the required replicas hold is held back, counted with reason="not_replicated", and queued for redrive. The subscription's own log reader stops at that offset Circuit breaker Open circuit skips send without burning credits Poison path After max retries → DLQ, and the event is recorded complete for the group so it is not delivered again. An attempt is a delivery the consumer failed, or did not acknowledge in time while still connected

Each subscription runs redriveRetained (internal/api/handlers.go), which reads the WAL from three sources in priority order:

  1. Queued ranges — offsets the dispatcher reported as held back (Dispatcher.RequestRedrive), re-read as soon as an ack returns credits.
  2. Backlog — records between the group's committed offset and the end of the log when the subscription started, read once at the pace credits allow.
  3. Sweep — 256 records every 500 ms from the group's first incomplete offset, as a safety net for anything not explicitly queued.

The dispatcher skips records already completed or in flight for the group, so a range offered twice is not delivered twice.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Redrive runs inside a subscription stream. A group with no connected subscriber makes no progress until one connects.
  • Redelivery does not preserve offset order, and duplicates remain possible after a crash or ack timeout (at-least-once).
  • Completion records are written on the partition leader and sent to its followers (see replication.md); a follower's copy trails the leader's.

docs.title: Operator guidance
docs.text:
1. Watch cronos_dispatcher_backpressure_skips_total: it counts events deferred to redrive. Sustained growth means consumers are slower than publishers.
  2. Ensure consumers ack; acks return credits and resume redrive.
  3. Scale consumer concurrency or credits (max_buffer_size) when a backlog builds.

Canonical cross-link: ARCHITECTURE.md § Known Limitations.

docs.title: Delivery state machine
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR

    [*] --> Pending
    Pending --> Delivered: stream send ok
    Delivered --> Acked: ack success
    Acked --> [*]

    Pending --> RetryQueued: send failed
    Delivered --> RetryQueued: nack or ack timeout
    RetryQueued --> Pending: retry_at reached
    RetryQueued --> DLQ: max retries exceeded
    DLQ --> [*]

    note right of RetryQueued
        The circuit breaker is per-subscription, not
        per-delivery: after the failure threshold it opens
        (gating dispatch via CanTry), half-opens after the
        open duration, and closes on a successful probe.
    end note

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The partition module is the core execution unit that groups WAL, scheduler, dedup, consumer, and delivery state.

docs.title: Key Files
docs.text:
• internal/partition/manager.go — partition lifecycle, leader promotion/demotion, SyncPartitionFromLeader (bulk install trigger).
  • internal/partition/split.go — online partition split. Experimental: PartitionService refuses a split unless the node runs with --dev --experimental-features.
  • internal/partition/retention.go — PruneWAL (compaction, retention and operator pruning; leader-only and log-start-only in a cluster) and FollowLogStart on followers.
  • internal/partition/disk_pressure.go — disk-pressure monitoring, emergency compaction callback.
  • internal/partition/backpressure.go — admission control across ready queue, timing wheel depth, and in-flight deliveries.
  • internal/partition/snapshot.go — partition-recovery snapshot.json (HWM + consumer offsets); distinct from the gRPC ReplicationService.Snapshot install path used for follower bootstrap.
  • internal/partition/lifecycle.go, replicated_lifecycle.go — lifecycle index, mutation/delivery exclusion and replicated activation.
  • internal/partition/term_start.go — durable format marker and current-term leadership proof.
  • internal/partition/recovery_snapshot.go — consistent lifecycle recovery-state capture and import across WAL generation swaps.

docs.title: Main Flow
docs.text:
1. Partition manager creates and starts partition runtime components.
  2. Routing resolves partition ownership for publish/replay paths.
  3. Leader/follower transitions attach replication responsibilities.
  4. Compaction removes finished segments; online split is experimental (see above).

docs.title: Production Decisions
docs.text:
• Partition-level encapsulation limits blast radius: each partition owns WAL, scheduler, dedup, dispatcher, worker, consumer groups, DLQ, and optional leader/follower replication roles.
  • Standalone mode creates all partitions at startup; cluster mode creates partition 0 for shared state and lazy-creates others on first use.
  • Create path wires NewDeadLetterQueue + NewDispatcherWithDLQ so delivery failures are durable.
  • Start path runs dedup WAL recovery and WAL timer replay (replayWALTimers): only events whose time has not come are scheduled again. Events already due stay in the log; each subscription reads what its group has not finished from the log at its consumers' pace (redriveRetained in handlers.go), so a restart does not load the undelivered backlog into memory.
  • Partition storage uses WAL v2 and default fsync mode batch.
  • Epoch handling fences stale leaders; ReplicateMu preserves offset order on the RF>1 write path only.
  • Admission control and disk monitor prevent overload and trigger emergency compaction.
  • --event-lifecycle enables future-event state queries, cancellation and rescheduling. The disk-backed index tracks heads without payloads and is rebuilt before readers run. A staged mutation suppresses its predecessor but does not make it removable; acceptance requires the current-term proof.
  • Lifecycle snapshot install captures the accepted boundary, epoch, consumer progress and dead letters with the WAL generation. Startup resumes an interrupted state import before serving; suffix replacement clears stale completions and rebuilds the index before offsets can be reused.
  • See the lifecycle contract and term-start protocol for rolling-upgrade requirements, internal offsets and unsupported combinations.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Replay serves historical data from WAL by time or offset, enabling debugging, backfills, and catch-up flows.

docs.title: Key Files
docs.text:
• internal/replay/engine.go
  • internal/api/handlers.go
  • proto/events.proto

docs.title: Main Flow
docs.text:
1. Replay request enters EventService replay handler.
  2. Handler validates partition ownership and policy constraints.
  3. Replay engine scans WAL ranges and applies query filters.
  4. Events are sent to the client one to a message, as they are read.

docs.title: Production Decisions
docs.text:
• speed paces a replay at 10 ms / speed between events: 0 sends as fast as the client takes them, and other values must be at least 0.001 (10 s between events); anything else is refused with INVALID_ARGUMENT. Cancelling a replay ends its pause. Before 1.0 the pause was a plain sleep, and a tiny speed asked for months of it: a cancelled replay kept its handler and the chunk of log it held until the sleep ended.
  • A replay reads the log 4 MiB at a time (replayChunkBytes) and sends each event before it reads on, so what it holds does not depend on the size of the range. The range is fixed when the replay starts: an event appended while it runs is not part of it.
  • A replay by offset returns 1,000 events unless the request gives a count.
  • A replay by time reads the segments that can hold an event in its window and looks at every event in those, because entries are not in time order. Each segment keeps the least and the greatest schedule time of its events, and one that the window does not meet is not read (WAL.TimeSpan). A window that events all over the log fall into still reads all of it.
  • Replay engine reads WAL v2 records with Raft term and trailing checksum validation.
  • Context cancellation is honored for long-running requests.
  • Follower-read policy gate protects consistency expectations.
  • On term-start partitions, public replay is bounded by the committed prefix. In lifecycle mode it emits only active event copies, strips internal mutation metadata, and excludes cancellations and superseded copies. Term-start records are always omitted. A replay is therefore not a physical WAL inventory; acceptance tests use authenticated physical snapshots to compare replicas. See current-term commitment.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Replication keeps partition data synchronized across intra-cluster followers and pushes events to remote regions for geo-resilience. Two distinct paths exist:

  • Intra-cluster replication (internal/replication/leader.go, internal/replication/follower.go) — synchronous, quorum-acked leader → follower streaming over a dedicated internal gRPC listener (internal/api/internal_grpc_server.go), with optional mTLS (internal/replication/mtls.go).
  • Cross-region replication (internal/replication/region.go) — asynchronous, best-effort batched push via the separate CrossRegionService gRPC service. No ISR semantics; fire-and-forget. Experimental: a node with CRONOS_REGIONS set refuses to start without --dev --experimental-features, and the service is registered only there.

docs.title: Key Files
docs.text:
• internal/replication/leader.go — Leader.Replicate, Leader.catchUpFollower, FollowerInfo management, ISR/quorum accounting.
  • internal/replication/follower.go — Follower.InstallSnapshot, Follower.dialCredentials, follower-side state.
  • internal/replication/mtls.go — MTLSConfig, BuildClientTLS (client configuration that re-reads the certificate, key and CA when their files change), BuildClientTLSConfig, BuildServerTLSConfig.
  • internal/replication/region.go — CrossRegionReplicator, per-region batched async push.
  • internal/api/replication_server.go — ReplicationServiceHandler.Append, .Sync, .Snapshot, .Position (where a replica's log ends; fences for elections), .LeaderReport (in-sync replicas and offsets of the partitions a node leads; the source of the admin topology), .SyncConsumerProgress (consumer progress and change-feed position from the leader).
  • internal/api/internal_grpc_server.go — InternalGRPCServer, registers ReplicationServiceServer and RaftServiceServer on a separate gRPC listener (default :7947).
  • internal/api/crossregion_server.go — CrossRegionServiceServer handler.
  • internal/partition/manager.go — PartitionManager.SyncPartitionFromLeader (the trigger path for bulk snapshot install during node join).
  • internal/cluster/manager.go — Manager.JoinCluster (calls SyncPartitionFromLeader for every partition the joining node owns; the cluster router also calls it during partition moves, internal/cluster/router.go).

docs.title: Main Flow (intra-cluster)
docs.text:
1. A publish enters Leader.Replicate(events) with a contiguous batch.
  2. Leader snapshots its follower list and minISR under a read lock.
  3. For each connected follower, sendToFollower issues a gRPC append carrying PartitionId, Events, ExpectedNextOffset, Term, PrevLogTerm, and an IEEE CRC32 batch checksum (computeBatchChecksum). Legacy partitions use Append; term-start partitions use AppendTermStart, including probes and catch-up, with separate term-start and lifecycle format versions. AppendLifecycle is the lifecycle-only compatibility transport. An incompatible receiver is refused; there is no downgrade to plain append.
  4. The follower handler (ReplicationServiceHandler.Append) verifies the batch checksum, then decides whether the sender may write: it rejects a term older than the one it has accepted and a second node claiming a term another node already holds, and records a newer term and its leader on disk before applying anything. Entries it already holds are compared with the leader's and appended via WAL.AppendReplicatedBatch (see Leadership and fencing).
  5. The leader returns success to the client only after at least min-insync-replicas replicas including the leader itself have acknowledged (i.e. minISR−1 followers). It returns as soon as that quorum is reached, or as soon as it can no longer be reached; sends to the remaining followers finish in the background, in offset order. Each Append RPC is bounded by --replication-timeout.

Replica counting alone cannot commit an earlier leader's entries. In v0.8.0 term-start mode, promotion or reactivation first appends and fsyncs a current-term control record. Leader.QuorumOffset exposes a committed prefix only once the required replicas hold that record or a later entry. Delivery, held-write resolution, retention and export share that boundary. See current-term commitment, including the legacy behavior retained during a mixed-version upgrade.

docs.title: Incremental catch-up (Sync)
docs.text: When a follower falls behind (f.NextOffset < events[0].Offset), Leader.catchUpFollower slices [from, to) from the leader's WAL into batchSize-sized chunks, and reads each chunk only as far as 8 MiB (catchUpBytes, through WAL.ReadEventsWithin); one larger event goes on its own. A request has to stay under the transport's 64 MiB limit whatever the events weigh, so a chunk that does not fit goes as several requests, each continuing from the follower's acknowledged offset, and replays them through the same format-appropriate append RPC. A follower with more than four batches outstanding is skipped for new batches instead of queueing without bound; it is caught up from the WAL by its next send, or by the leader's maintenance loop (every 500 ms) when the partition is otherwise idle. A follower whose log is empty is caught up from offset 0 the same way. A follower that has not acknowledged anything yet is first asked where its log ends, with an append that carries no entries; without that, an idle partition would neither catch it up nor learn what is on a quorum after a failover until somebody published. For very long catch-up ranges the leader may also serve ReplicationService.Sync, a server-streaming RPC that returns ReplicationSyncResponse chunks of decoded events.

docs.title: Bulk install (Snapshot)
docs.text:
Newly joined replicas or freshly wiped followers are initialized via Follower.InstallSnapshot(ctx, leaderAddr, partitionID, startOffset) (internal/replication/follower.go):

  1. Dial the leader over the internal gRPC listener, using mTLS when --replication-tls-enabled is set (see dialCredentials).
  2. Call ReplicationService.Snapshot. The leader flushes its active segment, then for each segment and sparse-index file, sends a ReplicationSnapshotHeader (filename, first/last offset, file size, per-file IEEE CRC32, is_index flag) followed by 1 MB ReplicationSnapshotChunk data frames.
  3. The follower stages files under <dataDir>/snapshot-staging/{segments,index}/, computing a running CRC32 over each file as it lands. If the transfer breaks, the files that arrived stay staged: the next attempt lists them with their sizes and checksums, and the leader sends only the files that are missing or different, answering the others with a header marked reuse. Staged files the leader no longer has are removed.
  4. Each file's size and CRC32 are checked against its header as it completes. The trailer carries the source's epoch: a source behind the epoch this replica has accepted was superseded as leader, and its snapshot is refused without touching the local log.
  5. Dead-letter journal pages, including payloads and removal tombstones, are applied and synced before the WAL is installed. A failed journal write leaves the existing WAL in place. A snapshot with dead-letter history requires a receiver that supports these pages.
  6. WAL.InstallCheckpoint then swaps the generations under a journal (snapshot-install.state): it writes prepared, moves segments and index aside as *.old, moves the staged directories into place, loads and verifies them against the announced last offset, writes installed, and removes the old directories. A failure, or a crash before installed, restores the old log; RecoverSnapshot finishes or undoes an interrupted install whenever the WAL is opened.
  7. The installed epoch is persisted, so the replica refuses appends from an older leader after a restart as well.

Lifecycle snapshots use recovery format 1: the WAL cut travels with a bounded, checksummed recovery file containing the epoch, accepted boundary, consumer progress and dead-letter state. Payload-bearing pages use the WAL encryption key when enabled. The receiver validates the complete generation before the swap, then clears stale completion state and imports and syncs the matching dead letters and progress before serving. A crash after WAL publication resumes that import on open. This generation protocol supplements the legacy dead-letter-page path described above. See consistent recovery.

The full install is wrapped in a 10-minute context by PartitionManager.SyncPartitionFromLeader (internal/partition/manager.go), which is itself invoked from Manager.JoinCluster (internal/cluster/manager.go) for every partition the joining node owns, and by the handoff target of a replication-factor-1 partition (pullForHandoff).

Manager.reconcileLocalLeadership (internal/cluster/leadership.go) runs whenever a committed assignment changes, and every 5s, and idempotently wires up PromoteToLeader + AddFollower on every partition committed to this node, which is what enables streaming Append on a healthy cluster.

The leader's checkpoint copies files without holding the WAL lock: appends are paused only while it notes where each file ends.

docs.title: Leadership and fencing
docs.text:
• One authority. A node leads a partition only when the Raft-committed assignment says so (internal/cluster/leadership.go). The hash ring decides where replicas belong and which node would ideally lead; it never makes a node the leader by itself.
  • One leader per epoch. Every committed change raises the partition's epoch. A replica stores {epoch, leader} in epoch.json and accepts appends at that epoch from that leader only.
  • Divergent tails. Log entries carry the term they were written in. When a leader sends an entry the follower already holds, the same offset and term is a retry and is skipped; a different term means the follower's entry and everything after it were written under another leader, and they are removed and replaced. Entries are never removed within a term.
  • Where an append continues from. A leader sends entries from where it believes the follower's log ends, so the comparison above only covers what it sends. Every append therefore also names the entry it follows and that entry's term. A follower that holds an entry of another term there refuses the append and reports that term and where its run of it starts; the leader resends from the point where the two logs still agree. An idle leader sends the same check with no entries, so an old leader that returns with a tail it never replicated is brought in line without waiting for a publish. What a follower holds counts as replicated only up to the entry the leader has checked.
  • What a refusal says. A follower that refuses an append reports where its log ends, which tells the leader where to resume sending and nothing else. It is no evidence of what the follower holds: a follower that has gone over to a newer leader reports a log that the newer leader wrote. The leader skips sending only what the follower has acknowledged of this leader's own log.
  • A replaced leader stops by itself. Every answer carries the term the follower has accepted. A leader that reads a newer term than its own there has been replaced, whatever the cluster's records on its node say so far: it refuses publishes, counts nothing more as replicated, records the term, and stops leading (PartitionManager.stepDownFor). After a network failure the followers' answers arrive seconds before the cluster's records do.
  • Beyond the end of the leader's log. Every request also says where the leader's log ends (leader_log_end). A follower that holds an entry there which was written in another term holds a tail the leader never had, and removes it. The checks above did not reach such a tail when the leader had nothing to send: the follower's log stayed longer than the leader's until somebody published, and a handoff of leadership, which waits for the two logs to be equal and refuses publishes while it waits, could not finish. An entry of the leader's own term at that offset stays: it came with a later request, and the one that says the log ends there arrived late.
  • Failover. When the committed leader is dead, the Raft leader asks the remaining replicas where their logs end (ReplicationService.Position) and elects the most complete one. It needs replicas - minISR + 1 answers to be sure every acknowledged write is on a replica that answered; with fewer it waits, except when the leader alone acknowledged writes (minISR 1). The new epoch is above every epoch the replicas report, not just above the cluster's own count.
  • An election fences before it asks. "Dead" is what the Raft leader sees. The leader it replaces may be running and reach other replicas, and what they confirm for it after they have answered would not be in the log of the replica chosen. So the election first commits that the partition has no leader, at a new epoch; clients are told to retry, and an election stays owed until one is committed, on whichever node decides next. Then every replica that is asked records that epoch before it answers (fence_epoch, PartitionManager.FenceLocalReplica). From there on it refuses the old leader, so nothing the old leader sends arrives behind its answer. A replica that held nothing of the partition is given an empty log to hold the epoch with, so that the old leader cannot fill it and count it. With replicas - minISR + 1 replicas fenced, the old leader cannot gather minISR confirmations any more. The leader is then committed at a higher epoch. The old leader learns of it from the first replica that refuses it, and stops.
  • First assignment. A partition's first leader is chosen the same way: the Raft leader asks the replicas what they hold. A restored cluster thereby continues from its backups, led by the most complete replica at an epoch above the ones stored with the data, without needing Raft metadata from the cluster that took the backups.
  • Handoff. When the ring prefers another live replica, the Raft leader commits the intent first. The current leader then refuses publishes; once it reports that none is in flight and the target's log ends at the same entry, the change of leader is committed. Until then nothing changes hands. A handoff that takes too long is abandoned and the leader stays.
  • Consumer progress. The leader sends each consumer group's completed work to its followers (ReplicationService.SyncConsumerProgress) whenever it changes and at least every 30 seconds, so a promoted follower does not redeliver it. The same message carries the position of the partition's change feed, so a promoted follower continues exporting where the old leader stopped (see cdc.md).
  • Sparse completion pages. Each follower has its own cursor over pages of at most 4,096 completed offsets across consumer groups. Failed pages are retried; version changes and periodic refreshes cover additions behind a cursor.
  • Dead-letter disposition. Durable journal pages carry failed payloads and removal tombstones. A follower syncs them before acknowledging, and the leader withholds completion transfer until that copy is durable. Retention also waits for every assigned follower to acknowledge the journal. See rolling upgrade behavior.
  • Progress stops at the end of the log. Completion is recorded by offset, so it is worth as much as the entry at that offset. A replica keeps none at or beyond the end of its own log: a follower takes its leader's progress only that far, and is sent it again once it has caught up; what was recorded for entries that a follower removes goes with them (Partition.CutLog); and whatever is left beyond the end of the log is removed when a partition starts and when a replica is made leader. Without this the events that later took those offsets counted as finished and were never delivered.
  • Only committed entries are delivered. Partition.DeliverableThrough bounds delivery by Leader.ReplicatedThrough. On a term-start partition, a new leader first establishes a durable current-term record on the required replicas; counting old-term copies is insufficient. Once proven, a prefix remains committed even if a follower disconnects. A new epoch needs a fresh proof, including on idle partitions. Non-leaders deliver nothing. Legacy partitions retain replica-count accounting until capability agreement; their old-term limitation is not fixed by merely upgrading one node.

docs.title: Log start
docs.text:
The leader of a partition removes finished segments from the start of its log (see storage.md). Every append, and an append without entries when a partition is idle, names the offset the leader's log starts at (log_start_offset), and a follower follows it (Partition.FollowLogStart):

  • It removes the segments of its own log that lie wholly below that offset. Its segments need not end where the leader's do, so its log may start a little earlier than the leader's.
  • If its log ends before that offset, it empties its log and restarts it there. The entries in between cannot be sent any more, and nobody needs them: they were finished before the leader removed them. This is how a replica with an empty disk joins a partition that has already removed entries, and how one that was away for long comes back, without a snapshot. It must durably receive the leader's dead-letter journal before skipping that prefix; an older follower that cannot acknowledge it is refused.
  • Either way the entries below that offset count as complete for every consumer group on that replica, so that it does not look for them if it leads next.

With opt-in relocation, a retained successor can represent a logical event whose original offset lies below the new start. Raising a completion floor for the removed prefix must not complete that successor's newer physical offset. Accepted cancellations and superseded copies are terminal; the replacement must reach the committed boundary before its predecessor can go.

A follower never removes anything by its own decision: its copy of the consumer progress trails the leader's. A new leader removes nothing until it has heard from enough followers to know what a quorum holds.

For ordinary completed events, the leader need not wait for a follower that is behind or down before removing entries. That follower restarts its log at the leader's start when it returns, so the completed range may temporarily exist on fewer replicas than the replication factor. Dead-letter journal replication adds a separate retention gate: every assigned follower must have acknowledged that journal before pruning can proceed.

docs.title: Publishes that fail after the append
docs.text:
A publish appends to the leader's log before replication, a requested fsync, and scheduling. If one of those fails the log cannot take the events back, so the partition holds them (internal/partition/unaccepted.go): they are not scheduled, and their message IDs are recorded as appended at offset N, not as accepted. They are accepted, and scheduled, when the log is known to be replicated that far:

  • by a retry of the publish, which is finished rather than appended again;
  • by the next publish that reaches the required replicas, since a follower holds a prefix of the log;
  • by the leader's maintenance loop once catch-up has taken them to a quorum.

After a restart or a promotion the events not yet due are scheduled, and the events already due stay in the log for their subscriptions to read. The dedup store is re-seeded from the log tail with appended records, so a retry is answered from the log. If the log no longer holds the event, because a newer leader replaced this node's unreplicated tail, the record is dropped and the retry is published as new.

docs.title: Production Decisions
docs.text:
• Wire format: gRPC over InternalGRPCServer (default :7947), a separate listener from the public client API on :9000. Public clients cannot reach replication traffic, and replication traffic does not contend for public-API rate limits or interceptors.
  • Integrity:
  • Every ReplicationAppendRequest carries a per-batch IEEE CRC32 (computeBatchChecksum), which the follower handler verifies before it applies the batch.
  • Every ReplicationSnapshotHeader carries a per-file IEEE CRC32 and size; the follower checks each file against its header and aborts the install on a mismatch.
  • Each WAL record (v2) carries its own CRC32 plus a payload checksum and Raft term, so per-record integrity is preserved on disk after install.
  • Term fencing: ReplicationServiceHandler.Append rejects req.Term < p.Epoch, rejects a second leader at the current term, and on a newer term persists it (stepping down first if this node was leading) before applying the sender's entries. See Leadership and fencing.
  • Quorum durability: Leader.Replicate returns success only after min-insync-replicas replicas including the leader have appended (--min-insync-replicas, default 1). With RF=3 / minISR=2 the leader
  • at least one follower must ack before the client write is acknowledged. If the cluster degrades below minISR, writes fail closed rather than silently succeeding on a leader-only ack. The count comes from what followers have acknowledged and, in term-start mode, the current-term commitment proof (Leader.QuorumOffset), not from the InSync flag; InSync feeds only reports (GetInSyncReplicas, the leader's stats). A follower of a partition whose log is empty on both sides counts as in sync, since it holds all of the leader's log (bothEmpty in Leader.appendToFollower). In the batch and every_event fsync modes a follower syncs an append before it acknowledges it, so a quorum-acknowledged write is on that many disks. In periodic mode it acknowledges first and syncs on a timer, and a simultaneous leader and follower crash inside one flush interval can lose acknowledged writes; production mode refuses periodic.
  • Snapshot trigger: bulk install is invoked by PartitionManager.SyncPartitionFromLeader (node join and router-driven partition moves). The --snapshot-catchup-threshold flag (default 10000) is defined and exposed but is currently a dead config key — nothing in internal/partition, internal/replication, or internal/cluster reads it; SyncPartitionFromLeader installs a snapshot unconditionally. Treated as a future-work knob here; flag stays so configuration is forward-compatible.
  • Journaled swap on install: the WAL is closed before the segments.old/index.old renames, staged dirs are renamed into place, and the old pair is kept until the new log has been loaded and verified. Every crash point recovers to one complete generation, never a mix (internal/storage/checkpoint_test.go).
  • mTLS: --replication-tls-enabled plus --replication-tls-{ca,cert,key}-file (all three are required, and the same certificates secure the membership and Raft ports; see cluster.md) enable cluster-only mTLS via replication.BuildClientTLSConfig / BuildServerTLSConfig. Server uses tls.RequireAndVerifyClientCert; both sides pin against --replication-tls-ca-file. Clients use BuildClientTLS, and the server configuration does the same: the certificate, its key and the CA are read again when their files change, so they are replaced without a restart. In dev mode the follower falls back to insecure credentials (Follower.dialCredentials, internal/replication/follower.go).
  • Cross-region path is separate: CrossRegionReplicator (internal/replication/region.go) batches outgoing events per region (100 events / 100 ms), pushes them via CrossRegionService.ReplicateEvents, and never participates in the intra-cluster quorum. Loss of a remote region does not stall local writes.
  • Conflict resolution: cross-region uses last-write-wins; intra-cluster uses Raft-style term fencing (the leader with the higher epoch wins).
  • Durable capability agreement: internal/cluster/capabilities.go commits format requirements only once every assigned replica, handoff target and Raft voter is alive and capable. Requirements constrain subsequent placement, elections, handoffs and voter admission. Lifecycle v1 additionally requires majority acknowledgements and excludes CDC and experimental features. Downgrading to a build that ignores committed requirements is unsupported.

docs.title: Trigger Policy & Known Limitation
docs.text: Path Trigger Code Bulk snapshot install (InstallSnapshot) New node joins and owns partitions it does not yet have data for (wipe/bootstrap), or the router moves a partition Manager.JoinCluster / router rebalance → PartitionManager.SyncPartitionFromLeader (unconditional) Incremental catch-up (Sync / Append loop) A connected follower reports NextOffset < nextBatchStart during normal Replicate, or is found behind while idle by the maintenance loop Leader.catchUpFollower, Leader.catchUpIdleFollowers Automatic lag-driven snapshot install Not implemented (documented gap). No mid-flight loop watches lag and switches to InstallSnapshot when lag > --snapshot-catchup-threshold — the flag is parsed but never read (dead config key). See ARCHITECTURE.md § Known Limitations

docs.title: Why mid-flight auto-snapshot is deferred
docs.text:
• Incremental catch-up preserves the normal leader→follower hot path and term fencing.
  • Full snapshot is heavyweight (segment + index stream, CRC, atomic dir swap, WAL close/reload).
  • Bootstrap/join already covers the common “empty or wiped follower” case.

Operator guidance: If a follower is hopelessly behind after network isolation, prefer re-provision / re-join so SyncPartitionFromLeader can InstallSnapshot, rather than waiting for unbounded incremental catch-up alone.

docs.text:

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The scheduler controls when events become deliverable, using a hot timing wheel and cold store hydration under a node-wide payload budget.

docs.title: Key Files
docs.text:
• internal/scheduler/scheduler.go
  • internal/scheduler/timing_wheel.go
  • internal/scheduler/cold_store.go

docs.title: Main Flow
docs.text:
1. Publish path schedules events by schedule timestamp.
  2. Near-future events live in hot timing wheel slots.
  3. Far-future events and payloads over the memory budget are staged as references in the cold store.
  4. Hydrator moves due-near events into hot wheel.
  5. Ready events are emitted to the worker queue.

docs.title: Production Decisions
docs.text:
• Hierarchical wheel gives near O(1) scheduling behavior.
  • Defaults: -tick-ms=10, -wheel-size=600 (6s root span); hot window default 60 minutes.
  • Adaptive hydrator interval (5s–5min) manages cold-store scan pressure.
  • --scheduler-memory defaults to 64 MiB across all partitions (minimum 32 MiB). Payloads, metadata and timer/accounting overhead count toward this budget. It excludes worker queues, Pebble caches and temporary WAL read buffers, so it is not an RSS limit.
  • Hydration scans at most 1,024 references per pass, with WAL payload reads serialized across partitions. Within a partition, earlier work can evict later timers back to disk. Draining ready events wakes hydration.
  • --hot-window-minutes=0 disables time-based cold routing; budget overflow still uses cold references.
  • Crash recovery: restore timer_state.json when present and rebase currentTick from the wall clock. replayWALTimers then walks the retained log from its first offset and schedules only the events that are not due yet. A replicated partition does this when its node becomes leader, not at start. Events that came due while the node was down are not queued: they stay in the log, and a subscription reads what its group has not finished from the log when it starts, at the pace its consumers take it (redriveRetained in internal/api/handlers.go). Nothing is dropped, and the backlog is not loaded into memory at start.
  • Ready-queue and wheel size admission limits reject publish under overload (ResourceExhausted).
  • In lifecycle mode, reconstruction and delivery consult the partition's active event index. Canceled and superseded copies, stale timers and internal term-start records are not delivered. The partition holds the same gate across the active-state check and send that a mutation takes while appending, so a cancellation cannot race between that check and delivery. A staged successor stays behind the accepted boundary. See the lifecycle contract.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Storage module provides durable append-only event persistence with indexed reads, compaction, backup, and optional encryption.

docs.title: Key Files
docs.text:
• internal/storage/wal.go — segmented WAL, append/replay/recovery. A follower's snapshot install goes through WAL.InstallCheckpoint (journaled swap of the staged log; see replication.md).
  • internal/storage/retention.go — WAL.Prune: verifies closed segments record by record against the caller's eligibility and terminal-state predicates.
  • internal/partition/retention.go — Partition.PruneWAL, the one path by which compaction, retention and operator pruning remove segments; FollowLogStart on followers.
  • internal/storage/segment.go, internal/storage/mmap_unix.go, internal/storage/mmap_windows.go — segment file format and platform mmap shims.
  • internal/storage/index.go — sparse index for O(log N) seeks.
  • internal/storage/fsync_coalescer.go — shared periodic flusher for many WALs (used with periodic / background flush; not the same as batch group-commit).
  • internal/storage/backup_scheduler.go — periodic backup scheduler loop.
  • internal/storage/backup.go — backup manifest / restore primitives (distinct from the scheduler).
  • internal/storage/crypto.go — AES-256-GCM at rest; record cipher v2 embeds a random 12-byte nonce per record (v1 counter nonce is decrypt-only).
  • internal/lifecycle — self-contained mutation records and the payload-free disk index of logical heads.
  • internal/recoverystate/file.go — bounded, checksummed recovery pages bound to a WAL generation; encrypted with its key when enabled.

docs.title: Main Flow
docs.text:
1. Append assigns offsets and writes WAL v2 records (8-byte Raft term + 4-byte payload checksum) to the active segment.
  2. Sparse index tracks offsets for read and replay efficiency.
  3. Durability depends on fsync mode:
  4. every_event — fsync each write
  5. batch (default) — group-commit fsync (concurrent writers share one sync)
  6. periodic — background / coalescer flush with a bounded loss window
  7. Segment rotation keeps prior segments readable; compaction and retention reclaim space.
  8. The backup scheduler periodically checkpoints every partition, including the active segment. A checkpoint pauses appends only while it notes where each file ends; the bytes are copied while appends continue. A backup cuts the logs of all partitions at one instant and starts at wall-clock multiples of the interval. These are independent node checkpoints, not a cluster-wide atomic cut; cluster restore uses the earliest required cut.

docs.title: Production Decisions
docs.text:
• WAL records use format v2: each record carries an 8-byte Raft term and a 4-byte payload checksum (written immediately after the payload, before metadata). Pre-v2 layouts have no automatic migration; this is separate from the capability-gated v0.7.0 to v0.8.0 upgrade.
  • CRC checks protect record integrity; critical metadata uses utils.AtomicWriteFile.
  • Default fsync mode is batch.
  • Encryption at rest v2 uses random GCM nonces to avoid cross-segment keystream reuse; v1 remains readable for migration.
  • Segment-level compaction supports retention and admin operations; retention never deletes the active segment and removes matching .index files.
  • Every record a log takes can be read back. A record's length field may say at most 10 MiB (storage.MaxRecordLength); readers and recovery take a larger length for damage. An event is therefore taken only if its record, metadata included, is at most storage.MaxEventRecordSize, 64 bytes less, which leaves room for encryption, so encrypted and plaintext replicas take the same events. Publishes check this before they claim the message ID (storage.CheckEventSize), and the log checks it again. Up to v0.6.0 a publish limited only the payload, to 4 MiB, and an event with a lot of metadata could be acknowledged and then not be read.
  • The term of an entry is the log's. An entry a log appends for itself (a publish, a cross-region event, a split, a transaction) is stored under the log's current term, whatever term the event carried; only a follower stores the term its leader sent. Elections and the matching of logs rely on terms saying which leader wrote an entry. Up to v0.6.0 a producer could put any term in an event and have it stored and replicated.
  • A failed write stops the log, and the node. After a write or fsync of a segment fails, nothing says what the disk holds: a failed fsync may drop the pages it did not write, so a later fsync that succeeds proves nothing about them. The log then takes no more appends (storage.ErrLogFailed), a follower whose log failed acknowledges nothing, and the node shuts down and exits with status 1, so that it is restarted, reads its logs again from disk, and other replicas lead its partitions meanwhile. An append reports whether its events reached the log (storage.EventsAppended): a publish whose events did is held for its retry to finish, as when replication fails, and only one whose events did not gives its message IDs back. Up to v0.6.0 every append error gave them back, so a retry could append the same event a second time, and background flush errors were only counted.
  • A segment that cannot be started does not fail an append. Rotation happens after the append that filled the segment, which is complete by then. If the new segment cannot be made, the full one takes the next append, which tries again; cronos_wal_rotation_errors_total counts the failures.
  • Opening a log reads each segment once, record by record, checking every CRC. It used to read each segment a second time to verify it, the whole segment into memory at once, so starting a node took as much memory as its largest segment (512 MiB by default).
  • Publishes stop before the disk is full. When the filesystem holding --data-dir is --max-disk-usage full (default 95%), publishes are refused with RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED until it is two points below; deliveries, acknowledgements, replication and retention go on. cronos_disk_publish_refused is 1 meanwhile. Usage is sampled every 2 seconds, so a publish costs one atomic load.
  • A segment holds a write buffer only while it is written through one. An unencrypted segment is written through its mapping and has none. An encrypted segment is written through a 4 MiB buffer, which is made on its first append and released when the segment stops taking appends. Every segment used to get the buffer when it was created or opened and keep it, so a node held 4 MiB of heap for each segment of its logs.
  • An encrypted record that was not completely written is a torn write, like a plaintext one. The buffer can put out part of a record and keep the rest until the next flush, so a crash can leave a final record that does not decrypt. When nothing is written after it and its last bytes are still unwritten zeros, it is treated like a plaintext record whose checksum fails (below): cut off at the end of the log, damage anywhere before it. The first record of a segment counts as torn only when its whole 16-byte authentication tag is unwritten, so that a wrong key, which fails every record, is never taken for a torn write; any other record that does not decrypt still stops the log from opening. Before 1.0 every decryption failure stopped it, and an encrypted node that crashed during a write could not start, nor be repaired with check-log --repair.
  • The sparse index only says where to start reading. Its file is written through a buffer that holds a whole number of 24-byte entries, so what the buffer puts out on its own is whole entries; before 1.0 it put out 64 KiB, 16 bytes into an entry, and in production nothing else flushed it until the segment closed. Opening an index keeps its entries up to the first that cannot be right (a partial entry, or an offset or position that does not follow the one before) and cuts the file there. A read that the index points to the wrong place reads the segment from its start. Before 1.0 a partial entry made later entries misaligned after the next restart, and reads of the events they pointed to returned nothing, without an error.
  • Bytes that are not valid records mean different things in different places, and the log treats them accordingly when it opens (wal.go, judgeInvalidTails):
  • At the end of the log, absent evidence of a later record, they are treated as a write that did not finish. The log ends before them, a warning says so, and they are overwritten with zeros. In the batch and every_event fsync modes an interrupted final write should not contain an acknowledged event.
  • Anywhere else, inside a segment that later segments follow, they are damage: segments are closed complete, so records were there. The partition refuses to open and the error names the segment, the byte and the offsets that cannot be read. Opening used to take such bytes for the end of the segment and carry on without the events behind them.
  • Repair depends on whether the partition has other replicas. In a cluster, stop the node and remove the partition's directory (partitions/<id>): the node rejoins the partition with nothing and the leader fills it again; nothing is lost. Without another replica, restore a backup (cronos-admin restore), or run cronos-admin check-log --data-dir <dir> --partition <id> --repair with the node stopped, which cuts the damaged segment after its last valid record and reports the offsets it gives up. cronos-admin check-log --data-dir <dir> alone only reports.
  • A newly created successor records its closed predecessor's durable offset and byte boundary in its checksummed header. Recovery and check-log reject a mismatch even if the erased area is all zeros and the sparse index is missing. The active tail does not have this evidence. A verified later indexed record can additionally prove some damage there. Explicit repair discards the remainder of the damaged segment, including any valid records after the damaged area; when there is no successor, the last discarded offset is unknown. Version 0.9.0 and later require a fresh data directory: they reject version-1 WALs, and older binaries reject version-2 WALs. See closed segment boundaries for deployment, repair and interrupted-truncation behavior.
  • What may go. Ordinary active events must be due and finished by every relevant consumer group, with at least one such group; export and durable dead-letter replication must also permit pruning. Accepted cancellations, superseded copies and term-start records can be terminal without a consumer completion. Unaccepted records cannot release a segment. A pass runs every --compaction-interval (default 10 minutes), checking one record at a time.
  • Prefix pruning. Replicated partitions and standalone lifecycle partitions remove only a contiguous prefix of closed segments. In a cluster the leader decides and followers follow its log start. Without relocation, one future event can still pin later segments. --wal-relocation-bytes can copy never-due work to a retained successor within a byte budget; it requires lifecycle mode and is off by default. A replicated copy must be committed before the original can go. Unfinished due work and the active segment are never evacuated. A standalone partition without lifecycle mode may remove finished segments elsewhere in its log. See the contract.
  • Retention by age and size (--retention-max-age-hours, --retention-max-size-gb) runs hourly (compliance/retention.go). It only picks segments; each is removed through PartitionManager.RemoveRetainedSegment → Partition.PruneWAL, with the same checks as compaction. In a cluster a replica that does not lead the partition removes nothing, and the leader removes only from the start of the log.
  • Consumer progress follows the log. What lies below the start of a log was finished before it was removed, so it counts as complete for every group, including one created later, and each group's completion floor is raised to the start. That also discards the per-event completion records below it.
  • Logical identity survives physical moves. A lifecycle successor retains the original reference but has a new physical offset. An old completion floor cannot finish it. Lifecycle backups and snapshots include the matching accepted boundary, epoch, group progress and dead letters; recovery resumes interrupted state import before delivery. A local index alone is not backup authority; it is reconstructed from retained WAL records.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The tenant module contains per-tenant accounting and quota code (publish rate, in-flight events, storage bytes).

Limits are not enforced. Accountant.SetLimits has no caller outside tests, and no flag, environment variable or RPC sets a limit. Without a configured limit the publish path skips the accountant entirely (HasConfiguredLimits is false), so no publish is checked or counted, and RecordDelivery only adjusts usage entries that already exist, of which there are none. AdminService.GetTenantUsage therefore reports zero usage and limits_configured: false.

docs.title: Key Files
docs.text:
• internal/tenant/tenant.go
  • internal/api/handlers.go
  • internal/partition/manager.go

docs.title: Main Flow
docs.text:
1. Startup creates a tenant accountant and hands it to the event handler, the partition manager (delivery callbacks) and the admin handler.
  2. If any limit were configured, the publish handlers would take the tenant from the JWT subject ("default" without claims), reserve quota with ReservePublishBatch, refuse with ResourceExhausted when it is exceeded, and tag the event with tenant_id.
  3. Delivery completion calls RecordDelivery for the event's tenant.

As shipped, step 2 never runs; see Purpose.

docs.title: Design Notes
docs.text:
• The accountant is built so that it costs nothing on the hot path when no limits are configured.
  • Delivery callbacks are wired through the partition manager, including partitions created later.
  • Tenant identity falls back to "default" when a request carries no claims.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The transaction module is an experimental two-phase commit coordinator: it runs prepare and commit phases across partition participants.

docs.title: Key Files
docs.text:
• internal/tx/coordinator.go
  • internal/tx/transaction_handler.go

docs.title: Main Flow
docs.text:

  2. Coordinator Prepare path executes phase-1 state transition and participant checks.
  3. Commit path applies phase-2 commit operations from prepared state.
  4. Recovery path replays durable transaction log on restart.

docs.title: Design of the Experimental Implementation
docs.text:
These describe what the code does. They are not tested or supported as guarantees.

  • Prepare and commit are separate phases.
  • State transitions are written to tx_log.json in the data directory, so the coordinator can find in-flight transactions after a restart.
  • tx.NewHandler(pm) gives the coordinator the PartitionManager, so Begin/Prepare/Commit write to real partitions. cmd/api/main.go creates it only with --experimental-features.
  • A recovery loop (every 30 s) re-drives Commit for Prepared and Committing transactions and aborts Pending ones past their timeout. Whether this holds up across crashes, failovers and replicated partitions has not been verified.

docs.text:

docs.title: Transaction state machine
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Pending : BeginTransaction
    Pending --> Prepared : PrepareTransaction - all participants vote yes
    Pending --> Aborted : any vote no / AbortTransaction / recovery timeout
    Pending --> Committing : CommitTransaction auto-prepares when Pending
    Prepared --> Committing : CommitTransaction
    Prepared --> Aborted : AbortTransaction
    Committing --> Committed : all participant commit markers written
    Committing --> Committing : commit callback failure - stays Committing, recovery loop retries with backoff
    Committed --> [*]
    Aborted --> [*]

    note right of Committing
        Coordinator statuses are exactly: Pending, Prepared,
        Committing, Committed, Aborted. There are no
        FailedCommit or Recovering states: the recovery loop
        (30s ticker) re-drives Commit for Prepared/Committing
        transactions and only aborts Pending transactions
        that exceeded their timeout.
